title: The Thirsty Crow
source: Indian folk tale · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A bird, a pot, and a rule it repeats until the world changes.

panels.text: It had not rained in weeks. A crow flew from field to field with a dry throat, finding every pond cracked and every trough empty. By afternoon it could barely call out.
panels.alt: A crow flying over dry, cracked ground under a hot sun.

panels.text: At the edge of a village it found a clay pot. There was water inside — but far down, past the reach of its beak. The crow pushed its head in as far as it would go. Nothing. The pot was too narrow to climb into and too heavy to tip.
panels.alt: A crow peering into a tall narrow clay pot with water far below the rim.

panels.text: The crow looked around and saw pebbles scattered in the dirt. It picked one up, dropped it into the pot, and looked again. The water was a little higher. Not enough. So it fetched another. And another. And another.
panels.alt: A crow dropping a pebble into the pot as the water level rises slightly.

panels.text: The crow did not count its pebbles. It only checked, each time, whether the water had come close enough to drink. When at last it had, the crow stopped fetching pebbles and drank.
panels.alt: The water risen to the rim of the pot and the crow drinking from it.

bridge.hook: The crow never decided how many pebbles it would need. It decided on a rule: keep dropping pebbles as long as the water is out of reach.

mapping.story: The water is still too low to drink
mapping.detail: Checked before every single pebble. While it stays true, the crow keeps working.

mapping.story: Fetch one pebble and drop it in
mapping.detail: One repetition, one small change. The body runs again and again, unchanged each time.

mapping.story: The water rises a little
mapping.python: The state the condition depends on
mapping.detail: Something inside the body has to move the world closer to stopping, or the loop never ends.

mapping.story: The water is close enough — the crow drinks
mapping.python: The condition becomes false and the loop exits
mapping.detail: The loop stops on its own. Nobody told it the number four hundred.

bridge.code:
water_level = 10
beak_reach = 25

while water_level < beak_reach:
    water_level = water_level + 3   # drop one pebble
    print("pebble dropped, water now at", water_level)

print("The crow drinks.")
bridge.codeNotes: Read the "while" line as the crow's rule, not as syntax: as long as the water is below my reach, keep going. Everything indented under it is one pebble.
bridge.gotcha: Delete the line that raises the water and the condition stays true forever — the crow fetches pebbles until the end of time. That is an infinite loop, and it is the most common way a "while" loop goes wrong.

quiz.question: In the crow's story, which moment is the loop condition?

options.text: Checking whether the water is still out of reach
options.why: Right. The condition is the test that runs before every repetition and decides whether there is another one.

options.text: Dropping a pebble into the pot
options.why: That is the loop body — the work done once per repetition. The condition is the check that comes before it.

options.text: Finding the pot at the edge of the village
options.why: That happens once, before any repeating starts. It is setup, not part of the loop.

options.text: Drinking the water at the end
options.why: That happens after the loop has already exited. It is what the loop was for, not part of it.

quiz.question: Which loop matches what the crow actually did?

options.text:
while water_level < beak_reach:
    water_level += 3
options.why: Yes. The crow repeats while the water is below its reach, and each repetition raises the water.

options.text:
for pebble in range(400):
    water_level += 3
options.why: This decides the number of pebbles in advance. The crow never knew the number — it only knew when to stop.

options.text:
if water_level < beak_reach:
    water_level += 3
options.why: An "if" checks once and moves on. That is one pebble, then a thirsty crow.

options.text:
while water_level < beak_reach:
    print("still thirsty")
options.why: The condition is right, but nothing in the body raises the water — so it never stops. This is an infinite loop.

quiz.question: A different situation: you are filling a bucket from a slow tap. You do not know how long it will take — you just keep the tap running until the bucket is full. Which construct fits?

options.text: A while loop, because the stopping point is a condition rather than a count
options.why: Exactly the crow's shape: repeat an action while something is not yet true. The number of repetitions is unknown until it happens.

options.text: A for loop over range(60), because filling a bucket takes about a minute
options.why: That guesses the count. If the tap runs slower today, the bucket is not full when the loop ends.

options.text: A single if statement checking whether the bucket is full
options.why: An if checks once. The bucket needs checking repeatedly, which is what a loop is for.

options.text: No loop is needed — just set the bucket to full
options.why: That skips the process. The point is that the filling takes an unknown number of steps.

title: The Blue Jackal
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A jackal changes what it looks like. It does not change what it is.

panels.text: A hungry jackal wandered into a village at night and was chased by dogs. Running blind through a dyer's yard, it fell into a great vat of indigo.
panels.alt: A jackal falling into a large vat of indigo dye in a dyer's yard.

panels.text: It climbed out soaked in blue. Back in the forest, no animal recognised it. They had never seen such a creature. The tiger stepped back. The elephant lowered its head.
panels.alt: A blue-dyed jackal standing before a tiger and an elephant who bow to it.

panels.text: The jackal saw its chance. "I was sent to rule this forest," it announced. The animals believed it and served it, and for many days it lived as king.
panels.alt: The blue jackal seated on a rock as forest animals bring it food.

panels.text: Then one evening a pack of jackals passed nearby and howled. The blue king forgot itself and howled back. Every animal turned. The colour had never been the animal — the howl was.
panels.alt: The blue jackal howling at night as the other animals turn and stare.

bridge.hook: The animals judged the jackal by how it looked. Python does not. Every value has a type underneath, and the way it prints is not that type.

mapping.story: The jackal's real nature
mapping.detail: Fixed and underneath. 5 is an int whether or not anything is looking at it.

mapping.story: The blue coat of dye
mapping.detail: print(5) and print("5") put the same mark on the screen. The screen is not the truth.

mapping.story: The forest animals believing the disguise
mapping.python: Assuming a type from how a value looks
mapping.detail: This is where beginners get caught: input() always hands you a string, even when it looks like a number.

mapping.story: The howl that gave it away
mapping.detail: Ask directly and the truth comes out. Or try to use the value and Python tells you what it really was.

bridge.code:
disguise = "5"      # a string that looks like a number
real = 5            # an actual number

print(disguise)     # 5
print(real)         # 5      <- identical on screen

print(type(disguise))   # <class 'str'>   <- the howl
print(type(real))       # <class 'int'>

print(real + 1)         # 6
print(disguise + 1)     # TypeError: can only concatenate str to str

print(int(disguise) + 1)   # 6   <- wash off the dye first
bridge.codeNotes: int(disguise) does not change the original value. It produces a new one of a different type — the way the rain would have washed the jackal clean rather than making it never have fallen in.
bridge.gotcha: input() hands back a string every single time. Ask for someone's age and you get "21", not 21. Adding to it fails, and comparing it to a number gives wrong answers rather than an error — which is worse, because nothing tells you.

quiz.question: In the story, what plays the role of type() — the thing that reveals what a value really is?

options.text: The howl
options.why: Right. It is the moment the underlying nature is exposed, regardless of appearance.

options.text: The indigo dye
options.why: The dye is the appearance — how the value prints. It is what hides the type, not what reveals it.

options.text: The tiger bowing
options.why: That is the mistake being made: judging by appearance. It reveals nothing true.

options.text: The dyer's yard
options.why: That is only where the disguise came from — setup, not revelation.

quiz.question: A program runs age = input("Your age: ") and the user types 21. What does age + 1 do?

options.text: Raises a TypeError, because age is the string "21"
options.why: Correct. input() always returns a string. It looks like a number on screen, but it howls like a string.

options.text: Gives 22, because Python sees it is a number
options.why: Python does not guess types from appearance. The value is a string and stays one until you cast it.

options.text: Gives "211", joining the two together
options.why: Close reasoning, but joining only works between two strings. 1 here is an int, so Python refuses.

options.text: Gives 21, ignoring the +1
options.why: Python never silently ignores part of an expression.

quiz.question: A form collects a price as "49.99" and a quantity as "3", both from input(). You need the total. What has to happen first?

options.text: Cast each one to a number — float("49.99") and int("3") — then multiply
options.why: Yes. Wash off the dye before you use the value. The cast produces new values of the right types.

options.text: Multiply them directly, since they both contain digits
options.why: Containing digits is appearance. Both are strings, and multiplying two strings is not allowed.

options.text: Use int() on both, since money is a number
options.why: int("49.99") fails — there is a decimal point in it. Price needs float().

options.text: Nothing — Python converts automatically when it sees multiplication
options.why: Python is explicit about this on purpose. It would rather raise an error than guess what you meant.

title: The Blind Men and the Elephant
source: Indian parable · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Six men, six answers, and one structure that could have held them all.

panels.text: Six men who had been blind since birth were brought to an elephant and asked to describe it. Each reached out and touched a different part.
panels.alt: Six figures standing around an elephant, each reaching toward a different part.

panels.text: The one holding a leg said the elephant was a pillar. The one at the trunk said it was a thick snake. The one at the ear said a great fan; the one at the side, a wall; the one at the tusk, a smooth spear; the one at the tail, a rope.
panels.alt: Each man touching one part of the elephant, with their descriptions beside them.

panels.text: They argued until nightfall. Every man was certain, and no man was lying. Each had found something true and none had found the whole.
panels.alt: The six men arguing as the sun sets behind the elephant.

panels.text: A traveller listening nearby said: you are not disagreeing. Write each answer next to the part it came from, and put the six together. That list is the elephant.
panels.alt: A traveller writing six labelled pairs on a slate, forming a picture of the elephant.

bridge.hook: The men had six answers with no labels on them. A dictionary is exactly that missing label: every value stored next to the thing it describes.

mapping.story: The part each man touched — leg, trunk, ear
mapping.detail: Unique and meaningful. You look things up by them, never by position.

mapping.story: What that man said it was — pillar, snake, fan
mapping.detail: The information itself. Values can repeat; keys cannot.

mapping.story: Writing each answer beside the part it came from
mapping.detail: This is the whole idea. The answer stops floating loose and gets attached to its question.

mapping.story: All six pairs together on the slate
mapping.detail: No single man is the elephant. The collection of labelled pairs is.

bridge.code:
elephant = {
    "leg": "a pillar",
    "trunk": "a thick snake",
    "ear": "a great fan",
    "side": "a wall",
    "tusk": "a smooth spear",
    "tail": "a rope"
}

print(elephant["trunk"])        # a thick snake

print("tail" in elephant)       # True
print(elephant.get("eye", "nobody reached it"))

for part, description in elephant.items():
    print(part, "->", description)
bridge.codeNotes: elephant["trunk"] is a man being asked what he found. .items() is every man reporting in turn, each one saying which part he held.
bridge.gotcha: elephant["eye"] raises a KeyError — nobody touched the eye, so there is no answer to give. .get("eye", default) asks the same question but accepts "nobody reached it" instead of crashing.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the key, and which is the value?

options.text: The body part touched is the key; the description given is the value
options.why: Right. You look things up by the part — that is what makes it the key.

options.text: The description is the key; the body part is the value
options.why: Backwards. You would be asking "which part felt like a rope?" — possible, but not how the men reported, and descriptions can repeat.

options.text: Each man is a key and the elephant is the value
options.why: Tempting, but the men are interchangeable. What matters is which part was touched, not who touched it.

options.text: There are no keys — it is just a list of six descriptions
options.why: That is the situation before the traveller arrives, and it is precisely the problem: six answers with nothing attached to them.

quiz.question: Nobody in the story touched the elephant's eye. What does elephant["eye"] do?

options.text: Raises a KeyError, because that key was never stored
options.why: Correct. Square brackets demand an answer, and there is none to give.

options.text: Returns None, since the key is missing
options.why: That is what .get("eye") does. Square brackets are stricter — they raise instead.

options.text: Returns an empty string
options.why: Python does not invent a blank answer. A missing key is an error, not an empty value.

options.text: Adds "eye" to the dictionary with no value
options.why: Reading never creates a key. Only assigning does.

quiz.question: You are storing the capital city of each Indian state so you can look up any state by name. List or dictionary?

options.text: A dictionary, because each capital belongs to a specific state you will look it up by
options.why: Yes. When one piece of data identifies another, that identifier is a key — same shape as part-to-description.

options.text: A list, because there are many states and lists hold many things
options.why: A list holds many things but only knows their positions. You would have to remember that Punjab is index 22.

options.text: Two lists kept in the same order, one of states and one of capitals
options.why: This works until one list is edited and the other is not — then every lookup is silently wrong. The dictionary makes the pairing unbreakable.

options.text: A dictionary with the capitals as keys
options.why: Right structure, wrong direction. You said you want to look up by state, so the state is the key.

title: The Brahmin and the Three Thieves
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: The animal never changed. The word for it did, three times.

panels.text: A Brahmin bought a goat at the market and set out for home with it across his shoulders. Three thieves saw him on the road. The goat was worth more than anything else they would find that day, and the Brahmin was bigger than any one of them.
panels.alt: A man walking a road with a goat across his shoulders, three figures watching from the trees.

panels.text: So they spread out along the road. The first stepped out of the trees and asked why a learned man was carrying a dog. The Brahmin told him it was a goat, and walked on.
panels.alt: A thief on the road speaking to the Brahmin, who still carries the goat.

panels.text: A mile later the second thief asked why he was carrying a dead calf. The Brahmin checked the animal, said nothing, and kept walking, slower now. Near the village the third asked him plainly why he had a dog on his back.
panels.alt: The Brahmin pausing to look at the animal on his shoulders as a second thief walks away.

panels.text: The Brahmin set the animal down, washed himself, and hurried home ashamed. The thieves came out of the trees and took it. It had been a goat the whole time. Only its name had changed, and only in one man's head.
panels.alt: The goat standing alone on the road as the Brahmin walks away and three thieves approach.

bridge.hook: Nothing was ever done to the animal. What changed was the word bound to it — and each new word threw the last one away.

mapping.story: The animal standing there on the road
mapping.detail: It has its own nature. Calling it something else does not reach it.

mapping.story: The word the Brahmin uses for it
mapping.detail: A label pointed at a value. The label is not the value and never was.

mapping.story: Each thief insisting it is a dog
mapping.detail: The name is unhooked from the old value and hooked onto a new one. Instant, silent, complete.

mapping.story: He can no longer say what he bought
mapping.python: The old value is unreachable through that name
mapping.detail: Assignment has no undo. Overwrite a name and what it held is gone, unless some other name still holds it.

bridge.code:
animal = "goat"          # what he bought
print(animal)            # goat

animal = "dog"           # the first thief
animal = "dead calf"     # the second
animal = "dog"           # the third

print(animal)            # dog   <- the only answer left

# nothing was ever done to the animal itself.
# to keep the first value, point a second name at it before overwriting:
bought = "goat"
animal = "dog"
print(bought, animal)    # goat dog
bridge.codeNotes: Read = as point this name at that value, not as these two are equal. Each line in the middle block is one thief pointing the name somewhere new.
bridge.gotcha: Reassignment is silent and there is no undo. total = total + 1 works because the right-hand side is worked out first, using the old value, and only then is the name repointed. Write total + 1 on a line by itself and Python computes it and throws it away — the name still holds the old number, and nothing warns you.

quiz.question: In the story, what plays the role of the variable name?

options.text: The word people use for the animal — "goat", then "dog"
options.why: Right. It is the label being moved around. The creature underneath it is a separate thing entirely.

options.text: The animal on the Brahmin's shoulders
options.why: That is the value the name points at. It never changed, which is the whole point of the tale.

options.text: The Brahmin himself
options.why: He is the program running, believing whatever the name currently says. He is not the name.

options.text: The road to the village
options.why: Setting, not structure. Nothing on it is bound or rebound.

quiz.question: What does this print?

options.text:
animal = "goat"
animal = "dog"
print(animal)

# prints: dog
options.why: Right. The second line repoints the name. Only the most recent binding survives.

options.text:
animal = "goat"
animal = "dog"
print(animal)

# prints: goat
options.why: The first line did run, but the second replaced what the name points at. Order matters and the last assignment wins.

options.text:
animal = "goat"
animal = "dog"
print(animal)

# prints: goat dog
options.why: A name does not accumulate values. Assigning replaces; it does not append.

options.text:
animal = "goat"
animal = "dog"
print(animal)

# raises NameError: animal was defined twice
options.why: Rebinding a name is ordinary and allowed. NameError is for names that were never bound at all.

quiz.question: A different situation: you are tracking a running score. You write score = 0, then on a later line score + 10, then print(score). What prints?

options.text: 0 — score + 10 computes a value and never binds it to anything
options.why: Yes. Addition produces a result; only = attaches it to a name. Without score = score + 10 the result is worked out and dropped.

options.text: 10 — Python updates score with the addition
options.why: Nothing on that line repoints the name. Python worked out 10 and discarded it.

options.text: 10 — + modifies the variable in place
options.why: + never modifies a name. It builds a new value and hands it back, and something has to catch it.

options.text: An error, because the line has no effect
options.why: Python allows expressions that go nowhere. That is exactly why this bug is hard to find — it runs perfectly and does nothing.

title: The Monkey and the Cap Seller
source: Indian folk tale · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A bundle that holds many things, in an order, and gives them up one at a time.

panels.text: A cap seller carried his stock to market in a bundle on his head — red caps, stacked one on top of the next. Halfway there the road ran under a banyan tree, and the afternoon was hot enough that he lay down in the shade and slept.
panels.alt: A cap seller asleep under a banyan tree with a bundle of red caps beside him.

panels.text: The tree was full of monkeys. They came down while he slept, took the caps one at a time from the top of the stack, and carried them up into the branches. When he woke, the bundle was empty and every monkey above him was wearing red.
panels.alt: Monkeys in the branches wearing red caps above an empty bundle.

panels.text: He shouted. They shouted back. He waved his arms and the branches waved theirs. Whatever he did, the tree did after him. He sat down in the dirt and thought about the walk home with nothing.
panels.alt: The seller waving his arms while the capped monkeys copy him.

panels.text: Then he pulled off his own cap and flung it on the ground. Every monkey pulled off its cap and flung it down. He gathered them up — all of them back in the bundle, though not in the order they had left it.
panels.alt: Red caps scattered on the ground below the tree as the seller collects them.

bridge.hook: The bundle is one thing holding many things in a definite order, and every move in the story has a name in Python.

mapping.story: The bundle of caps
mapping.detail: One object holding many, keeping them in order, growing and shrinking as needed.

mapping.story: A single red cap
mapping.detail: Elements need not be unique. Six identical caps are six separate items.

mapping.story: A monkey lifting the top cap
mapping.detail: Removes an item and hands it back. Both halves matter, and the bundle is one shorter after.

mapping.story: Every cap thrown back down
mapping.detail: Adds to the end. Which is exactly why the stack comes back in a different order.

bridge.code:
caps = ["red", "red", "red", "red", "red", "red"]
print(len(caps))            # 6

# the monkeys empty the bundle, one cap at a time
taken = []
while caps:
    taken.append(caps.pop())

print(caps)                 # []
print(len(taken))           # 6

# he throws his own down; every monkey copies
caps.append("the seller's own")
for cap in taken:
    caps.append(cap)

print(len(caps))            # 7
print(caps[0])              # the seller's own   <- his hit the ground first
bridge.codeNotes: caps.pop() takes from the end, caps.append() puts on the end, and caps[0] asks for whatever sits at position zero. Positions start at 0, so the first cap on the ground is caps[0], not caps[1].
bridge.gotcha: A list remembers order, and removing from the middle moves everything after it. caps.remove("red") deletes only the first match and shifts every later item down one position. Code that walks a list while deleting from it will skip items, because the positions moved underneath it while it was reading.

quiz.question: A monkey lifts one cap off the top of the stack. Which list operation is that?

options.text: .pop() — it removes an item and hands it back
options.why: Right. The cap leaves the bundle and ends up in the monkey's hands. Both halves matter: removed, and returned.

options.text: .append() — it adds an item
options.why: Backwards. That is a cap going onto the pile, not coming off it.

options.text: len() — it counts the items
options.why: Counting tells the seller how many he has lost. It removes nothing.

options.text: Indexing with caps[0]
options.why: Indexing reads an item and leaves it where it is. The monkey did not read the cap.

quiz.question: The seller wants to print how many caps he has left, then add one more to the bundle. Which lines do that?

options.text:
print(len(caps))
caps.append("red")
options.why: Yes. len() counts what is there; append() puts one on the end.

options.text:
print(caps.count())
caps.add("red")
options.why: count() needs to be told what to count, and lists have no .add() — that belongs to sets.

options.text:
print(len(caps))
caps.pop("red")
options.why: The count is right, but pop() removes rather than adds, and it takes a position, not a value.

options.text:
print(caps.length)
caps += "red"
options.why: Lists have no .length attribute, and += "red" adds three separate items: 'r', 'e', 'd'.

quiz.question: A different situation: you are holding the queue of people waiting at a clinic. People join at the back and are called from the front. Which pair of operations models that?

options.text: queue.append(name) to join, queue.pop(0) to call the next
options.why: Yes. Append adds at the end, pop(0) takes from the front. Order is the whole point of a queue, and a list keeps order.

options.text: queue.append(name) to join, queue.pop() to call the next
options.why: That calls whoever arrived most recently. It is a stack — the monkeys' behaviour, not a clinic's.

options.text: queue.add(name) to join, queue.first() to call the next
options.why: Neither method exists on a list. Method names are worth checking rather than guessing.

options.text: A dictionary keyed by each person's name
options.why: A dictionary answers "what belongs to this key". It cannot answer "who is next", which is a question about order.

title: The Talkative Tortoise
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Safe only while two things were true at once. Either one was enough to end it.

panels.text: A tortoise lived in a lake with two geese for company, and they talked all day, which the tortoise was better at than anything else. Then the rains failed. The lake shrank to mud, and the geese said they would have to leave.
panels.alt: A tortoise and two geese beside a lake dried down to cracked mud.

panels.text: The tortoise could not fly and would not be left behind. So the geese fetched a stick. They would hold each end in their beaks; the tortoise would bite the middle and not let go. One more thing, they said: whatever happens, do not open your mouth.
panels.alt: Two geese holding the ends of a stick with a tortoise gripping the middle in its mouth.

panels.text: They rose over the fields. People came out of their houses to look, because a tortoise in the sky is not a thing anyone sees twice. Some of them laughed. Some called up that the geese were clever birds to have thought of it.
panels.alt: Villagers below pointing up at two geese carrying a tortoise on a stick.

panels.text: The tortoise held the stick and held its tongue for three villages. In the fourth, someone shouted that the geese must have caught their supper. The tortoise opened its mouth to say whose idea it had been.
panels.alt: The stick held by two geese with nothing in the middle, and the ground far below.

bridge.hook: The tortoise was safe only while two things were true at the same time. Losing either one was enough.

mapping.story: Its jaws stay clamped on the stick
mapping.detail: True or false on its own, evaluated independently of anything else.

mapping.story: Its mouth stays shut
mapping.detail: Also true or false on its own — and here, unusually, the same jaws serve both.

mapping.story: Both at once, or nothing
mapping.detail: A and B is true only when both parts are. One false part settles the whole expression.

mapping.story: It opens its mouth to answer
mapping.python: The condition turns False and the else branch runs
mapping.detail: No partial credit. The flight ends the instant the expression stops being true.

bridge.codeNotes: Read "and" as "both", and read the "else" as the ground. Python also stops early: if "holding_stick" is False it never bothers to check "mouth_shut", because the answer is already settled. A tortoise that has let go is falling whether or not it kept quiet.
bridge.gotcha: Writing "or" where you meant "and" gives you a program that mostly works, which is worse than one that fails. holding_stick or mouth_shut is true when only the mouth is shut — a tortoise gripping nothing, silently, in the air. Nothing crashes. The answer is simply wrong.

quiz.question: The geese gave the tortoise two conditions. What joins them?

options.text: "and" — both had to hold at every moment
options.why: Right. Either one failing ends the flight, which is exactly what "and" means.

options.text: "or" — either one was enough
options.why: That would mean the tortoise could talk freely as long as it kept gripping. The story turns on the fact that it could not.

options.text: "not" — it only had to avoid one thing
options.why: "Do not open your mouth" does contain a negation, but that is one condition. The question is how the two combine.

options.text: Nothing — they were separate rules, checked at different times
options.why: They were checked continuously and together. Two rules that must hold at once are one compound condition.

quiz.question: Which expression describes when the tortoise is safe?

options.text:
if holding_stick and mouth_shut:
    print("still flying")
options.why: Yes. Both parts true, or the else branch runs.

options.text:
if holding_stick or mouth_shut:
    print("still flying")
options.why: True when only one part holds. This says a silent tortoise gripping nothing is fine, and it is not.

options.text:
if holding_stick and not mouth_shut:
    print("still flying")
options.why: This makes talking a requirement for safety, which inverts the instruction the geese gave.

options.text:
if holding_stick and mouth_shut == False:
    print("still flying")
options.why: mouth_shut == False means the mouth is open. This describes the moment before the fall, not safety.

quiz.question: A different situation: a door should unlock only when the badge is valid and the time is within office hours. A colleague writes if badge_valid or in_office_hours:. What happens?

options.text: It opens for a valid badge at midnight, and for anyone at all during office hours
options.why: Yes. "or" needs only one part to hold, so each condition alone becomes sufficient. That is two separate holes, not one.

options.text: It never opens, because "or" requires neither condition
options.why: "or" is true when at least one part is true. The door opens too often, not too rarely.

options.text: It behaves correctly — "and" and "or" are interchangeable here
options.why: They are never interchangeable. They differ on exactly the cases that matter: when one part is true and the other is not.

options.text: It raises an error, because two conditions must be joined with "and"
options.why: Both are valid Python. That is the danger — the code runs, and the bug shows up only in behaviour.

title: The Lion and the Rabbit
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: One animal a day, in order, until one of them ended the sequence early.

panels.text: A lion hunted the forest without counting. He killed what he wanted and left most of it, and the animals began to find their families thinner every season. So they went to him with an arrangement.
panels.alt: A lion on a rock above a gathering of forest animals.

panels.text: Every day, they said, one animal will come to you. You will not have to hunt and we will not have to lose ten for one. The lion agreed. From then on the forest sent one animal each day, in turn, and each day the lion ate what arrived.
panels.alt: A line of animals waiting their turn along a forest path leading to the lion.

panels.text: In time the turn reached a rabbit. It walked slowly, and arrived late, and the lion was already angry. The rabbit said it was sorry — it had been held up by another lion on the far side of the forest, one who claimed the whole place was his.
panels.alt: A small rabbit standing before an angry lion.

panels.text: Show me, said the lion. The rabbit led him to an old stone well and stood back. The lion looked over the edge, saw the other lion looking up at him, and jumped. Nobody walked to the lion the next day, or any day after.
panels.alt: A rabbit beside a stone well with a lion leaning over the edge.

bridge.hook: The forest handed over its animals one at a time, in order — exactly what a for loop does to a list. The rabbit is the line that ends it early.

mapping.story: The animals waiting their turn
mapping.detail: A sequence known in advance. The loop walks it from the beginning.

mapping.story: Whichever animal walks up that day
mapping.detail: One item at a time, bound to a name for the length of a single repetition.

mapping.story: One day, one animal, in order
mapping.detail: The loop stops by running out of items — unless something inside it interrupts.

mapping.story: The rabbit's trick at the well
mapping.detail: Leaves the loop immediately. Everything still queued is never reached.

bridge.code:
animals = ["deer", "boar", "monkey", "rabbit", "elephant", "peacock"]

for animal in animals:
    print("the", animal, "walks to the lion")
    if animal == "rabbit":
        print("the lion follows it to the well")
        break                 # the arrangement ends here

print("the forest is quiet")

# the elephant and the peacock were never reached.
bridge.codeNotes: for animal in animals reads as take them one at a time, in this order. "break" is the only thing in the story that was not part of the arrangement. Python also offers for ... else, where the "else" runs only if the loop finished without a break — here that would mean the queue emptied and every animal was eaten.
bridge.gotcha: "break" leaves one loop: the innermost one it sits inside. Put this inside another loop and the outer one carries on as if nothing happened. And do not reach for "continue" by mistake — that skips the rest of "this" repetition and moves to the next animal, which would leave the lion waiting for tomorrow rather than gone.

quiz.question: What is the loop variable in the arrangement the animals made?

options.text: The animal whose turn it is that day
options.why: Right. Each repetition binds one item out of the sequence to a name, and the body works with that one.

options.text: The list of all the animals in the forest
options.why: That is the iterable — what the loop walks through. The loop variable is a single item taken out of it.

options.text: The lion
options.why: The lion is the loop body: the thing that happens once per repetition. He is not what changes each time.

options.text: The number of days that pass
options.why: A count does exist here, but nothing in the code tracks it. The loop moves through animals, not days.

quiz.question: Which loop matches the arrangement, including the way it ended?

options.why: Yes. One item at a time out of a known sequence, stopped early by a condition inside the body.

options.text:
while animals:
    eaten(animals.pop())
options.why: This also empties the queue, but nothing stops it early — the rabbit is eaten along with everybody else.
"continue" skips the rabbit's turn and carries on to the next animal. The lion is still there tomorrow.
This breaks on the very first animal. The deer goes and the arrangement collapses on day one.

quiz.question: A different situation: you are searching a list of orders for the first one over ₹10,000. Once you have it, the rest do not matter. What belongs in the loop?

options.text: "break", the moment the first match is found
options.why: Yes. The work is done and every remaining item is wasted effort — the same shape as the rabbit. The sequence had more in it, and none of it mattered.

options.text: "continue", to move past the orders that are too small
options.why: "continue" is harmless here and pointless — the loop advances on its own. It does nothing about stopping when you are finished.

options.text: Nothing — let the loop finish and keep the last match
options.why: That gives you the "last" order over ₹10,000 rather than the first, and it reads the entire list to get there.

options.text: "return" — a loop cannot be stopped any other way
options.why: "return" does stop it, but only inside a function, and it exits the function too. "break" stops the loop exactly where it stands.

title: The Four Friends
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Four animals, one skill each, called by name when needed — and one of them called twice.

panels.text: A deer, a crow, a mouse and a tortoise lived near the same water and were friends, which is unusual. They were friends because each of them could do one thing well and none of them could do all four.
panels.alt: A deer, a crow, a mouse and a tortoise beside a pool of water.

panels.text: The crow saw far, from high up. The mouse could cut through anything with its teeth. The tortoise was slow but hard to hurt. The deer could outrun anything in the forest, and did, until the afternoon it ran into a hunter's net.
panels.alt: A deer tangled in a hunter's net among the trees.

panels.text: The crow found it, because finding things was what the crow did. It fetched the mouse. The mouse gnawed through the net's cords, one after another, and the deer stepped out of it.
panels.alt: A mouse gnawing the cords of a net while a crow watches from a branch.

panels.text: The tortoise had come too, slowly, and was still in the open when the hunter returned. So the mouse was called again, and did the same work on the sack the tortoise had been put in. It had not needed to learn anything new.
panels.alt: The mouse gnawing open a sack, with the freed tortoise beside it.

bridge.hook: Each animal is one job, written down once, called by name when it is needed. The mouse's second rescue is the whole reason functions exist.

mapping.story: What one animal is good at
mapping.detail: The steps that run when it is called. Written once, in one place.

mapping.story: Calling on that animal by name
mapping.detail: Naming it makes it run. The describing was done earlier and separately.

mapping.story: Telling it which trap, and where
mapping.detail: Called with the net, called later with the sack. Same steps, different input.

mapping.story: The freed animal walking away
mapping.detail: What the call hands back to whoever asked for it.

bridge.code:
def spot(area):
    print("the crow searches the", area)
    return "the deer, in a net"

def gnaw(trap):
    """The mouse's one skill. Written down once."""
    print("the mouse cuts through the", trap)
    return "freed"

found = spot("north field")     # the crow's job
print(found)

gnaw("net")                     # the first rescue
gnaw("sack")                    # the second, same function
bridge.codeNotes: def gnaw(trap): is the mouse being able to gnaw. gnaw("net") is somebody calling for the mouse. The last two lines are the point of the tale and the point of functions: the skill was written down once and used twice, on two different traps, with nothing rewritten in between.
bridge.gotcha: Defining a function does not run it. def gnaw(trap): on its own frees nobody — the body waits until some line says gnaw("net"). Forgetting the call, or writing "gnaw" without the brackets, is the most common way a function appears to do nothing at all: Python evaluates the name, gets the function object back, and quietly discards it.

quiz.question: What corresponds to "defining" a function, as opposed to calling one?

options.text: The mouse being able to gnaw, before anyone has asked it to
options.why: Right. The skill exists and is written down. Nothing happens until something asks for it.

options.text: The crow flying off to fetch the mouse
options.why: That is the call — the moment the skill is actually invoked.

options.text: The deer stepping out of the net
options.why: That is the result the call produced, which in Python is the return value.

options.text: The four animals being friends
options.why: That is only the arrangement that makes calling possible. It is not the writing-down of any one skill.

quiz.question: The mouse frees the deer from a net, then the tortoise from a sack. Which code says that?

options.text:
def gnaw(trap):
    ...

gnaw("net")
gnaw("sack")
options.why: Yes. One definition, two calls, the trap passed in as a parameter. Nothing is rewritten.
This runs, and it is exactly what the mouse did "not" do. Two copies of the same steps means two places to fix when the steps change.

options.text:
def gnaw(trap):
    ...

gnaw
gnaw
options.why: A name without brackets does not call anything. Python looks the name up, gets the function object, and throws it away.

options.text:
gnaw("net")
gnaw("sack")

def gnaw(trap):
    ...
options.why: The calls come before the definition exists, so the first line raises NameError. Python reads the file from the top down.

quiz.question: A different situation: three screens in your app each format a price as ₹1,234.50, and each one has its own copy of the same three lines. What does the mouse suggest?

options.text: One format_price(amount) function, called from all three screens
options.why: Yes. Write the steps once and call them wherever needed. When the format changes, it changes in exactly one place.

options.text: Copy the three lines again when you build the fourth screen
options.why: That is four copies to keep in step. The first time one is fixed and the others are not, they disagree silently.

options.text: A variable holding the formatted price, shared between the screens
options.why: A variable holds one result. The screens need the "steps", run on different amounts.

options.text: Nothing — three lines is too short to be worth a function
options.why: Length is not the test. Being needed in more than one place is.

title: The Crows and the Serpent
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A problem too big for your own beak, solved by calling in something that already worked.

panels.text: A pair of crows nested in a tree by a temple, and every season a black serpent came up the trunk and ate their eggs. The crows attacked it once. What they learned was that they could do nothing to it at all.
panels.alt: A serpent coiled around the trunk of a tree with two crows above it.

panels.text: They went to a jackal they knew and told him. The jackal thought about it and said the problem was not that the serpent was strong. The problem was that they had been trying to solve it with beaks.
panels.alt: Two crows perched near a jackal at the foot of a tree.

panels.text: Fly to the lake where the king's women bathe, he said, and take the gold necklace one of them leaves on the bank. Do not be quiet about it. Let the guards see you carry it, and drop it into the hollow at the foot of your tree.
panels.alt: A crow flying away from a lakeside with a gold necklace in its beak.

panels.text: The crows did exactly that. The guards followed the necklace to the hollow, found the serpent coiled around it, and killed it with the sticks they were already carrying. The crows had not touched the snake.
panels.alt: Guards with sticks at the foot of the tree, the necklace and the serpent in the hollow.

bridge.hook: The crows solved the problem without gaining a single new ability. They called in something that already existed and already worked.

mapping.story: What a crow can do with its own beak
mapping.detail: Always in reach, no import needed. Python hands you these the moment it starts.

mapping.story: The jackal's advice
mapping.detail: One line that brings a capability you did not write into reach. It does not create the guards; it points you at them.

mapping.story: The guards, already armed and trained
mapping.detail: Written, tested and used by many people before you. Calling one is far cheaper than becoming one.

mapping.story: The serpent dealt with
mapping.detail: The problem is solved by code you never wrote and do not have to maintain.

bridge.code:
# already in reach — nothing to import
print(len([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))      # 5
print(max([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))      # 5

# not in reach until you say so
import math
import random

print(math.sqrt(144))            # 12.0
print(random.choice(["crow", "serpent", "jackal"]))

# or bring in one name instead of the whole module
from statistics import mean
print(mean([3, 1, 4, 1, 5]))     # 2.8
bridge.codeNotes: import math is the jackal telling the crows that the guards exist. math.sqrt(144) is the guards arriving. Keeping the dotted name is worth something: six months later it still says where that capability came from.
bridge.gotcha: from math import * drags every name in the module into your file at once. If any of them collide with names of your own, yours are quietly replaced and the error surfaces somewhere else entirely. Name the module, or name the one function you want. The guards will do the job — and they will also take the necklace back. A dependency arrives with everything it carries, not only the part you asked for.

quiz.question: In the story, what plays the role of an import statement?

options.text: The jackal's advice — the thing that puts the guards within reach
options.why: Right. It does not create the capability. It connects the crows to one that already existed.

options.text: The guards killing the serpent
options.why: That is the call doing its work. The import only made it possible to ask.

options.text: The crows attacking the serpent themselves
options.why: That is code you write yourself — and in this story it is the part that failed.

options.text: The necklace
options.why: The necklace is what gets handed over to make the call happen. That is closer to an argument than to the import.

quiz.question: Which line lets you write sqrt(144) with no math. in front of it?

options.text: from math import sqrt
options.why: Yes. This brings the one name directly into your file, so you call it unqualified.

options.text: import math
options.why: This works, but you then have to write math.sqrt(144). The module name stays attached.

options.text: import sqrt from math
options.why: Right pieces, wrong order. Python's syntax is from <module> import <name>.

options.text: include math.sqrt
options.why: "include" is not Python. You are thinking of C or PHP.

quiz.question: A different situation: you need to generate a secure random password. You could write your own shuffling logic in about thirty lines. What should you do?

options.text: Use the "secrets" module from the standard library
options.why: Yes. It is already written, and for anything security-shaped its authors have considered attacks you have not. Thirty lines of your own is thirty lines of new risk.

options.text: Write the thirty lines — fewer dependencies is always safer
options.why: The standard library is not a dependency you took on; it ships with Python. And hand-rolled randomness is a well-known way to produce guessable passwords.

options.text: Use random.choice(), since "random" is already imported in that file
options.why: "random" is fine for shuffling a playlist and unfit for secrets — it is predictable by design. This is exactly why "which" module matters.

options.text: Copy a snippet from the first search result and move on
options.why: That is calling in a capability you have not looked at. The crows knew what the guards would do before they sent for them.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: He could not stop the betrayal. He could have an answer ready for it.

panels.text: A monkey lived in a jamun tree on the riverbank and ate the fruit all season. A crocodile took to resting under it, and the monkey began dropping fruit down to him, and then more to carry home, and they became friends the way daily small kindnesses do it.
panels.alt: A monkey in a fruit tree dropping fruit to a crocodile resting on the riverbank.

panels.text: The crocodile's wife ate that fruit for months and then said a monkey who lived on it must have a very sweet heart, and that she wanted it. The crocodile argued. Then he stopped arguing, went to the tree, and offered his friend a ride across the river.
panels.alt: A crocodile at the foot of the tree looking up at the monkey.

panels.text: Midstream, with no bank in reach and nothing to hold, the crocodile told him why they were going. The monkey said nothing for a moment. Then he said it was a pity the crocodile had not mentioned it earlier.
panels.alt: A monkey sitting on a crocodile's back in the middle of a wide river.

panels.text: Monkeys, he said, leave their hearts in the tree. Go back and I will fetch it. The crocodile turned around. At the bank the monkey climbed into the branches, sat where he could not be reached, and stayed there.
panels.alt: The monkey high in the jamun tree with the crocodile waiting below in the water.

bridge.hook: The dangerous stretch was the part the monkey could not control. He did not avoid it — he crossed it with an answer ready in case it went wrong.

mapping.story: The river crossing
mapping.detail: The stretch where something outside your control might fail. You mark it; you do not refuse to cross.

mapping.story: The confession midstream
mapping.detail: Normal execution stops right there. Nothing further down the try block runs.

mapping.story: "My heart is back in the tree"
mapping.detail: The prepared response. It runs instead of the crash, and only for the failure it was written for.

mapping.story: Climbing back into the branches
mapping.python: Recovery — the program carries on in a safe state
mapping.detail: The point is not that nothing went wrong. It is that the program is still running and still correct.

bridge.codeNotes: Everything under try: is the crossing. The "raise" is the confession. except Betrayal is the sentence about the heart — prepared in advance, for that one specific problem. "finally" runs whichever way the crossing went, which is where the things that must happen regardless belong: closing a file, hanging up the call, getting off the crocodile.
bridge.gotcha: A bare except: catches everything — your own typos included, and the interrupt you press to stop the program. The monkey did not agree to whatever story he was told; he had an answer for one specific betrayal. Catch the exception you expect, by name, and keep the "try" block short, or you will never know which line actually failed.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the "except" block?

options.text: The monkey's answer about leaving his heart in the tree
options.why: Right. It is the prepared response that runs instead of the disaster, and it was thought of before it was needed.

options.text: The crocodile telling him midstream
options.why: That is the exception being raised — the failure itself, not the handling of it.

options.text: The ride across the river
options.why: That is the try block: the stretch that might fail, marked as such.

options.text: The wife asking for the heart
options.why: That is the cause, upstream of everything. Nothing in the code corresponds to a motive.

quiz.question: Which version survives a missing file "and" tells you what went wrong?

options.why: Yes. One specific exception, caught by name, with the detail kept and reported.
This swallows every failure in silence, including ones you never anticipated. When something breaks later there is nothing at all to read.
open() raises before "if" ever receives a value to test. This kind of failure cannot be checked for with a condition.
This catches the exception and immediately re-raises it, so the program still stops. Sometimes that is deliberate; here it handles nothing.

quiz.question: A different situation: your app calls a payment API over the network. It usually works. Occasionally the network times out. Where does the try block go?

options.text: Around the API call itself, catching the timeout, with a retry or a clear message for the user
options.why: Yes. Wrap the part that can fail for reasons outside your program, and handle the specific failure you expect.

options.text: Around the whole function, catching everything, so nothing can ever crash
options.why: A large try with a broad except hides where the failure was. A typo three lines down would be reported to the user as a payment problem.

options.text: Nowhere — check the network connection first with an "if"
options.why: The connection can drop between the check and the call. Failures that come from outside cannot be prevented by asking politely first.

options.text: Around the call, catching "Exception", then carrying on as though the payment succeeded
options.why: The worst of both: the failure is hidden and the program continues on a false belief. Money is involved.

title: The Frog in the Well
source: Indian parable · public domain · original retelling
blurb: The well was the whole world, until something arrived from outside it.

panels.text: A frog was born in a well and lived its whole life there. It knew the wall, the water, the ring of sky overhead, and the insects that fell in. It had measured the well end to end and found it large.
panels.alt: A cross-section of a stone well with a frog on the water at the bottom and a small circle of sky above.

panels.text: One day a frog from the sea fell in. The well frog asked where it had come from. The sea, said the visitor. The well frog leapt from one wall to the other and asked whether the sea was that big.
panels.alt: Two frogs on the water at the bottom of the well, one darker than the other.

panels.text: Bigger, said the visitor. The well frog swam a full circle around the water and asked whether the sea was that big. Bigger, said the visitor, and could not explain how much bigger, because there was nothing in the well to compare it to.
panels.alt: The well frog swimming a circle traced on the water while the visitor watches.

panels.text: The well frog decided its guest was a liar and went back to counting insects. It was not stupid. It had simply never been given a name for anything outside its own walls.
panels.alt: The well frog alone again on the water with a few insects above it.

bridge.hook: The frog was not wrong about the well. It was wrong about the well being everything. Every name it had was a name that only existed inside those walls.

mapping.story: The inside of the well
mapping.detail: Names created in here exist in here. They are made when the function runs and gone when it returns.

mapping.story: The world outside the well
mapping.detail: Names defined at the top level of the file. They exist for the whole run of the program.

mapping.story: The frog can hear about the sea
mapping.python: A function can read a global
mapping.detail: Looking outward is allowed. Python checks local names first, then enclosing ones, then globals.

mapping.story: The sea cannot see into the well
mapping.python: Code outside cannot read a local
mapping.detail: Ask for a name that only ever existed inside the function and you get a NameError. Out here it was never created.

bridge.code:
sea = "very large"              # global — the world outside the well

def in_the_well():
    wall_to_wall = "two hops"   # local — made when this runs, gone when it ends
    print("I have heard of the", sea)     # looking outward is allowed
    print("the well is", wall_to_wall)

in_the_well()

print(sea)                      # very large
print(wall_to_wall)             # NameError: name 'wall_to_wall' is not defined
bridge.codeNotes: "wall_to_wall" is created when in_the_well() starts and destroyed when it ends. The last line is the sea trying to look down into the well: from out here, that name never existed at all.
bridge.gotcha: Assigning to a name anywhere inside a function makes it local for the "whole" function, including lines above the assignment. So def f(): print(sea); sea = "small" raises "UnboundLocalError" on the print — Python decided "sea" was local the moment it saw the assignment, and the global became unreachable from inside. If you genuinely mean to change the outer one, say global sea; usually you want to return a value instead.

quiz.question: What does the inside of the well correspond to?

options.text: A function's local scope — names that exist only while it is running
options.why: Right. The well is a world with its own names, created when you enter it and gone when you leave.

options.text: The whole program
options.why: That is the mistake the frog makes, not the structure it corresponds to. The well is one enclosed part of something larger.

options.text: A single variable
options.why: The well holds many names. It is the space they live in, not one of them.

options.text: A comment at the top of the file
options.why: Comments neither create names nor hold them. Nothing lives in a comment.

quiz.question: What happens when this runs?

options.text:
def well():
    depth = 3
    print(depth)

well()
print(depth)

# prints 3, then raises NameError
options.why: Right. "depth" exists only while well() is running. Outside it, that name was never created.

options.text:
def well():
    depth = 3
    print(depth)

well()
print(depth)

# prints 3, then 3
options.why: The call does print 3, but the name does not survive the return. Locals are not left behind for the rest of the program to use.

options.text:
def well():
    depth = 3
    print(depth)

well()
print(depth)

# raises NameError on the first print
options.why: Inside the function "depth" is perfectly visible — it was assigned on the line above. The failure happens outside.

options.text:
def well():
    depth = 3
    print(depth)

well()
print(depth)

# prints nothing; both lines are skipped
options.why: well() with brackets does call the function. Nothing here is skipped.

quiz.question: A different situation: you write a function that reads a config file and sets "api_key" inside it. Code at the bottom of the file then uses "api_key" and crashes with NameError. Why?

options.text: The function created "api_key" in its own local scope, so it never existed outside
options.why: Yes. Assigning inside a function makes a local name. To get the value out, "return" it and bind it to a name outside.

options.text: The config file was empty, so "api_key" was never assigned
options.why: Possible in principle, but then the failure would happen inside the function. A NameError at the bottom of the file says the name never reached that scope at all.

options.text: You must declare "api_key" at the top of the file before any function can use it
options.why: Python has no declaration step. A name exists once something binds it, in whichever scope that binding happened.

options.text: Functions cannot create variables, only read them
options.why: They can and constantly do. What they cannot do is leave those names behind after they return.

title: The Fox and the Crow
source: Aesop · public domain · original retelling
blurb: What it said was well formed. That was not the same as it being true.

panels.text: A crow found a piece of cheese in a yard and carried it up into a tree to eat where nothing could reach it. A fox came past below, looked up, and worked out that it had no way to climb.
panels.alt: A crow on a branch holding cheese in its beak, a fox on the ground looking up.

panels.text: So it spoke instead. It said the crow's feathers were the finest it had seen, that its shape was better than any bird's, and that if its voice matched the rest of it, then the crow was first among birds.
panels.alt: The fox speaking up at the crow, with its words written across the space between them.

panels.text: None of this was checkable from where the crow sat. It was pleasant, and it was specific, and it arrived in complete sentences. The crow accepted all of it and opened its beak to prove the last part.
panels.alt: The crow with its beak open and the cheese beginning to fall from the branch.

panels.text: The cheese fell. The fox took it, and said before leaving that the crow had a fine voice and no judgement at all, and that it should have asked itself who was asking.
panels.alt: The fox walking away with the cheese while the crow watches from the branch.

bridge.hook: Everything the fox said was well formed. Not one word of it had been checked. Those are two different properties, and only one of them was the crow's job.

mapping.story: What the fox said
mapping.detail: It arrives in the right shape. That tells you nothing about whether it is true or safe to act on.

mapping.story: It sounded correct and complete
mapping.detail: Parsing succeeded. int("-5") works perfectly; -5 may still be nonsense for what you are about to do.

mapping.story: It never asked who was asking
mapping.detail: One "if" between the value arriving and the value being used. That is the whole of the defence.

mapping.story: Opening its beak
mapping.detail: The point of no return. After this the cheese is gone and any check you add is too late.

bridge.codeNotes: Two checks, not one. The "try" asks whether the value is the right "kind" of thing. The "if"s ask whether it is a "sensible" thing to act on. "-5" passes the first and fails the second, which is exactly the fox's trick: correctly formed, and still not to be acted on.
bridge.gotcha: Checking the type is not checking the value. int("-5") succeeds, float("1e400") quietly gives "inf", and an empty name passes any test that only asks whether it is a string. Decide what range, length and shape you actually need and check for that. The crow's mistake was not that it failed to parse the fox — it was that it never asked whether the source could be trusted at all.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the missing validation check?

options.text: The question the crow never asked about who was speaking, and why
options.why: Right. One check between the input arriving and it being acted on. That is what validation is.

options.text: The fox's speech
options.why: That is the input itself. It is not a check; it is the thing that needed checking.

options.text: The cheese falling
options.why: That is the consequence, well past the point where a check would have helped.

options.text: The crow flying up into the tree
options.why: That is a real defence and it worked — against climbing. It simply does not defend against what actually arrived.

quiz.question: A form asks for an age. Which version is actually validated?

options.why: Yes. First whether it is a number at all, then whether it is a number that makes sense here.

options.text:
raw = input("Age: ")
age = int(raw)
register(age)
options.why: This crashes on any non-number, and cheerfully registers -5 or 900 when it does parse. No check at either layer.
This only checks that something was typed. "abc" is truthy and still crashes on int().
input() always returns a string, so this test is always True. It looks like a check and is guaranteed to pass.

quiz.question: A different situation: your API receives a JSON order with quantity: 1000000. The field is present and is an integer. What still has to happen before you use it?

options.text: A range check — it is well formed and still not a value you should act on
options.why: Yes. Schema validation says the shape is right. Whether a million of something is a sane order is a separate question, and only your code knows the answer.

options.text: Nothing — it parsed as an integer, so it is valid
options.why: That is the crow's reasoning exactly. Parsing tells you what kind of thing you have, not whether to act on it.

options.text: Convert it to a string so it cannot be used in arithmetic
options.why: That hides the value rather than checking it, and the problem returns the moment something casts it back.

options.text: Wrap the whole request handler in a try/except
options.why: That catches failures after they happen. A million-unit order may not fail at all — it may succeed, and be wrong.

title: The Mice and the Elephants
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Not one herd and one colony. Every elephant against every burrow.

panels.text: A colony of mice lived in the ruins of an old town, in burrows under what had once been streets. There were thousands of them, and they had been there for generations, and nothing had ever come through big enough to matter.
panels.alt: Broken walls of a ruined town with burrow mounds between them and mice on the ground.

panels.text: Then a herd of elephants began crossing the ruins twice a day on the way to a lake. There were hundreds of elephants. Each one, on each crossing, came down on burrow after burrow after burrow.
panels.alt: Elephants walking across the ruins over a line of burrow mounds.

panels.text: The mice counted their losses and found the number did not make sense at first. It was not the hundreds of elephants. It was not the thousands of mice. It was every elephant meeting every burrow in its path, one after another.
panels.alt: A grid of lines connecting each elephant to each burrow, with the count written beside it.

panels.text: So the mouse king went to the elephant king and asked for a different road to the lake. The elephants had no reason to refuse, and took it. The cost went to nothing, and it went to nothing all at once.
panels.alt: The elephants following a new path curving away from the intact burrows.

bridge.hook: The damage was not the number of elephants, and it was not the number of mice. It was the two numbers multiplied.

mapping.story: The herd, crossed one elephant at a time
mapping.detail: Runs once per elephant. Everything inside it happens all over again for the next one.

mapping.story: The burrows in one elephant's path
mapping.detail: Runs from the start, in full, for every single pass of the outer loop.

mapping.story: One elephant, one burrow
mapping.detail: The unit of work. Count these and you know what the pair of loops actually costs.

mapping.story: Hundreds times thousands
mapping.detail: Not hundreds plus thousands. Loops of n and m do n × m units of work, and products grow fast.

bridge.code:
elephants = ["tusker", "matriarch", "calf"]
burrows = ["north", "east", "south", "well", "gate"]

crushed = 0
for elephant in elephants:            # outer: once per elephant
    for burrow in burrows:            # inner: all of them, every time
        crushed = crushed + 1
        print(elephant, "passes over the", burrow, "burrow")

print(crushed)        # 15, which is 3 * 5 — not 3 + 5
bridge.codeNotes: The inner loop starts again from the beginning every time the outer one advances. Read the indentation as the herd: everything indented twice happens once per elephant per burrow. The final number is the one to watch, because it is a product.
bridge.gotcha: Nested loops are how a program that is fine on your test data dies on real data. Three elephants and five burrows is fifteen steps; three hundred and five thousand is one and a half million, with nothing in the code changed. If the inner loop is only searching for something, a "set" or a "dict" can usually replace it with a single lookup — and note that the mice's answer was to stop the crossing happening at all, not to make each crossing faster.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the inner loop?

options.text: The burrows one elephant passes over during a single crossing
options.why: Right. It runs all the way through, and then it runs all the way through again for the next elephant.

options.text: The herd of elephants
options.why: That is the outer loop — the one that advances once per complete pass of the inner one.

options.text: The mouse king going to the elephant king
options.why: That happens once, after the loops. It is what fixed the problem, not part of it.

options.text: The lake the elephants were walking to
options.why: That is why the loop exists at all. It is the goal, not a repetition.

quiz.question: Which version prints every elephant-and-burrow pair?

options.why: Yes. The inner loop runs in full for each pass of the outer one, which gives every combination.

options.text:
for elephant in elephants:
    print(elephant, burrows)
options.why: This prints the whole burrow list as one object, once per elephant. It never visits a single burrow.
The "break" ends the inner loop after the first burrow, so each elephant is paired with only one.
This is an IndentationError. The second "for" has to be indented inside the first to be nested at all.

quiz.question: A different situation: you have 2,000 customers and 5,000 orders, and for each customer you loop through every order to find theirs. It works on ten test rows and times out in production. Why?

options.text: The work is 2,000 × 5,000 — ten million comparisons, not seven thousand
options.why: Yes. Nested loops multiply. Ten test rows hid it because 10 × 10 is nothing; the real numbers are the product.

options.text: Production hardware is slower than your machine
options.why: Hardware is not the difference between seven thousand steps and ten million. The shape of the loop is.

options.text: 5,000 orders is simply too much data for Python
options.why: Reading 5,000 orders once is trivial. Reading them 2,000 times is not.

options.text: The two loops should be combined into one loop with an "and"
options.why: There is no single loop over two independent collections. The fix is a lookup — group the orders by customer once, then read each customer's orders directly.

title: The Monkey and the Wedge
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: It was sitting in the gap it decided to close.

panels.text: Carpenters were building a temple at the edge of the town. At midday they left a log half split, with an iron wedge driven into the cut to hold the two halves apart, and went into the shade to eat.
panels.alt: A half-split log on the ground with an iron wedge holding the cut open, workers walking away.

panels.text: A troop of monkeys came down into the yard. Most of them went through the tools and the wood shavings, looking for something to eat. One of them found the log, and the gap running down it, and sat in the gap with a leg on either side.
panels.alt: Monkeys in a carpenter's yard, one of them sitting astride the gap in the split log.

panels.text: It could see the wedge in the cut below it and had no idea what the wedge was for. It took hold with both hands and worked the thing back and forth until it began to give.
panels.alt: The monkey gripping the wedge below it and pulling.

panels.text: The wedge came free. The log closed. The monkey had been holding the one thing keeping open the space it was sitting in, and it had pulled that thing out itself, from the inside.
panels.alt: The log shut with no gap in it and the iron wedge lying on the ground beside it.

bridge.hook: The monkey was inside the structure and it changed the structure. What broke was not the log — it was the position the monkey was occupying.

mapping.story: The half-split log
mapping.python: The list you are looping over
mapping.detail: A structure with positions in it. Its shape is exactly what the loop depends on.

mapping.story: The monkey sitting in the gap
mapping.detail: A "for" holds an index into the list. That index is only meaningful while the list stays the same length.

mapping.story: Pulling the wedge out
mapping.detail: for x in items: items.remove(x). The list shrinks while something is still counting through it.

mapping.story: The log closing on it
mapping.detail: Everything after the removal shifts down one, the index moves up one, and the loop steps straight over an element it never saw.

bridge.code:
animals = ["monkey", "monkey", "crow"]

for animal in animals:            # the log
    if animal == "monkey":
        animals.remove(animal)    # the wedge

print(animals)    # ['monkey', 'crow']   <- one monkey survived

# it did not crash. it quietly gave the wrong answer.

# loop over a copy, change the original:
animals = ["monkey", "monkey", "crow"]
for animal in list(animals):
    if animal == "monkey":
        animals.remove(animal)
print(animals)    # ['crow']

# or build a new list instead of editing in place:
animals = ["monkey", "monkey", "crow"]
animals = [a for a in animals if a != "monkey"]
print(animals)    # ['crow']
bridge.codeNotes: The loop is counting positions while the list is losing them. Trace the first block: the loop is at position 0 and removes what it finds there, so the list becomes ["monkey", "crow"] and everything slides down one. The loop then moves to position 1 — which now holds the crow. The second monkey slid down into position 0, which the loop has already been past, so it is never looked at. One pass, one survivor, no error.
bridge.gotcha: It does not raise an error, and that is the dangerous part. The loop finishes, the program carries on, and the list is quietly wrong — a monkey left in a list you asked to have no monkeys in it. Removing while iterating fails silently; only running off the end fails loudly. Loop over list(items), or build a new list with a comprehension.

quiz.question: What does the wedge correspond to?

options.text: The list keeping its shape while the loop runs through it
options.why: Right. The loop depends on the length and the positions staying put. The wedge is that assumption, and the monkey removes it.

options.text: The loop's condition
options.why: A "for" over a list has no written condition. What it has is the assumption the wedge stands for.

options.text: The item being removed
options.why: The item is what the monkey grabs. The wedge is what its removal destroys — the stable gap the monkey was sitting in.

options.text: The carpenters
options.why: They set the structure up before any of this started. That is the code above the "for", not part of the loop.

quiz.question: animals = ["monkey", "monkey", "crow"]. What does this leave behind?

options.why: Right. Removing index 0 slides everything down; the loop moves to index 1 and steps straight over the second monkey. No error, wrong answer.
That is what you asked for and not what you get. The loop skips an element because the positions moved underneath it.
A "for" over a list stops when it runs out of positions, so it ends quietly. The silence is what makes this bug expensive.
remove() does work — it deletes the first match. The problem is what the loop does afterwards, not that the removal failed.

quiz.question: A different situation: you loop over a dictionary of sessions and delete the expired ones inside the loop. Python raises RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. What is the fix?

options.text: Loop over a copy of the keys — for sid in list(sessions): — and delete from the original
options.why: Yes. The copy is a stable thing to walk; the original is then free to change. Same fix as the log: do not remove what you are standing on.

options.text: Catch the RuntimeError and carry on
options.why: That abandons the loop partway through, leaving an unknown number of expired sessions behind. The error is the diagnosis, not the problem.

options.text: Use a "while" loop instead, since only "for" has this restriction
options.why: The restriction is on changing the dictionary while any iteration over it is live. Changing the loop keyword does not change that.

options.text: Nothing — dictionaries are unordered, so removing from them mid-loop is safe
options.why: Being unordered is exactly why it is not safe. Python refuses outright rather than silently skipping, which is more than a list will do for you.

title: The Brahmin's Dream
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Everything he had was in one pot, and the pot was only hanging there.

panels.text: A poor Brahmin was given a pot of rice flour, more than he could eat at once. He hung it from a nail in the wall above his bed, where the rats and the damp could not get at it, and lay down to look at it.
panels.alt: A clay pot hanging from a nail on a dark wall above a man lying on the floor.

panels.text: He worked out what it was worth. Sell the flour in a famine year and he would have goats; the goats would give him a herd; the herd would buy cattle, and the cattle a house, and the house a wife.
panels.alt: A pale dream shape above the sleeping man containing goats and a small house.

panels.text: He got as far as a son. He imagined the boy running underfoot while his wife was busy at the stove, and imagined calling out to her to come and take the child away, and imagined her not hearing him.
panels.alt: The dream shape now containing two figures and a smaller one beside a house.

panels.text: So he kicked out, in the dark, to get her attention. His foot caught the pot. The flour went across the floor, and everything he had built that evening had been standing on it.
panels.alt: An empty nail with a cut rope, broken pot pieces and spilled flour across the floor.

bridge.hook: Everything he owned, and everything he had planned on top of it, existed in exactly one place — and that place was only hanging on a nail.

mapping.story: The pot on the nail
mapping.detail: Fast to reach, and gone the instant something goes wrong. Nothing outside the program knows it exists.

mapping.story: Everything built on top of it
mapping.detail: The goats, the cattle, the house. All of it depends on the pot and none of it is stored anywhere else.

mapping.story: The kick
mapping.python: The process ending — a crash, a restart, a power cut
mapping.detail: It does not have to be dramatic. It only has to happen once.

mapping.story: Writing it down, or selling the flour that morning
mapping.detail: The moment the value leaves the program and lands somewhere that outlives it.

bridge.code:
# in memory only — the pot on the nail
plans = ["goats", "cattle", "a house"]
plans.append("a son")

# the kick: if the program ends here, so do the plans.

# on disk — this survives the process
with open("plans.txt", "w") as handle:
    for plan in plans:
        handle.write(plan + "\n")

# a later run can pick it up again
with open("plans.txt") as handle:
    recovered = [line.strip() for line in handle]

print(recovered)      # ['goats', 'cattle', 'a house', 'a son']
bridge.codeNotes: with open(...) opens the file and closes it again when the block ends, even if something fails inside — which is the point. An unclosed file may still be sitting in a buffer, written nowhere, when the process dies. The "with" is what takes the pot off the nail.
bridge.gotcha: open(path, "w") empties the file before writing a single byte. Point it at the wrong name and the old contents are gone, with no warning and no undo — the kick, delivered by your own code. Use "a" to append and "r" to read, and check the path before you open anything for writing.

quiz.question: What does the pot hanging on the nail correspond to?

options.text: Data that exists only in memory while the program is running
