options.why: Right. Reachable, useful, and gone the moment the process stops. Nothing outside it holds a copy.

options.text: A file saved to disk
options.why: That is the opposite — the thing the Brahmin never did. A file survives the kick.

options.text: A variable name
options.why: A name points at data; the pot is the data itself. The problem is where it is kept, not what it is called.

options.text: His plans for the goats and the cattle
options.why: Those are built on the pot. They are the derived state, not the thing everything rests on.

quiz.question: You want to add a line to an existing log file without destroying what is in it. Which is right?

options.text:
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("one more line\n")
options.why: Yes. "a" appends, and "with" closes the file even if something fails partway through.

options.text:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("one more line\n")
options.why: "w" truncates the file to nothing before writing. The old log is gone and nothing warns you.

options.text:
f = open("log.txt", "a")
f.write("one more line\n")
options.why: The mode is right, but the file is never closed. If the process dies first, the line may still be in a buffer and never reach the disk.

options.text:
with open("log.txt", "r") as f:
    f.write("one more line\n")
options.why: "r" opens for reading only. The write raises io.UnsupportedOperation.

quiz.question: A different situation: a shopping cart is held in a Python list on the server. A deploy restarts the process and every cart in progress vanishes. What was the mistake?

options.text: Treating memory as storage — the carts were never written anywhere that outlives the process
options.why: Yes. A restart is not an accident to be prevented; it is a thing that will happen. Anything that must survive it has to be written down.

options.text: Deploying during business hours
options.why: That makes it hurt more, not different. The carts would still be lost at the next restart, crash or power cut.

options.text: Not using a server with more memory
options.why: Memory size is not the issue. Nothing in memory survives the process ending, however much of it there is.

options.text: Not wrapping the deploy in a try/except
options.why: You cannot catch a process being stopped from inside it. The fix is where the data lives, not how the failure is handled.

title: Nasruddin Counts the Donkeys
source: Mulla Nasruddin · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A man counts his animals twice and gets two different answers. Both counts are careful.

panels.text: Nasruddin bought ten donkeys at the spring fair and set out for home. He climbed onto the back of one and let the rest walk ahead of him down the road. The morning was long and the road was dusty, and somewhere past the second village it occurred to him that he ought to check.
panels.alt: A man seated on a donkey at the right of a dusty road, with a loose line of donkeys walking ahead of him toward the left.

panels.text: He counted the animals ahead of him. Nine. He counted them again, slower. Nine. He counted a third time, touching each one with his eyes and moving his lips as he went, and there were nine, and he had paid for ten.
panels.alt: Nine donkeys walking ahead, each with a small gold mark floating above it. The tenth, the one the man is sitting on, is drawn pale and washed out, and the mark above it is an empty dashed ring.

panels.text: He got down to look along the road for the missing one. Standing in the dust with the reins still in his hand, he counted what was in front of him. Ten. Every animal he had paid for was there, and not one of them had wandered off.
panels.alt: The man standing on the ground at the right, arm out toward the animals. All ten donkeys are gathered in front of him now, his own among them, and every one carries a solid gold mark above it.

panels.text: He climbed back up, satisfied, and counted once more out of habit. Nine. He got down. Ten. He got up. Nine. Nasruddin walked the rest of the way to his own gate, leading all ten, and did not try it again.
panels.alt: A wooden field gate at the left. The man walks on foot just past it with his arm stretched back toward the animals, and the whole group follows behind him in a bunched line.

bridge.hook: Nasruddin never miscounted. He counted correctly, from a place that left one animal out.

mapping.story: The ten donkeys he paid for
mapping.detail: The group itself is never in doubt. What changes between his two answers is how much of it the counting reaches.

mapping.story: Counting from the saddle
mapping.detail: A count that begins one place in. The animal underneath him is the item the walk starts just after.

mapping.story: Nine
mapping.python: A total that is one short
mapping.detail: Nothing was lost and nothing wandered off. The boundary of the count moved, and the answer moved with it.

mapping.story: Getting down to count
mapping.detail: Standing where nothing is excluded. The fix is where you start, not how carefully you count.

bridge.code:
donkeys = ["grey", "brown", "black", "roan", "dun",
           "white", "piebald", "bay", "cream", "dapple"]

counted = []
for i in range(1, len(donkeys)):      # counted from the saddle
    counted.append(donkeys[i])
print(len(counted))                   # 9

counted = []
for i in range(len(donkeys)):         # counted from the ground
    counted.append(donkeys[i])
print(len(counted))                   # 10
bridge.codeNotes: The two walks differ by one character. range(1, len(donkeys)) starts at the second animal, because the first one is the one he is sitting on — it is in the group, but the count never arrives at it. range(len(donkeys)) starts at the first. Nothing was lost either time; only the starting place changed.
bridge.gotcha: range(1, len(items)) is the version that skips the first item; range(len(items) - 1) is the version that skips the last. Both are off by exactly one and both look reasonable on the page. The same mistake shows up as items[len(items)], which raises IndexError: the last position is len(items) - 1, because positions start at zero and the animal underneath you was never in the count.

quiz.question: Nasruddin's count is wrong in the same way an off-by-one error is wrong. Which part of the story is the item that falls outside the boundary of the count?

options.text: The donkey he is sitting on
options.why: It is in the group he paid for and it is never in the number he says. That is exactly what an off-by-one error drops — an item that belongs to the collection but sits outside the stretch the count walks.

options.text: The nine donkeys walking ahead of him
options.why: These are the animals the count actually reaches, and it counts them correctly. The error is in what the walk never arrives at, not in what it visits.

options.text: Buying ten donkeys at the spring fair
options.why: This happens before any counting and it is not wrong. Setting the collection up is not where an off-by-one error lives; it lives in the walk across it.

options.text: Walking the rest of the way to his gate
options.why: This is what he does after he stops counting. By then the boundary has already been chosen — an off-by-one error is decided before the walk starts, not after it ends.

quiz.question: Ten donkeys are in donkeys. Which snippet counts all ten?

options.why: range(len(donkeys)) produces 0 through 9 — ten positions, every animal reached. This is Nasruddin standing on the ground.
This is Nasruddin in the saddle. Starting at 1 means position 0 is never reached, so the first animal is left out and the total is nine.
This drops the last one instead of the first — the same error from the other end. range(9) stops at 8, so the tenth animal is never counted.

options.text: counted = donkeys.length
options.why: Python has no .length attribute; that is JavaScript. The built-in is len(donkeys), which counts every item without a walk at all.

quiz.question:
A school prints name badges. There are thirty names in students, and the code is:

for i in range(1, len(students)):
    print_badge(students[i])

Thirty pupils arrive and one has no badge. Which one?

options.text: The first pupil in students
options.why: range(1, 30) starts at position 1, and the first name sits at position 0. It is the saddle again — the name is in the collection, and the walk begins just past it.

options.text: The last pupil in students
options.why: range(1, 30) runs up to 29, and the last name is at position 29 — so it is reached. Skipping the last one is the other off-by-one, written range(len(students) - 1).

options.text: A pupil somewhere in the middle
options.why: Nothing here is random. The walk visits positions in order, so the one it misses is always at a boundary — the start or the end, never the middle.

options.text: None of them — all thirty get a badge
options.why: range(1, 30) produces twenty-nine numbers, not thirty. One badge short is exactly the symptom, and the position that never came up is 0.

title: The Word of Harishchandra
source: Indian epic tradition · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A king says one sentence in the morning. Nothing afterwards can reach back into it.

panels.text: Harishchandra was known for one thing before he was known for anything else: what he said was what happened. A sage came to his court one morning and asked for a gift. The king answered without waiting. Whatever you name from my house is yours.
panels.alt: A robed king with his arm out toward a shorter robed figure. To their right stands a broad stone tablet with three cut lines across it, and beyond it an open store stacked with coin.

panels.text: The sage named the kingdom. The ministers were on their feet at once, saying it had been a courtesy, a form of words, that he should take it back before the hour was out. Harishchandra said that a thing already spoken is not a thing you can reach into.
panels.alt: The same tablet, in the same place, with the same three cut lines across it. Three court figures stand beside it with their arms raised toward it.

panels.text: So he spoke again, beside it rather than over it. He would give up the throne, and he would serve until whatever remained was paid. The first sentence stood where it was, word for word. There were simply two of them now.
panels.alt: The first tablet standing unchanged, with a second, smaller and paler tablet now set beside it carrying a single cut line.

panels.text: He left before evening and served for years, and the name held. Only one thing had moved: the sentence had named the treasury, and coin had gone in and out of the treasury all year. What the words pointed at was never as fixed as the words.
panels.alt: Both tablets unchanged in the foreground. Behind them the same open store, now holding two coins where it had held eight.

bridge.hook: The king could add a sentence. He could not reach back into the one he had already spoken.

mapping.story: The sentence he spoke to the sage
mapping.detail: Both are settled at the moment they are made. Nothing that happens later reaches back and edits one part of them.

mapping.story: The ministers asking him to unsay it
mapping.detail: The refusal is not stubbornness. There is no route into a thing already made that would let one piece of it be swapped.

mapping.story: Speaking a second sentence beside the first
mapping.detail: He does not alter the old sentence, he builds another from it. The original survives the operation exactly as spoken.

mapping.story: The treasury the sentence named
mapping.python: A list held inside the tuple
mapping.detail: The words naming the store never moved, and the store emptied anyway. Naming a thing does not freeze the thing.

bridge.code:
word = ("the kingdom", "the treasury")

try:
    word[0] = "a smaller gift"        # the court, asking him to unsay it
except TypeError as e:
    print("cannot alter:", e)

spoken_again = word + ("and I will serve",)
print(word)                           # unchanged
print(spoken_again)

promise = ("the treasury", ["gold", "grain"])
promise[1].append("silver")           # the walls were named, not what stands inside
print(promise)
bridge.codeNotes: The first block is the ministers asking him to take the word back, and Python refuses for the same reason he does — the sentence is already made. The second block is what he does instead: a new sentence built out of the old one, leaving the first exactly as spoken. The last block is the treasury. The promise still names the same store, and the store's contents moved anyway.
bridge.gotcha: A tuple holding a list is not as frozen as it looks. promise[1] = [...] raises TypeError, but promise[1].append(...) succeeds — a tuple fixes which objects it holds, not what those objects contain. The other reliable trap is the missing comma: ("only one",) is a one-item tuple, while ("only one") is just a string in brackets.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the thing that cannot be changed once it is made?

options.text: The sentence the king spoke to the sage
options.why: It is settled the moment it leaves him, and everything afterwards has to work around it rather than inside it. That is exactly what a tuple is — a value that is finished when it is built.

title: The Hydra
source: Greek myth · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Cutting the heads off was the easy part, and on its own it made the problem larger.

panels.text: The thing in the marsh at Lerna had nine heads, and it had killed everyone who had come before. Heracles waded in with a sword and took the nearest head off at the neck. That part was not difficult.
panels.alt: A figure at the left with a raised sword, facing a dark green creature rising out of still water. Nine long necks fan out above the marsh, each ending in a small head.

panels.text: Two grew back from the stump while he watched. He took another, and there were two more. Cutting was work he could do all day, and at the end of the day there would be more of the creature than there had been at the start.
panels.alt: The same creature with more necks than before. Two of them are paler and thinner than the rest, rising together from one point on the body.

panels.text: His nephew Iolaus came down to the water with a torch. Heracles cut, and Iolaus put the fire to the open neck before it could answer. Nothing came back. What stood in the marsh was the same creature it had been, with one head fewer.
panels.alt: A second, smaller figure holding a lit torch stands beside the swordsman. The creature now has five necks where it had nine.

panels.text: So they did that. Cut, then burn, then look at what was left — which was always the same thing, one head smaller than the last time they had looked. When there were none, there was nothing left to do, and they stopped.
panels.alt: The water is quiet and the creature is a bare mound with no necks at all. The two figures stand at the left, turned away, the torch lowered and out.

bridge.hook: Each head was dealt with the same way, and each time it left them the same creature with one head fewer.

mapping.python: The value the function is called with
mapping.detail: What they face at each step is never a new problem. It is the same problem, arriving at a smaller size.

mapping.story: Cut, then burn the stump
mapping.python: The work done in the body, before the next call
mapping.detail: One head is handled here and now. Everything else is handed on unchanged in kind, which is what makes the next step identical in shape.

mapping.story: One head fewer, every time
mapping.detail: Descent is the whole requirement. If what is handed on is not smaller, the chain has no reason to ever end.

def cut_and_burn(n):
    print("head", n, "dealt with")

def clear(heads):
    if heads == 0:               # none left: nothing to do
        return 0
    cut_and_burn(heads)          # one head, handled here
    return 1 + clear(heads - 1)  # the same creature, one head smaller

print(clear(9))                  # 9
bridge.codeNotes: clear is called on a creature, and the first thing it asks is whether there is anything left — that is the pair of them looking at the water at the end. If there is, one head is handled here and the rest is handed straight back to clear with a smaller number. Every call does the same work on a smaller creature, and the whole chain unwinds once the count reaches zero.
bridge.gotcha: The torch is the base case. Remove the if heads == 0 line and nothing ever refuses to call again; remove the - 1 and every call hands on a creature exactly as big as the one it received, which is Heracles cutting all day. Both give RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded — the same failure reached from two directions. A base case also has to be reachable: clear(heads - 2) starting from nine steps straight over zero and never stops.

options.why: It is the one look that ends with nothing being handed on. Every other step passes a smaller creature to the next round; this one has nothing to pass, so the chain stops here.

options.text: Putting the torch to the cut neck
options.why: This is the work done at each step, and it is what makes the next creature smaller. Necessary, but it happens on every round except the last — the base case is the round where the work is not done at all.

options.text: Two heads growing back from the first stump
options.why: This is the case with no descent: what is handed on is bigger than what arrived. It is what a missing base case feels like from the inside, not the base case itself.

options.text: Heracles wading into the marsh at the start
options.why: This is the first call, the one that begins the chain. The base case sits at the other end — the point where the chain declines to make another call.

quiz.question: Which version clears a nine-headed creature and actually stops?

options.why: There is a branch that does not call again, and every call that does hands on a strictly smaller number. Nine reaches zero in nine steps, and the chain unwinds.

The base case is written but never reached, because every call hands on exactly the number it received. This is Heracles cutting all day — the same RecursionError, arrived at from the other direction.

options.text: Reaching a folder that has no sub-folders inside it
options.why: There is nothing left to descend into, so that call returns instead of handing the job on. It is the empty marsh — the one place the chain has no smaller version of itself to pass along.

options.text: Counting the files sitting directly in the current folder
options.why: That is the work done at each step, the cut-and-burn. It happens on nearly every call, including the ones that then go deeper, so it cannot be the place the descent ends.

options.text: Opening a sub-folder and counting inside it

options.text: Reaching a folder containing a shortcut that points back to itself
options.why: That is the failure, not the base case. The job hands on something no smaller than what it received, so it never ends — Heracles without the torch, and it raises RecursionError.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
source: Aesop · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Two ways of paying the same price. One of them stops working in December.

panels.text: All summer the ant went out and came back, out and came back, carrying what she found to a hole under a flat stone. It took her the whole season. The grasshopper watched her do it, then went to look for his own supper, which took him about an hour.
panels.alt: A flat stone with a dark chamber beneath it holding a few seeds. An ant walks toward it across ground thick with tall stems, and a grasshopper sits at the far right.

panels.text: He was not idle. Every day he went out, and every day he found enough, and an hour was a fair price for a day of food. He paid it on the Monday and paid it again on the Tuesday, and in June that was a perfectly good arrangement.
panels.alt: The grasshopper alone in the middle of the panel under a high sun, one seed on the ground beside him, tall seed-heavy stems standing all around.

panels.text: In December the ant went down to the hole under the stone, took what she needed, and came back up. It cost her nothing at all; she had spent the whole of it in July. The grasshopper went out as he always did. He was gone all day and came back with very little.
panels.alt: Night, with a moon. The chamber under the stone is packed with seed and the ant stands beside it. The ground is bare and pale, and the grasshopper is small and far off at the right.

panels.text: Her price had never changed either. She had simply paid all of it at once, in a month when she had the time, and every day after that was free. He had paid a small price every day of his life, and one day the price was more than he had.
panels.alt: Daylight again. The chamber under the stone is still packed with seed and the ant is climbing out of it carrying one. Far to the right the grasshopper stands on bare pale ground with nothing around him.

bridge.hook: The ant did not do less work than the grasshopper. She did all of it at once, in a season when it was cheap.

mapping.story: Carrying seed to the hole all summer
mapping.python: Building the lookup once, above the loop
mapping.detail: One long stretch of work done when there is room for it, producing something that will be read many times afterwards.

mapping.story: The hole under the stone
mapping.python: The stored result — a dict, a list, a cached value
mapping.detail: It exists so the expensive part never has to happen again. Its entire value is that it was filled earlier.

mapping.story: Going down and taking what she needs
mapping.detail: Cheap only because the work behind it is already done. The cost was moved, not removed.

mapping.story: Going out to search every single day
mapping.python: Rebuilding the lookup inside the loop
mapping.detail: The same answer found again from scratch on every pass. It is affordable right up until the day it is not.

bridge.code:
def build_index(rows):
    print("indexing...")          # the whole season's work
    return {name: price for name, price in rows}

rows = [("rice", 60), ("dal", 110), ("oil", 180)]
orders = [("rice", 3), ("dal", 2), ("oil", 1), ("rice", 5)]

total = 0
for item, qty in orders:
    index = build_index(rows)     # the grasshopper: pays on every pass
    total += index[item] * qty

index = build_index(rows)         # the ant: pays once
total = 0
for item, qty in orders:
    total += index[item] * qty

print(total)                      # 880
bridge.codeNotes: build_index is the summer. The first loop calls it on every order, which is the grasshopper going out each day — it works, it gives exactly the right answer, and it does the whole job four times over. The second loop calls it once before the loop starts and only reads it inside. Same rows, same total. Count the "indexing..." lines and you are counting how many times the season was paid for.
bridge.gotcha: The dangerous version is the one that still returns the right answer. Nothing raises, nothing looks broken — it is just slower every time the data grows, so it passes review and fails in production. Watch for a build, load, open, sorted or database call sitting in a loop body when nothing inside it depends on the loop variable. If the result would be identical on every pass, it belongs above the loop.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the work done once so that all the later work is free?

options.text: The ant carrying seed to the hole all summer
options.why: It is one long stretch of work, paid in a season when there was room for it, and it is what makes every December trip cost nothing. That is precomputation — the same total work, moved to a moment when it is cheap.

options.text: The ant going down to the hole in December
options.why: This is the cheap part, the reading. It is cheap because of the work done months earlier — it is what precomputing buys you, not the precomputing itself.

options.text: The grasshopper's hour of searching each day
options.why: This is the cost paid on every pass. It is the thing precomputing replaces: the same work repeated, rather than one block of it done in advance.

options.text: The hole under the flat stone
options.why: This is where the result is kept, not the work of producing it. An empty hole would have cost nothing to have and been worth nothing in December.

quiz.question: rows never changes while the orders are processed. Which version pays for the index once?

options.why: The expensive call sits above the loop, so it happens once no matter how many orders arrive. Inside the loop there is only a lookup, which is the December trip to the stone.
This rebuilds the whole index on every order. It gives the right total, which is exactly why it survives review — nothing fails, it is just the grasshopper going out again every single day.

options.text:
for item, qty in orders:
    total += build_index(rows)[item] * qty
options.why: Identical cost to rebuilding it on its own line; the call is still inside the loop, just harder to spot. Writing an expensive call inline does not make it cheaper.
This raises NameError: name 'index' is not defined on the first pass. Paying in advance means before the thing that reads it, not merely once somewhere in the file.

quiz.question: A page lists 500 comments and shows each commenter's display name. The 500 comments were written by only 40 different people. Which arrangement is the ant's?

options.text: Fetch all 40 people once before the loop into a dict keyed by id, then look each name up inside the loop
options.why: One trip pays for all 500 rows, and everything inside the loop is a lookup. The number of comments can grow without the expensive part growing with it — the hole under the stone, filled once.

options.text: Fetch the commenter from the database inside the loop, once per comment
options.why: That is 500 trips to answer 40 distinct questions. It returns entirely correct names, which is what makes it easy to ship and painful later.

options.text: Fetch all 40 people from the database inside the loop, once per comment
options.why: This is the worst of both: the whole season of work, repeated on every pass. It is the grasshopper going out each morning and searching the entire field.

options.text: Re-fetch all 500 comments inside the loop each time a name is needed
options.why: This fetches again the thing you already have, and the names still are not indexed. It adds a second daily price on top of the first without removing either.

title: The Titibha Bird and the Sea
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A bird decides to empty the sea one beakful at a time. The method is sound.

panels.text: The titibha bird laid her eggs above the tideline, where the water had never come. The water came that night and took them. In the morning there was smooth wet sand where the nest had been, and nothing in it.
panels.alt: A small long-legged shorebird standing on pale sand. To her right is a shallow flattened hollow where a nest has been washed over. A broad band of sea lies across the upper half of the panel.

panels.text: She stood at the edge and asked the sea to give them back. The sea did what it had been doing before she arrived. So she decided she would take the water out herself, and she started that afternoon.
panels.alt: The bird alone on the sand facing a wide flat expanse of water. The sea sits at exactly the same height in the panel as it did before.

panels.text: A beakful carried up the beach and tipped into the sand. Back to the edge, look at the water, another beakful. She was not working to a number. She was looking each time to see whether there was still sea in front of her, and there was.
panels.alt: The bird further down the sand tipping a small arc of water onto the beach, with a trail of six damp patches behind her. The sea is unchanged at the same height.

panels.text: Behind her the tide came in over everything she had emptied. Other birds heard about it and joined her, and a thousand beaks made no more difference than one. What ended it was the sea giving the eggs back. Nothing she did to the water was ever going to.
panels.alt: Five birds of different sizes scattered across the sand, all working. Behind them the sea stands at precisely the height it has held in every panel.

bridge.hook: She was not working to a number. She was checking, each time, whether there was still sea in front of her — and there always was.

mapping.story: Still sea in front of her
mapping.python: The condition, tested before every pass
mapping.detail: Both are looked at again each time round rather than settled once at the start. This much she has exactly right.

mapping.story: One beakful, carried and tipped out
mapping.detail: The work done on each pass. It runs, and it genuinely moves water — this is not where it goes wrong.

mapping.story: The tide filling in behind her
mapping.python: The body's effect undone before the next test
mapping.detail: She did change the sea. The net change across a pass was zero, so a test that was true stays true.

mapping.story: A thousand beaks, no difference
mapping.python: A faster body does not make a loop end
mapping.detail: If nothing drives the condition toward false, more speed only reaches nowhere sooner.

bridge.code:
sea = 1000
beakfuls = 0

while sea > 0:
    sea = sea - 1          # one beakful carried up the beach
    sea = sea + 1          # the tide, filling in behind her
    beakfuls += 1
    if beakfuls == 5:
        break              # only here so this example can finish

print("beakfuls:", beakfuls)   # 5
print("sea:", sea)             # 1000 — exactly where it started
bridge.codeNotes: The test at the top is the right shape: it looks at the water every time round instead of deciding a number in advance. The body works too — the first line really does remove a beakful. The second line is the tide, and between them the water finishes each pass exactly where it began. Take the break out and this runs until you stop it, and sea still prints 1000.
bridge.gotcha: The crow shows you a while loop that forgets to change the variable at all. This one is harder to see, because the body does change it — the change is simply cancelled, or moves the wrong way, or is too small ever to arrive. The loop reads correctly on the page and never ends. When a while hangs, print the condition's variable at the top of every pass and watch whether it is actually travelling toward false.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the reason her loop never ends?

options.text: The tide filling in behind her every time
options.why: The body ran and it did remove water, and the tide put back exactly as much. The test at the top asks whether there is still sea, and after every pass there still is. A loop ends only when something drives its condition toward false.

options.text: Carrying one beakful up the beach
options.why: This is the body, and it works — it really does move water. A working body is not enough on its own; what matters is whether its effect survives to the next test.

options.text: Looking at the water each time she came back
options.why: This is the condition being tested, and testing it on every pass is the correct shape. The crow at the pot does exactly the same thing and its loop ends.

options.text: The other birds coming to join her
options.why: This makes each pass faster, not fewer. If nothing moves the condition toward false, a thousand beaks arrive at nowhere sooner than one does.

quiz.question: sea starts at 1000. Which of these loops actually ends?

options.text:
while sea > 0:
    sea = sea - 1
options.why: Every pass leaves sea strictly smaller than it was, so the test is driven toward false and eventually reaches it. This is the crow, whose water really does rise and stay risen.
The body does change sea — twice — and the two changes cancel. Each pass finishes exactly where it started, so a test that was true stays true. This is the tide filling in behind her.

options.text:
while sea > 0:
    beakfuls = beakfuls + 1
options.why: This counts the passes but never touches the value being tested. The body is busy and the condition is untouched, which is the version of this mistake the crow warns about.

options.text:
while sea > 0:
    sea = sea + 1
options.why: This drives the value the wrong way. Every pass makes the test more true than it was, so the loop is not merely failing to end — it is travelling away from ending.

quiz.question: A script clears out a download folder: while count_files(folder) > 0, delete the oldest file. It runs on a machine where a camera saves a new photo into that same folder about once a second, and deleting one file takes about a second. What happens?

options.text: It never finishes, even though the body really does delete a file on every pass
options.why: One file out, about one file in. The count is tested every pass and never reaches zero, so the loop runs until something stops it from outside — the tide, with a camera instead of a sea.

options.text: It finishes as soon as the folder is empty, because the condition is rechecked every pass
options.why: Rechecking is necessary but it does not make the answer change. The test is honest each time; it keeps honestly reporting that files are still there.

options.text: It raises an error when a new file appears part-way through the loop
options.why: Nothing raises. That is exactly what makes this hard to find — the code is valid, the body succeeds every time, and the only symptom is that the script never returns.

options.text: It deletes one file and stops, because the condition was only true once
options.why: That is what an if would do. A while returns to the test after every pass and runs the body again for as long as the answer is true.

title: The Donkey in the Tiger Skin
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A disguise that works perfectly, until something asks him to make a sound.

panels.text: The washerman had a donkey who was worked hard and fed badly, and there was good barley growing in fields that were not theirs. One night the washerman brought out a tiger skin that had been folded in a box for years, and put it over the donkey.
panels.alt: Night. A thin donkey stands in a bare field with a hut behind it. A man holds out a striped orange pelt with a tiger head still attached.

panels.text: It worked. The villagers saw the shape moving through the barley in the dark and stayed behind their doors, and the donkey ate as much as he wanted and walked home at dawn. He did this for many nights, and nothing about the skin ever failed.
panels.alt: The donkey standing in tall barley wearing the striped pelt across its back, the tiger head sitting over its own. The hut in the distance is shut.

panels.text: Then one night a donkey called from somewhere across the field, the ordinary complaining call of a donkey wanting company. He heard it, and he answered it, because that is the sound he had.
panels.alt: The disguised donkey with three curved lines spreading from its mouth, and a small plain donkey standing far off at the other side of the field.

panels.text: They came out with sticks before he had finished. The skin lay in the barley afterwards, exactly as orange and exactly as striped as it had been the whole time. It had never been the thing they were afraid of.
panels.alt: Two villagers approaching, one carrying a stick. The striped pelt lies flat and empty on the ground apart from the donkey, which stands uncovered.

bridge.hook: The skin was a perfect tiger right up to the moment he had to make a sound.

mapping.story: The tiger skin
mapping.python: How a value looks when you print it
mapping.detail: Both are surface. print(3) and print("3") put the identical character on your screen and tell you nothing about what you are holding.

mapping.story: Villagers keeping their doors shut
mapping.detail: It behaved correctly for many nights. Working for a while is not the same as being the right type.

mapping.story: The bray
mapping.python: type(x), or any operation only one type supports
mapping.detail: The moment something needs what the thing actually is, the surface stops counting.

mapping.story: Sticks, and no surprise
mapping.detail: The failure lands far from the disguise, at whatever line first needed the truth.

bridge.code:
grazed = "3"            # read from a file, and it looks like a number

print(grazed)          # 3    <- the skin
print(3)               # 3    <- identical on screen

print(type(grazed))    # <class 'str'>   <- the bray

print(grazed * 2)      # 33, not 6
print(sorted(["10", "9", "100"]))
# ['10', '100', '9'] — compared one character at a time
bridge.codeNotes: The first two lines are the disguise: the screen shows the same character either way, so nothing you can see distinguishes them. type() is the bray — it makes the thing say what it is. The last two lines are the sticks: multiplying gives "33" instead of 6, and sorting puts "100" before "9" because it is comparing characters, not quantities. Neither of them raises.
bridge.gotcha: The screen cannot tell you what you have. Because print("3") and print(3) look the same, a value read from a file, a form or a spreadsheet can travel a long way through your code wearing the wrong type without anything complaining. "3" * 2 gives "33", and "10" < "9" is True. Use type(x) or isinstance(x, int) when you want to know, and convert at the edge where the data comes in rather than at the line that finally breaks.

options.text: The bray
options.why: It is the one thing the skin could not do for him. An operation that only his actual kind can perform is exactly what type() is — it makes the value state what it is rather than what it resembles.

options.text: The tiger skin going on
options.why: This is the surface being applied, not the truth coming out. It is the moment the value starts looking like something it is not.

options.text: The villagers staying behind their doors
options.why: This is the code working by accident. It ran correctly for many nights, which is what makes this kind of bug survive so long.

options.text: The sticks
options.why: This is the consequence, and it arrives last. By then the type has already been revealed — the sticks are what the wrong answer costs, not how it was discovered.

quiz.question: values = ["10", "9", "100"] was read from a file. Which line gives the true largest number?

options.text: max(int(v) for v in values)
options.why: Each value is converted before anything is compared, so the comparison is between numbers. This returns 100.

options.text: max(values)
options.why: This compares strings one character at a time, so "9" wins because "9" is later than "1". It returns "9" and raises nothing at all.

options.text: max(values, key=len)
options.why: This returns "100", which happens to be right, but only because it is the longest string. Give it ["7", "100"] with a real answer of 100 and it still picks by length — it is right by accident, which is worse than being wrong.

options.text: int(max(values))
options.why: The conversion happens after the comparison has already gone wrong. max() picks "9" from the strings, and int() faithfully turns that into 9. Convert at the edge, not at the end.

quiz.question: A spreadsheet of exam scores is exported and read back in. The report sorts the column and prints the top score as 9, when several pupils clearly scored higher. Nothing raised an error. What happened?

options.text: The scores are strings, so they were compared one character at a time
options.why: Text out of a spreadsheet arrives as text. "9" sorts after "100" because the first character decides it, and no line ever asked what type it was holding — the skin, all the way to the report.

options.text: The scores are numbers, but sorted() returned them in reverse order
options.why: sorted() goes smallest to largest by default, and reversing a list of real numbers would still not make 9 the largest of that set.

options.text: The scores are floats and lost precision on the way out of the file
options.why: Precision loss changes digits far to the right of the point; it does not reorder 9 above 100. Floats would also still compare as quantities.

options.text: sorted() always needs key=int, even for numbers
options.why: sorted() handles real numbers perfectly well with no key at all. The key is only needed here because these values are text wearing a number's appearance.

title: The Cat as Judge
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Two animals need someone impartial. They pick the one who says he is.

panels.text: The partridge went away for a season, and when she came back a hare was living in her burrow. She said it was hers because she had dug it. He said it was his because it had been empty when he found it. Neither of them was lying.
panels.alt: A plump ground bird facing a hare beside a low mound with a dark opening in it. Both are turned toward each other.

panels.text: They agreed to put it to someone outside the quarrel. Down at the river there was an old cat who sat very still with his eyes shut, and everyone along that bank said he had given up meat years ago and lived on air and river water.
panels.alt: An old cat sitting upright and motionless by a band of river water with his eyes closed, a thin ring of light drawn behind his head. The bird and the hare stand well back.

panels.text: He said he was glad they had come. He said his hearing had gone with age and they would have to come closer, since a judge who cannot hear the case cannot rule on it fairly. He said this without opening his eyes.
panels.alt: The cat in the same position with two small curved lines by his mouth. The hare and the bird have both moved noticeably nearer to him.

panels.text: They came close enough to be heard, and that was the end of the case. Everything anyone knew about the judge, the judge had said about himself, and nobody had thought to check it against anything else.
panels.alt: The cat alone by the river, in the same upright pose. The burrow sits empty on the far side of the panel with nothing beside it.

bridge.hook: Every fact they had about the judge was a fact the judge had supplied.

mapping.story: His holiness, his age, his deafness
mapping.detail: All of it arrived from the thing being judged. A value that describes itself has told you what it wants you to believe.

mapping.story: Everyone along the bank saying so
mapping.detail: The corroboration came from the same place as the claim. Repeating an assertion does not turn it into a check.

mapping.story: Come closer so I can hear you
mapping.python: A validation step the source designed
mapping.detail: The instruction sounds like due process. It was written by the party it is meant to constrain.

mapping.story: Checking him against nothing
mapping.detail: The condition passes exactly when the sender wants it to. Nothing was verified except that the sender said so.

bridge.codeNotes: The first check reads a field out of the parcel and asks the parcel whether the parcel is fine. It prints accepted, because it passes whenever the sender wants it to — which means it is not a check. The second compares against a set that lives on your side and a range you decided, neither of which the sender can reach, and it stays silent: this order carries no trusted source, so it does not get through. The last line is the same trap in its commonest costume — a filename ending in .png is a claim, not a fact about the file.
bridge.gotcha: The crow at least got real information from the fox. Here the whole of the evidence is the source describing itself, which is a check that passes by construction. Watch for anything the sender both supplies and is judged by: a verified flag in a payload, a Content-Type header, a file extension, a role field in an unsigned token. Validate against something you hold — a signature you compute, a record you look up, a list you own — and treat everything in the parcel as a claim.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the check that could never have failed?

options.text: The cat's own account of his holiness and his deafness
options.why: It is evidence produced by the thing being evaluated. A test whose input the subject controls returns whatever the subject wants, so it passes by construction — nothing was ever actually examined.

options.text: The partridge and the hare disagreeing about the burrow
options.why: This is the problem that needed deciding, not the flawed check. The dispute itself was honest — both of them had a real claim.

options.text: Choosing to ask someone outside the quarrel
options.why: This part is sound. Going to a third party is the right shape; the failure is in what they accepted as evidence about that third party.

options.text: Coming closer so that he could hear
options.why: This is the consequence of trusting him — the moment the data is handed over. The decision to trust had already been made on his say-so before either of them moved.

quiz.question: An order arrives from outside your system as {"item": "lamp", "quantity": 4, "verified": true}. Which line is an actual check?

options.text: if order.get("source") in TRUSTED and 0 < order["quantity"] <= 50:
options.why: TRUSTED is a set you hold and the range is one you decided, so neither can be altered by whoever sent the order. This compares the claim against something the sender cannot reach.

options.text: if order["verified"]:
options.why: This asks the parcel whether the parcel is fine. Anyone who can send the order can send verified: true with it, so the branch passes exactly when the sender wants — the cat, describing his own piety.

options.text: if isinstance(order["quantity"], int):
options.why: This confirms the type and stops there. A quantity of 1000000 is an int, and so is -4. Knowing what kind of thing you have is not knowing whether you should act on it.

options.text: if "verified" in order and "quantity" in order:
options.why: This checks that fields are present, which says nothing about whether their contents are true or sane. A hostile sender will happily include every field you ask for.

quiz.question: Your site lets people upload a profile picture. The handler accepts the file if its name ends in .png and the browser's Content-Type header says image/png. What is wrong with that?

options.text: Both the filename and the header are chosen by whoever is uploading, so neither one checks anything
options.why: They are two claims from the same source, which is one claim. Anyone can name a file report.png and send whatever header they like — the cat telling you twice that he is holy.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because two independent checks are being made
options.why: They are not independent. Both values travel in the same upload from the same party, so they agree whenever the uploader wants them to.

options.text: It is too strict, and will reject valid images that use .jpg
options.why: Being narrow is not the problem here. A check can be as narrow as you like and still be worthless if the thing it examines is written by the sender.

options.text: The header should be checked before the filename, not after
options.why: The order makes no difference when both values come from the same untrusted place. Read the file's actual bytes, or hand it to a library that does, and compare against something you control.

title: The Jackal and the War Drum
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: A noise loud enough to be worth running from. He goes and looks at it instead.

panels.text: The jackal had eaten nothing for two days and was working his way along a dry thicket when a sound came out of it that he had never heard before. It was enormous and it kept coming, at intervals, always the same.
panels.alt: Night. A jackal stands with its head up at the right. Three curved lines spread outward from a patch of dark scrub and trees at the left.

panels.text: Everything he had told him to leave. Nothing that made a noise that size was smaller than he was, and the sensible thing, the thing that had kept him alive so far, was to be somewhere else before it came out.
panels.alt: The jackal turned the other way with the sound lines drawn larger and closer behind it, filling more of the panel than before.

panels.text: He went towards it instead, slowly, and a good deal of the afternoon went on it. In the middle of the thicket was a war drum an army had left behind, with a branch above it that knocked against the skin whenever the wind moved.
panels.alt: A large drum with a stretched pale skin and red hoops standing in the scrub, a bent branch hanging down against it, and the jackal watching from a short distance.

panels.text: There was nothing inside it and nothing to eat anywhere near it. But he had spent an afternoon and come away knowing exactly what the sound was, which is more than he would ever have known from the far side of the field.
panels.alt: The drum from above with its open dark interior visible and empty. The jackal stands beside it, unhurried.

bridge.hook: The noise told him something was wrong. Going and reading it told him what.

mapping.story: The sound out of the thicket
mapping.detail: Both announce that something has happened. Neither one is the thing that happened.

mapping.story: The urge to be elsewhere
mapping.detail: The program keeps running and you keep your ignorance. The noise stops mattering and the cause is still there.

mapping.story: Walking into the thicket
mapping.detail: Binding the exception is the walk. It is the difference between knowing something failed and holding the thing that failed.

mapping.story: A branch on a drum skin
mapping.detail: The specific, dull, useful fact. It was available the whole time to anyone willing to go and look.

bridge.code:
rows = ["12", "7", "not a number", "5"]
total = 0

for row in rows:
    try:
        total += int(row)
    except ValueError as e:
        print("skipped:", e)
        # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'not a number'

print(total)   # 24

# the other jackal, the one who ran:
#     except ValueError:
#         pass
# same total, and you never find out which row was bad
bridge.codeNotes: The try block holds one line, so when it fails there is no question about which line it was. Binding with as e is the walk into the thicket — e carries the offending text, so the message names the exact row that could not be read. The commented version at the bottom produces an identical total and tells you nothing, which is the version that gets shipped because it looks tidy.
bridge.gotcha: The monkey's mistake would be catching everything. This one is catching something and then throwing away what it said. except Exception: pass and except Exception: print("something went wrong") are the same bug — the drum booms, you leave, and you never learn it was hollow. Bind the exception with as e and put e in the message, or let it raise. An error you cannot read costs far more than the failure it was reporting.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is reading the exception rather than merely surviving it?

options.text: Walking into the thicket to find the drum
options.why: He ends the afternoon holding the actual cause instead of a memory of the noise. That is what binding an exception and reading its message gets you — the specific fact, not just the fact that something happened.

options.text: Hearing the sound come out of the thicket
options.why: This is the exception being raised. It tells him something is happening and nothing about what, which is exactly as much as an unread error tells you.

options.text: The urge to be somewhere else
options.why: This is the instinct that becomes except: pass. It keeps him alive and keeps him ignorant, and the cause of the noise is entirely unaffected by his leaving.

options.text: Finding nothing inside the drum to eat
options.why: This is what the investigation returned, and it is a real result — sometimes the answer is that there was nothing there. But it is the outcome of looking, not the looking itself.

quiz.question: Some rows in a file cannot be read as numbers. Which version lets you find out which ones?

options.why: as e binds the exception, and printing it names the exact text that could not be converted. The try block holds one line, so there is no doubt about what failed either.
This produces the correct total and destroys the evidence. It is the jackal leaving — the run succeeds, and nobody ever learns which rows were dropped or why.
This looks like it handles the error and carries exactly the same amount of information as pass. A message that does not include e tells you only what you already knew: that the noise happened.
A bare except swallows everything, including your own typos and the interrupt you press to stop the program. It also still discards the message — two separate mistakes in one line.

quiz.question: A nightly job reads two hundred config files. It finishes successfully every night, but a few settings never take effect. The log line for each failure reads "could not load config, skipping". Where is the real problem?

options.text: The handler catches the error but never records which file failed or what was wrong with it
options.why: The job is reporting the noise and discarding the drum. Bind the exception and log the filename with str(e), and the same run that hides the fault becomes the run that names it.

options.text: The job should not be catching the error at all, so that it crashes on the first bad file
options.why: Crashing on file three of two hundred is its own failure. Continuing is a reasonable choice — the bug is continuing without writing down what you skipped and why.

options.text: The job needs to be run more often so the failures are noticed sooner
options.why: Running it hourly gives you the same unreadable line more often. Frequency does not add information to a message that never had any.

options.text: The config files should be validated before the job starts
options.why: A useful habit, and it does not fix this. Whatever validator you add will hit the same malformed file, and if it reports failures the same way you are no better off.

title: The Four Scholars and the Lion
source: Panchatantra · public domain · original retelling
blurb: Each of them could do one thing perfectly. That turned out to be the problem.

panels.text: Four young men set out together to look for work. Three of them had studied for years and each had come away with one thing he could do better than anyone. The fourth had studied nothing much and was mostly useful for noticing things.
panels.alt: Four robed figures of different sizes walking together along a road past a tree, all facing the same way.

panels.text: Beside the road, half covered, were the bones of some large animal. The first said he could put bones in their proper order, and did, and a skeleton stood up out of the dust while the others watched.
panels.alt: A scatter of pale bone shapes lying at angles in the dirt, with one figure standing over them and another watching from further off.

panels.text: The second said he could cover a frame with flesh and hide, and did. The third said he could put breath into a thing that had none. The fourth said that was fine, and that he would say the rest of it from the tree, and started walking.
panels.alt: A pale, bone-coloured lion standing complete but lifeless. Two figures stand close to it, and a smaller figure sits high in a tree at the far side.

panels.text: From up there he asked whether anyone had thought about what the thing would want first. Nobody answered, because the third had already done his part, and it had worked exactly as well as he had promised.
panels.alt: The same lion, now in full tawny colour with a dark mane, standing alone in the road. One figure remains up in the tree; there is nobody else in the panel.

bridge.hook: Every one of them did precisely what he said he could do, and one of those was a call that should never have been made.

mapping.story: Each scholar with his one skill
mapping.python: A function — one job, called by name
mapping.detail: The same shape as the four friends: work written down once and invoked when wanted.

mapping.story: Handing the same bones on
mapping.python: Passing the same object to each call
mapping.detail: Nobody makes a copy. Each one works on the thing itself, so every change is waiting for the next.

mapping.story: Putting breath into it
mapping.python: A call with a side effect
mapping.detail: It returns nothing useful and changes the world. The value of a call is not the only thing a call does.

mapping.story: Going up the tree first
mapping.python: Reading what a function does before calling it
mapping.detail: The one precaution available. After the call, being right about it is worth nothing.

bridge.code:
def add_flesh(bones):
    bones.append("hide")     # changes the caller's list
    return bones

mine = ["skull", "ribs"]
result = add_flesh(mine)

print(result)            # ['skull', 'ribs', 'hide']
print(mine)              # ['skull', 'ribs', 'hide']  <- yours too
print(result is mine)    # True — one object, not two
bridge.codeNotes: add_flesh looks like it builds something and hands it back. It does hand something back, and it is the very list you passed in — the same bones, altered where they lay. result is mine prints True, which is the whole story: there was never a second set. If you want the caller's list left alone, copy it first with bones[:] or list(bones) and work on that.
bridge.gotcha: The four friends warn you about the call you forgot to make. This is the opposite: a call that runs perfectly and does more than you wanted. A function handed a list, dict or set can change it in place, and nothing in the call site tells you so — names.sort() reorders the caller's list and returns None. The deeper version is a mutable default, def add(item, cart=[]), where every call shares one list that survives between them. Read what a function does to what you hand it, before you hand it over.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the call that succeeds and should not have been made?

options.text: Putting breath into the finished shape
options.why: It did exactly what it promised, on the first attempt. That is what makes it dangerous — a call that fails is a call you notice, and this one worked.

options.text: Arranging the bones into order
options.why: A call that runs, and on its own it harms nobody. It sets up the object the later calls act on, which is a different job from the one that turns out to matter.

options.text: Climbing the tree
options.why: This is the precaution taken before the call, not the call itself. It changes nothing about what the third scholar does — it only changes who is standing next to it.

options.text: Four men setting out to look for work
options.why: This is the setup, before any of the work is invoked. Nothing has been called yet, so nothing has happened that could be regretted.

quiz.question: mine = ["skull", "ribs"], then result = add_flesh(mine), where add_flesh appends to the list it is given. What does mine hold afterwards?

options.text: ['skull', 'ribs', 'hide'] — the same list the function changed
options.why: Passing a list hands over the list itself, not a copy, so appending inside the function is appending to yours. result is mine is True — the two names point at one object.

options.text: ['skull', 'ribs'] — the function worked on its own copy
options.why: Python passes a reference, not a copy. The parameter name is simply a second name for the same list, which is why the change is visible from both.

options.text: It raises an error, because a function cannot change its argument
options.why: Nothing raises. Mutating a list inside a function is entirely legal and extremely common, which is exactly why the surprise is so expensive.

options.text: None — because .append() returns None
options.why: .append() does return None, but that is the return value of the method, not what mine holds. mine is a list and stays a list; only its contents changed.

quiz.question: A helper def tidy(names): names.sort(); return names is called to print a sorted guest list for a report. Afterwards the seating plan, built from the same list, has come out in the wrong order. Why?

options.text: sort() reorders the list in place, so the helper rearranged the caller's own list
options.why: The helper was handed the list itself, and sort() rewrites it where it sits. The report got what it wanted and the seating plan quietly inherited the damage — the same bones, altered by a call that looked read-only.

options.text: return names hands back a copy, so the original could not have changed
options.why: Returning a name does not copy anything. It gives back a reference to the very list that was just sorted, so both names still point at one reordered list.

options.text: The report and the seating plan were generated in the wrong order
options.why: Sequencing is not the fault. Whenever tidy runs, the caller's list is reordered; moving the calls around only changes which part of the program notices first.

options.text: sort() returns None, so nothing was ever assigned
options.why: It is true that list.sort() returns None, but this helper returns names explicitly, so the call site gets a list. The harm was done by the in-place sort, not by the return value.

title: The Milkmaid and her Pail
source: Aesop · public domain · original retelling
blurb: She had it all worked out. None of it had been put anywhere yet.

panels.text: The morning's milk went into one pail and the pail went onto her head, and she set off for the market at the other end of the valley. It was a long walk and there was nothing to do on it but think.
panels.alt: A woman walking away from a small hut with a full pail balanced on her head, the milk showing pale at the brim.

panels.text: The milk would buy eggs. The eggs would come to something like a dozen birds by spring, and the birds would pay for the dress with the deep red hem she had been looking at since the last fair.
panels.alt: The woman walking with the pail on her head. Ahead of her float two pale eggs, a bird, and a plain red dress shape.

panels.text: None of it was written anywhere. It did not need to be, because she was carrying the beginning of it on her head and had both hands free, and the pail had never once come off on any of the mornings before this one.
panels.alt: The woman upright with the pail balanced on her head and neither hand touching it, a dotted line drawn under the rim.

panels.text: She tossed her head at something, the way anyone does. The pail went over. The milk went into the road and the dress went with it, and the eggs and the birds, none of which had ever been anywhere but in the pail.
panels.alt: The pail lying tipped on its side and empty, with a wide pale spill spreading across the road. The woman stands apart from it.

bridge.hook: Everything she owned that morning was in one container, and the container was in motion.

mapping.story: The milk in the pail
mapping.python: Bytes sitting in the write buffer
mapping.detail: Real, and yours, and not yet anywhere that would survive you dropping it.

mapping.story: The walk to market
mapping.python: The stretch between write() and close()
mapping.detail: The window in which everything is true and none of it is safe.

mapping.story: Both hands free
mapping.python: No with block, no close in a finally
mapping.detail: Nothing arranged for the case where the journey does not finish the way it usually does.

mapping.story: The toss of the head
mapping.python: An exception, or the process being killed
mapping.detail: Ordinary, unremarkable, and enough. The file on disk is empty and the code that wrote it never failed.

bridge.code:
f = open("milk.txt", "w")
f.write("three eggs, then birds, then the dress")

print(repr(open("milk.txt").read()))   # ''  <- nothing on disk yet

f.close()
print(repr(open("milk.txt").read()))   # 'three eggs, then birds, ...'

# the pail, carried properly:
with open("milk.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("safe")                    # closed even if this block raises
bridge.codeNotes: The middle line is the point of the whole story. The write has happened, the program believes it, and reading the file from disk at that moment gives back an empty string — the milk is in the pail and the pail is still on her head. Only close() puts it somewhere. The with block does the close for you, including on the way out of an exception, which is the toss of the head.
bridge.gotcha: Writing is not saving. f.write() puts characters in a buffer in memory and they reach the disk when the file is closed or the buffer fills, so a process that is killed — or an exception that jumps over your f.close() — leaves a file that is empty or half written, with no error anywhere. Always use with open(path) as f:. Note this is a different failure from the Brahmin's: his pot existed and got kicked, while her milk had never been anywhere but the pail.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the stretch where the data exists but is not yet safe?

options.text: The walk to market with the pail on her head
options.why: The milk is real and it is hers for the whole walk, and it is in the one place that cannot survive a stumble. That is the gap between write() and close(), where the bytes are in memory and not on the disk.

options.text: The milk being poured into the pail that morning
options.why: This is the write itself — the moment the data comes into being. The danger is not in producing it; it is in the time that passes before it is put somewhere that keeps it.

options.text: The plans about eggs and birds and the dress
options.why: These are conclusions drawn from the data, not the data. They are lost with the milk, but they were never the thing that needed saving.

options.text: The toss of the head
options.why: This is the interruption — the exception, or the process being killed. It is what the unsafe stretch leaves you exposed to, not the stretch itself.

quiz.question: f = open("out.txt", "w") then f.write("hello"), and the program is killed before anything else runs. What is in out.txt?

options.text: Nothing — the file exists and is empty
options.why: open(..., "w") creates and empties the file immediately, but write() only fills a buffer in memory. Without a close or a flush, those characters never reach the disk, so an empty file is left behind by code that never failed.

options.text: "hello", because write() puts it on the disk straight away
options.why: write() hands the characters to a buffer, not to the disk. Reading the file from another handle before the close gives back an empty string, which you can watch happen.

options.text: The file does not exist, because it was never closed
options.why: The file is created the moment open() is called with "w" — that is also what truncates any existing file of that name. It exists; it is simply empty.

options.text: "hello" but with no newline, which makes it unreadable
options.why: A missing newline would be harmless, and it is not what happened. Nothing was written to the disk at all.

quiz.question: A service appends to a log file with f.write() and keeps the handle open for its whole run. While it is running you watch the log, and the newest lines are missing — then a batch of them all appears at once. What is going on?

options.text: The lines are sitting in the write buffer and only reach the file when it is closed or the buffer fills
options.why: The all-at-once arrival is the tell: that is the buffer flushing when it fills. The service is honestly writing every line, and every line spends time on the milkmaid's head before it lands.

options.text: The service is writing to a different path than the one being watched
options.why: Then the lines would never appear in the watched file at all. They do appear, in order, in a batch — which points at when they arrive, not where.

options.text: The tool watching the file cannot show lines written after it started
options.why: Following a growing file is exactly what such tools do. It is showing everything the file contains; the file simply does not contain the newest lines yet.

options.text: The service is writing faster than the disk accepts, so lines are dropped
options.why: Nothing is dropped — every line turns up in the end. Loss and delay look different, and a complete batch arriving late is delay.

title: The Day Every Zune Froze
source: Real incident · 31 December 2008 · original account

sources.label: CNN — Leap-year glitch freezes Zune MP3 players (31 Dec 2008)
Princeton CITP — Debugging the Zune blackout (12 Jan 2009)

blurb: One day in four years, a date routine asked the same question forever.

panels.text: On the last day of 2008, owners of the 30 GB Zune music player switched it on and saw the loading screen. Then they kept seeing it. The logo sat there and nothing came after it. Not on one player — on every one of that model, at the same time.
panels.alt: A row of identical music players, every screen showing the same loading logo.

panels.text: When the player starts, it reads one number from its clock chip: how many days have passed since 1 January 1980. To show today's date it has to turn that count into a year. It does it the way you would by hand. Take away a year's worth of days, move the year on by one, and look at what is left.
panels.alt: A counter showing a large day count, with a year worth of days being taken away and the year moving on by one.

panels.text: It keeps taking away years as long as more than 365 days remain. In a leap year it takes away 366 instead, but only if more than 366 remain. On 31 December 2008, day 366 of a leap year, exactly 366 remained. More than 365, so keep going. Not more than 366, so take nothing away. Look again. Same answer.
panels.alt: The counter stuck at 366 and the year stuck at 2008, with an arrow circling back to the same question.

panels.text: Every player was stuck asking one question and getting one answer. The makers' advice was simple: let the battery run flat, then switch on again once the new year had begun. By then the count had moved past the bad day, the answer came out differently, and every Zune woke up.
panels.alt: A player with an empty battery icon beside a calendar turned to 1 January, and the player's screen working again.

bridge.hook: The player's rule was right for years: keep subtracting as long as too many days remain. But once every four years, the body of that rule changed nothing at all.

mapping.story: More than 365 days still remain
mapping.detail: Asked before every pass. While it is true, the player goes round again.

mapping.story: Take away a year of days and move the year on
mapping.detail: It exists to shrink days, so that the condition can one day come out false.

mapping.story: In a leap year, subtract only if more than 366 remain
mapping.python: An if inside the body that can skip the only line changing days
mapping.detail: On day 366 the if is false, the body runs, and nothing moves.

mapping.story: Stuck on the logo until the date changed
mapping.detail: The condition is still true and the state is the same, so the next check must say the same thing.

bridge.codeNotes: Read while days > 365 as the player's question, and the indented block as one attempt to answer it. The "max_passes" guard is not in the real player. Without it, the second call would freeze your terminal the way the players froze.
bridge.gotcha: A "while" loop ends only if every path through its body moves the condition toward false. Here one path, a leap year with exactly 366 days left, moves nothing. Testing ordinary days cannot find it: the routine works on 1,460 of every 1,461 days. The fix is one else: break on that path, because 366 days into a leap year is simply 31 December.

quiz.question: In the player's date routine, what is the loop condition?

options.text: More than 365 days still remain
options.why: Right. It is asked before every pass, and while it is true the player goes round again.

options.text: Take away 366 days and move the year on
options.why: That is work inside the body. On the bad day it is exactly the part that got skipped.

options.text: Reading the day count from the clock chip
options.why: That happens once, before any repeating starts. It is setup, not the loop.

options.text: The battery running flat
options.why: That stopped the player from outside. The loop never ended on its own, which is the bug.

quiz.question: Which change to the leap-year branch stops the freeze on 31 December?

options.why: Yes. The path that changed nothing now leaves the loop, and 366 days into a leap year really is 31 December, so stopping gives the right date.

options.text: while days >= 365:
options.why: That makes the condition true in more cases, not fewer. Day 366 still changes nothing, and now day 365 of a leap year sticks as well.
It no longer freezes, but on 31 December 2008 it subtracts a whole year and lands on day 0 of 2009. A wrong date has replaced a frozen screen.

options.text: print(days)   # added at the top of the body
options.why: Useful for finding the bug, since it would show 366 again and again. It fixes nothing.

quiz.question: A different situation: a phone app keeps retrying a photo upload as long as the upload has not succeeded. With no signal, each try fails instantly. What is wrong, and what fixes it?

options.text: Offline, nothing in the body can change the outcome, so it may retry forever. Add a limit on attempts, with a point where it gives up.
