options.why: That removes the only exit. Even a successful upload would no longer end it without a break.

title: Three Tries at the Counter
source: Real system · UPI payments in India · original account

sources.label: Google Pay Help — Fix an incorrect UPI PIN
ICICI Bank — UPI payer FAQs

blurb: A fixed number of chances, one way out early, and one outcome for running out.

panels.text: You are at the counter of a medicine shop, paying ₹340 through UPI. The app asks for your four-digit PIN. Out of habit you type the one you use at the ATM. The app tells you the PIN is incorrect.
panels.alt: A phone showing a payment of 340 rupees beside a number pad, and one of three attempt markers crossed out.

panels.text: You try the PIN you had before you changed it last year. Incorrect again. The shopkeeper is waiting, and the queue behind you is getting longer. You stop typing and think, because you have a feeling about what comes next.
panels.alt: The same payment screen, two of three attempt markers crossed out, and three people waiting in a queue.

panels.text: The rule was fixed before you ever opened the app: three tries. Each one is checked on its own. If one is right, the payment goes through at that moment and nobody asks you for another. If all three are wrong, the app stops asking.
panels.alt: Three boxes for try one, two and three in a row, each with an arrow up to pay if right, and an arrow down after the third to stop asking.

panels.text: Your third try is wrong too. Now UPI payments from your account are blocked for the next twenty-four hours. Money sent to you still arrives; you just cannot send any. To pay sooner you would have to reset the PIN with your debit card and an OTP. You pay the shopkeeper in cash.
panels.alt: The phone showing that sending is blocked, all three attempt markers crossed out, a stamp reading blocked 24 hours, and an arrow showing incoming money still arrives.

bridge.hook: The number of tries was decided before the first one: three. A correct PIN ends the asking early, and running out of tries is an outcome of its own.

mapping.story: Three tries, fixed in advance
mapping.detail: The count is known before the first try, which is exactly what a for loop is for.

mapping.story: Checking one PIN you typed
mapping.detail: Runs once per try, with the attempt number bound to a name.

mapping.story: A correct PIN pays at once, and no more asking
mapping.detail: Leaves the loop immediately. The tries not yet used are never reached.

mapping.story: All three wrong: sending blocked for 24 hours
mapping.detail: The else runs only if the loop finished without a break, the one case where every try failed.

bridge.codeNotes: The "else" lines up with the "for", not the "if", and it means the loop ran out without a break. Change the third entry to "2580" and the last line never prints: the loop broke before it could run out.
bridge.gotcha: Leave out the "break" and a PIN that is right on the first try gets asked for twice more. If the payment happens inside the loop, it happens up to three times. The other common slip is putting the block message after the loop with no "else". It then runs every time, including straight after a successful payment.

quiz.question: In the PIN rule, what does break correspond to?

options.text: A correct PIN ending the asking at once
options.why: Right. The loop stops the moment its work is done, and the unused tries are never reached.

options.text: Sending being blocked after three wrong tries
options.why: That happens when the loop runs out without a break. It is the else branch, the opposite case.

options.text: Typing the PIN
options.why: That is what happens inside the body, once on every try.

options.text: The limit of three tries
options.why: That is the sequence the loop walks, fixed before it starts: range(3).

quiz.question: Which code blocks sending only when all three tries fail?

options.why: Yes. The else belongs to the for, and runs only if the loop was never broken: three wrong tries.
block() sits after the loop with no else, so it runs every time, even straight after a successful payment.
This else belongs to the if. Sending is blocked after the first wrong try, with two tries still unused.
No limit at all, so someone with your phone could guess forever. The whole rule is that the number of tries is fixed.

quiz.question: A different situation: an exam portal holds a paper of 50 questions. You want code that opens the first question you have not answered yet, or says "all answered" if there is none. What does the loop need?

options.text: A for over the 50 questions, break at the first unanswered one, and an else that says all answered
options.why: The PIN rule's shape: a known sequence, stop at the first match, and a separate outcome for when nothing matched.

options.text: A for over the 50 questions with continue at every answered one
options.why: continue skips ahead but never stops, so it would open every unanswered question, not the first.

options.text: A while loop that runs until the exam's time is up
options.why: The number of questions is known, 50. Waiting on the clock does not find anything.

options.text: No loop. Open question 1.
options.why: That is only right if you skipped question 1. The point is finding the first gap, wherever it is.

title: WL 7
source: Real system · Indian Railways reservations · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — Reservation against Cancellation (Indian Railways)

blurb: Nobody's ticket changes. The line moves, and so does every number in it.

panels.text: You book a sleeper ticket from Pune to Patna three weeks ahead, and the train is already full. The booking goes through anyway, with a status where the berth should be: WL 7. You are seventh in the waiting line for that train and class.
panels.alt: A ticket reading Pune to Patna, sleeper class, status WL 7, above seven people standing in a row with the last one marked as you.

panels.text: You check the PNR every morning. WL 7 becomes WL 5, then WL 4. You have done nothing. Other people have cancelled, and every cancellation ahead of you moves the whole line forward by one. Your ticket and your PNR stay exactly the same. Only the number beside your name changes.
panels.alt: The first three people in the row faded out and leaving, the rest still standing, and a status changing from WL 7 to WL 4.

panels.text: A week before the journey it shows RAC 2: you may board and share a berth. Two days before, it shows CNF, with a coach and a berth number. Everyone who was ahead of you moved up first. The line only ever moves from the front, one place at a time.
panels.alt: A sequence reading WL 7, WL 4, RAC 2, then CNF, above a ticket stamped confirmed for coach S4, berth 32.

panels.text: Your friend booked the same train a day later and is still WL 9 when the chart is prepared, a few hours before departure. An e-ticket that is still waiting then is cancelled on its own, and the fare is refunded. Same line, same rule. It ran out of cancellations before it reached her.
panels.alt: Your ticket stamped confirmed beside your friend's ticket still at WL 9, with a cancelled and refunded stamp beneath it and the chart page below.

bridge.hook: The waiting line is one ordered collection. Nobody's ticket ever changes. People leave from the front, and everyone else's position shifts.

mapping.story: The waiting line for the train
mapping.detail: One object holding many, in a definite order that it keeps.

mapping.story: WL 7: seventh in line
mapping.detail: Python counts positions from 0, so seventh in line is index 6.

mapping.story: A cancellation lets the front of the line move up
mapping.detail: Removes the first item and hands it back, on to a berth.

mapping.story: Your number drops, though your ticket never changed
mapping.python: Every later item shifts down one position
mapping.detail: Removing from the front renumbers everything behind it.

bridge.code:
waitlist = ["Asha", "Ravi", "Kiran", "Dev", "Meena", "Imran", "you"]
print("status: WL", waitlist.index("you") + 1)   # WL 7

# three cancellations ahead of you
for _ in range(3):
    moved_up = waitlist.pop(0)
    print(moved_up, "moves up")

print("status: WL", waitlist.index("you") + 1)   # WL 4
print(len(waitlist), "still waiting")             # 4
bridge.codeNotes: "you" is never touched. Three pop(0) calls take from the front, and index("you") quietly comes out three smaller. The + 1 is only there because the railway counts from 1 and Python counts from 0.
bridge.gotcha: A saved position goes stale the moment anyone in front of it leaves. mine = waitlist.index("you") is 6. After one cancellation the list is six long, and waitlist[6] raises IndexError. Save the position of someone in the middle and it is worse: the number now points at whoever was behind them, and no error appears. Look people up by name when you need them, not by a number you stored earlier. And watch pop() with no argument: it takes from the back, which gives the berth to the last person who booked.

quiz.question: Your status reads WL 4. In the list, what is that?

options.text: Your position in it, which Python counts from 0 as index 3
options.why: Right. The railway counts from 1 and a list counts from 0. Same place, different counting.

options.text: Your PNR
options.why: The PNR is the item itself, and it never changes. WL 4 is where that item sits right now.

options.text: The number of people still waiting
options.why: That would be len(waitlist). You can be WL 4 in a line of twenty.

options.text: The number of cancellations so far
options.why: Cancellations change your position, but the position is not a count of them.

quiz.question: Someone at the front of the line gets a berth. Which line updates the waiting list correctly?

options.text: moved_up = waitlist.pop(0)
options.why: Yes. The front item leaves the list and is handed back to be given a berth, and everyone behind moves up one.

options.text: moved_up = waitlist.pop()
options.why: pop() with no argument takes from the back. That gives the berth to whoever booked last.

options.text: waitlist.remove(0)
options.why: remove() searches for a matching value. There is no passenger called 0, so this raises ValueError.

options.text: del waitlist
options.why: That deletes the whole list, name and all. Nobody moves up; the line stops existing.

quiz.question: A different situation: your favourite song is number 5 in a playlist. You delete two songs that sit above it, then tap number 5. Which song plays?

options.text: The song that used to be number 7
options.why: The waiting line's rule: removing items shifts everything after them up, so position 5 now holds what was at 7. Your favourite is now number 3.

options.text: Your favourite, because a song's number is fixed when you add it
options.why: The number is a position, not a label. Removing songs above it renumbers it.

options.text: Nothing. It raises an error, because number 5 changed.
options.why: Removing items is silent. Position 5 still exists; it just holds a different song.

options.text: The song that used to be number 3
options.why: Wrong direction. Deleting above a position shifts later songs up to fill the gap, so number 5 now holds what was number 7.

title: The Year 00
source: Real incident · 1999–2000 · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — Year 2000 problem
Computerworld — India IT officials relieved as Y2K passes without incident

blurb: Two digits saved memory for decades, and then the calendar ran out of them.

panels.text: In the 1960s, computer memory was expensive enough that every character had to earn its place. So programmers wrote years with two digits. 1965 was stored as 65, and 1999 as 99. The machine put the 19 in front whenever it needed a whole year. It worked for decades.
panels.alt: The number 65 in two boxes, with a faded 19 in front of it that the machine was trusted to supply.

panels.text: A bank works out a customer's age by taking the birth year away from this year. In 1999 that is 99 minus 65: thirty-four. Its reports put accounts in order from oldest to newest by comparing the stored years. Everything lines up, because every year it has ever seen begins with 19.
panels.alt: A sum reading 99 minus 65 equals 34, beside a page of years in order: 65, 71, 88, 99.

panels.text: Now turn the calendar to 1 January 2000. This year is stored as 00. The customer's age comes out as 00 minus 65: minus sixty-five. An account opened that morning goes to the top, ahead of one opened in 1965. Nothing has crashed. The answers are simply, confidently wrong.
panels.alt: A calendar at 1 January 2000, the sum 00 minus 65 equals minus 65 in red, and the page of years with 00 now at the top.

panels.text: Through the late 1990s, programmers around the world went through old code line by line, much of it written in COBOL, and a large share of that work was done by Indian IT firms. They widened years to four digits, or taught the code where a century began. When midnight came, very little broke. That is what a finished fix looks like.
panels.alt: A two-digit year being widened to four digits, from 65 to 1965, with a stamp reading fixed.

bridge.hook: The data never held a year. It held the last two digits of one, and trusted everyone to remember the rest. A date type holds the whole thing.

mapping.story: Writing 1965 as 65
mapping.python: A year kept as the text "65" or the number 65
mapping.detail: The century is not in the data. It lives only in the programmer's head.

mapping.story: Age = this year minus birth year
mapping.detail: Right only when both numbers mean the same thing. 00 − 65 is valid maths and a wrong age.

mapping.story: Putting accounts in order by stored year
mapping.detail: Text compares character by character, so the year 2000 comes first.

mapping.story: Widening years to four digits
mapping.detail: A real date type holds the full year, and compares and subtracts correctly.

bridge.code:
from datetime import date

# the 1960s way: two characters, century assumed
born, today = "65", "00"
print(int(today) - int(born))        # -65, as an age
print(sorted(["99", "00", "65"]))    # ['00', '65', '99']  2000 comes first

# the fixed way: whole dates
born = date(1965, 3, 14)
today = date(2000, 1, 1)
age = today.year - born.year - ((today.month, today.day) < (born.month, born.day))
print(age)                           # 34
print(sorted([date(2000, 1, 1), date(1999, 12, 31)])[0])   # 1999-12-31
bridge.codeNotes: today.year - born.year on its own gets the age wrong for anyone whose birthday has not come round yet this year. The comparison of (month, day) pairs takes one off in that case. Dates are full of edges like this, which is the reason to let "datetime" handle them.
bridge.gotcha: Two-digit years did not die in 2000. They come back whenever a form asks for YY, or a file named 24-03-01 is sorted as text. And text dates sort correctly only in year-month-day order: "2024-03-01" sorts properly, "01-03-2024" does not. Turn text into a "date" as soon as it arrives, and turn it back into text only for display.

quiz.question: In the story, where is the actual defect?

options.text: In the data: the year is stored without its century
options.why: Right. Every later calculation is correct maths on an incomplete value.

options.text: In the age calculation, which subtracts wrongly
options.why: The subtraction is fine. It is handed 00 and 65, and it subtracts them faithfully.

options.text: In the computers, which could not count past 1999
options.why: They could. The storage format kept only two digits, so 2000 and 1900 looked the same.

options.text: In the price of memory
options.why: That is why the shortcut was taken. It is the reason for the defect, not the defect.

quiz.question: Which comparison correctly puts 31 December 1999 before 1 January 2000?

options.why: Yes. Date objects compare as dates, full year included. This is True.
Text compares character by character, and "0" comes before "9". This is False, so 2000 comes first.
Two-digit years as numbers make 2000 the smallest year of all. This is the Y2K bug in one line.
The full year is there, but in the wrong place. Day-first text compares the days first, and "3" > "0" makes this False.

quiz.question: A different situation: a library app stores due dates as day-month text like "05-11", and sends a reminder for every book whose due date is less than today's text. What goes wrong?

options.text: Day-first text compares days before months, so 5 November counts as earlier than 12 October
options.why: Y2K's failure again: the text looks like a date but compares like characters. Converting to date objects fixes it, and fixes the missing year too.

options.text: Nothing, as long as every date is written with the same number of characters
options.why: Equal length helps text sort, but day-first order still compares the days before the months.

options.text: It raises an error, because Python cannot compare dates written as text
options.why: Python compares text happily, character by character. It returns an answer, just the wrong one.

options.text: Only the missing year is a problem, so it breaks on 1 January
options.why: The missing year does break it at New Year, but day-first order breaks it every month, much sooner.

title: The Index That Lost Half Its Value
source: Real incident · Vancouver, 1982–83 · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — Vancouver Stock Exchange (the 1982–83 index error)
Wolfram MathWorld — Roundoff error

blurb: It was never wrong by more than a thousandth. It was wrong the same way, millions of times.

panels.text: In January 1982 the Vancouver Stock Exchange launched a new index: a single number meant to show how its shares were doing overall. It started at 1,000. After every trade, a computer worked the index out again from the new prices.
panels.alt: The number 1000.000 labelled the index, above a row of small tick marks for trades, each one recalculating it.

panels.text: Each result had more decimal places than the exchange kept. It kept three. The computer did not round the rest; it simply cut them off. 1000.4567 became 1000.456. The part it dropped was never as much as a thousandth of a point, and usually far less. Nobody would ever notice one.
panels.alt: The number 1000.4567 with its last digit struck out, and an arrow down to 1000.456, the part kept.

panels.text: But the index was worked out again thousands of times a day, every trading day, for twenty-two months, and every cut went the same way: down. By November 1983 the index stood at 524.811, about half where it began, while the market it measured seemed to be rising.
panels.alt: A line chart from January 1982 to November 1983: the index falling to 524.811 while a dashed line for the market drifts upward.

panels.text: Over one weekend the index was recalculated from the same trades, this time rounding each result to the nearest thousandth. It came back at 1098.892. No trade had earned those 574 points. They had been lost a sliver at a time, and every sliver in the same direction.
panels.alt: The value 524.811 struck through, an arrow to 1098.892, and a stamp reading recalculated.

bridge.hook: Each cut threw away less than a thousandth of a point. The damage came from doing it thousands of times a day, always in the same direction.

mapping.story: Keeping three decimal places
mapping.detail: A stored number almost never holds every digit of the true one. What matters is what happens to the rest.

mapping.story: Cutting the extra digits off
mapping.detail: For positive numbers it always moves the value down. Rounding moves it up or down, so the errors cancel.

mapping.story: Worked out again after every trade
mapping.python: Each calculation starting from the last result
mapping.detail: Every step inherits the previous step's error, so errors accumulate instead of staying small.
Not one big mistake. Millions of tiny ones, all pointing the same way.

bridge.code:
import math, random

def cut(x):                      # what the exchange did
    return math.floor(x * 1000) / 1000

random.seed(1982)
chopped = rounded = 1000.0
for trade in range(600_000):     # roughly 22 months of recalculations
    move = random.gauss(0, 0.02)  # both get exactly the same moves
    chopped = cut(chopped + move)
    rounded = round(rounded + move, 3)

print(round(chopped, 3), round(rounded, 3))   # 688.725 988.59

# and underneath it all, floats are binary approximations
print(0.1 + 0.2)                  # 0.30000000000000004
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)           # False
print(cut(1.005))                 # 1.004  (1.005 * 1000 is 1004.999...)
bridge.codeNotes: Both numbers receive exactly the same 600,000 moves. The only difference is the last step of each update, so the whole gap of about 300 points was made by where the extra digits went.
bridge.gotcha: Floats set a second trap underneath the first. Python stores 0.1 in binary, where it cannot be exact, so 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004 and 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False. The same thing makes cut(1.005) give 1.004: 1.005 * 1000 comes out a hair under 1005, and the floor cuts one thousandth more than you meant. For money, count whole paise as integers or use decimal.Decimal. Compare floats with math.isclose, never ==.

quiz.question: In the story, what corresponds to the rounding rule that caused the damage?

options.text: Cutting off everything after the third decimal place
options.why: Right. It is the one step, repeated every time, that decided where the extra digits went: always down.

options.text: Starting the index at 1,000
options.why: That is only the starting value. The drift would have happened from any starting point.

options.text: The trades on the exchange
options.why: The trades are the input. The broken index and the corrected one used the very same trades.

options.text: The weekend recalculation
options.why: That was the fix: every step done again, rounding instead of cutting.

quiz.question: Which update keeps the index honest over thousands of recalculations?

options.text: index = round(index + move, 3)
options.why: Yes. Rounding sends some results up and some down, so the tiny errors cancel instead of piling up.

options.text: index = math.floor((index + move) * 1000) / 1000
options.why: That is exactly what the exchange did. Every result moves down, and the losses add up.

options.text: index = int(index + move)
options.why: That cuts off every decimal place, not only the fourth. It drifts down far faster.

options.text: index = math.ceil((index + move) * 1000) / 1000
options.why: The same mistake in the other direction. Every result moves up, and the index drifts up instead.

quiz.question: A different situation: a food-delivery app gives 2.5% cashback on every order, with any fraction of a paisa dropped. It handles a million orders a day. What happens to customers' total cashback over a year?

options.text: Customers are paid measurably less than 2.5% in total, because every order loses a fraction of a paisa and none gains one
options.why: Vancouver's shape: a tiny cut, always in the same direction, repeated until it is real money.

options.text: Nothing noticeable, since each order loses less than a paisa
options.why: That is what the exchange assumed. One loss is nothing; a million a day, every day, is not.

options.text: It evens out, because some orders round up
options.why: Dropping the fraction never rounds up. That is the whole difference between cutting and rounding.

options.text: Python raises an error when a paisa is split
options.why: Python computes fractions of a paisa without complaint. The rule you apply afterwards decides who keeps them.

title: Pending
source: Real system · failed UPI payments and the RBI's reversal rule · original account

sources.label: Business Standard — RBI tightens norms, penalties for failed transactions (20 Sep 2019)
Medianama — RBI introduces penalties for failed transactions on UPI and more

blurb: The money left one account and arrived nowhere, until the failure was caught and undone.

panels.text: You pay ₹1,200 to a friend over UPI. The app spins for a long time, then shows a word you did not want: pending. A minute later your bank sends an SMS. ₹1,200 has left your account. Your friend checks their phone. Nothing has arrived.
panels.alt: Your phone showing a 1,200 rupee payment as pending, a bank message saying it was debited, and your friend's phone showing nothing yet.

panels.text: Somewhere between your bank and theirs, the payment stopped halfway. The first step, taking the money out of your account, finished. The second step, putting it into theirs, did not. For now the money is in neither place you can see.
panels.alt: Two bank buildings. The arrow from yours is solid and marked debit done; the line to theirs is broken and crossed, marked credit failed.

panels.text: This half-finished state happens often enough that there is a rule for it. Since October 2019 the Reserve Bank of India has required that when a UPI payment debits you but never reaches the other side, your bank reverses it by the day after. If it is late, the bank pays you ₹100 for every day of delay.
panels.alt: A page headed RBI, from October 2019, listing: debited but never credited, reverse by the next day, and 100 rupees for each day late.

panels.text: The next morning another SMS arrives: ₹1,200 credited back, the reversal of a failed payment. Your balance is whole again. You send the money a second time and it goes through at once. Nothing about the failure was hidden. It was caught, undone, and reported.
panels.alt: Your phone showing a whole balance, a bank message saying 1,200 rupees credited back, and a stamp reading reversed.

bridge.hook: A payment is two steps that must both happen or neither. When the second one fails after the first has finished, something has to catch that and put the first one back.

mapping.story: Taking the money out, then putting it into their account
mapping.detail: The steps that might fail, in the order they run.

mapping.story: The credit to your friend fails halfway
mapping.python: An exception raised after the debit
mapping.detail: Control jumps out of try at that line. The lines after it never run.

mapping.story: Your bank reverses the debit by the next day
mapping.detail: Catching the error is only half of it. The handler has to put things back the way they were.

mapping.story: The SMS that tells you what happened
mapping.python: finally, with else for the success case
mapping.detail: Whatever happened, the customer is told. Silence is how money goes missing.

bridge.codeNotes: The debit sits before the "try" on purpose: it is the step that already succeeded, and the "except" exists to undo it. Read "else" as nothing went wrong, and "finally" as tell the customer either way.
bridge.gotcha: The dangerous version catches the error and does nothing: except CreditFailed: pass. The program carries on happily, and ₹1,200 has left one account and arrived nowhere. The opposite trap is catching too much. A bare except: also swallows your own bugs, such as a mistyped name, and turns them into mysterious reversals nobody can explain.

options.why: Right. It runs only because something failed, and its job is to leave the accounts in a consistent state.

options.text: The credit to your friend's account
options.why: That is the risky step inside try, the one that raised the error.

options.text: The ₹1,200 leaving your account
options.why: That is the first step, which succeeded. The handler exists to undo it.

options.text: Sending the money again the next day
options.why: That is a new payment, a fresh attempt made after the handler had finished.

options.why: Yes. If the credit fails, the handler puts the debit back; if it succeeds, there is nothing to undo.
The error is caught and forgotten. Your money has left and arrived nowhere, and nothing says so.

debit(amount)
credit(amount)

quiz.question: A different situation: a cinema app reserves your seat, then charges your card. If the charge fails, what should the error handler do?

options.text: Release the seat it just reserved, then tell you the payment failed
options.why: The UPI shape: the first step succeeded, the second failed, and the handler undoes the first so nothing is left half-done.

options.text: Keep the seat reserved, since the reservation itself worked
options.why: Then the seat is held for nobody who has paid. A half-finished pair of steps is exactly the state to avoid.

options.text: Retry the charge until it works
options.why: A retry or two can help, but with no limit it can hang, and it never releases the seat if the card is simply declined.

options.text: Hide the error so you are not worried
options.why: Silent handling is how money and seats go missing. Undo what was done, and say what happened.

title: Sixty-Four Present
source: Hypothetical practical case · a college attendance system · original account
blurb: The register counted taps. It should have counted students.

panels.text: Your college moves attendance online. At every lecture, students tap their ID card on a reader beside the door, and every tap is written down. At the end of the day the software counts the taps to see who attended.
panels.alt: A card reader beside a classroom door, a student standing by it, and an ID card held up to the reader.

panels.text: On Monday the maths lecture shows 64 present in a class of 60. Nobody has sneaked in. The reader simply wrote down every tap, and some students tapped twice: once when the card did not seem to register, and once more to be sure. One tapped three times.
panels.alt: An attendance page for Monday's maths lecture showing 60 enrolled and 64 present, beside a column of card taps with the repeats in red.

panels.text: Counting taps answers the wrong question. The register does not need to know how many times a card touched the reader. It needs to know which students were in the room. A student who tapped three times is still one student, present once.
panels.alt: Three taps from the same card, S12, a second apart, joining into a single tick for one student.

panels.text: The fix is to keep each ID once, however many times it arrives. Tap again and nothing changes. Monday's count comes out at 58, the real number, and the two students who were missing are now easy to find: the whole class, minus everyone who tapped.
panels.alt: The attendance page corrected to 58 present, with the two absent students named, and a stamp reading fixed.

bridge.hook: The register kept every tap. What it needed was every student, once. That is the difference between a list and a set.

mapping.story: Every tap written down
mapping.detail: Keeps everything in order, repeats included. len() counts taps, not people.

mapping.story: Each student kept once, however often they tap
mapping.detail: A set holds each value at most once. Adding one that is already there changes nothing.

mapping.story: The real count: 58
mapping.detail: Counting the different values is counting the set.

mapping.story: The whole class, minus everyone who tapped
mapping.detail: Set difference: on the roster, but not in the room.

bridge.code:
roster = set(f"S{n:02}" for n in range(1, 61))       # 60 students, S01 to S60
taps = [f"S{n:02}" for n in range(1, 59)]            # 58 students tapped once...
taps += ["S07", "S12", "S12", "S33", "S41", "S58"]    # ...and some tapped again

print(len(taps))                  # 64, counting taps
present = set(taps)
print(len(present))               # 58, counting students
print(sorted(roster - present))   # ['S59', 'S60']
bridge.codeNotes: set(taps) throws the repeats away and keeps who, not how often. roster - present reads exactly like the sentence in the story: the whole class, minus everyone who tapped.
bridge.gotcha: A set has no order and no positions, so present[0] raises TypeError; sort it when you need to show it. A set also knows only what is exactly equal. "S07", "s07" and "S07 " with a trailing space are three different students to it, so clean the IDs before you add them. And an empty set is set(): {} makes an empty dictionary.

quiz.question: In the register story, what should the set hold?

options.text: Each student ID that tapped, once
options.why: Right. The question is who was there, and a set answers it by keeping each ID once.

options.text: Every tap, in the order it happened
options.why: That is the list the reader already had, and it is exactly what gave 64.

options.text: How many times each student tapped
options.why: That is a tally per student, which is a dictionary. Useful for finding the double-tappers, but it is not the register.

options.text: The students who were absent
options.why: That is what you work out afterwards, roster minus present. The set built from the taps holds who came.

quiz.question: Which expression gives the real number of students present?

options.text: len(set(taps))
options.why: Yes. set() keeps each ID once, and len() counts them.

options.text: len(taps)
options.why: That counts taps. It is the 64.

options.text: taps.count("S12")
options.why: That counts how often one student tapped, 3 for S12 here. It says nothing about the class.

options.text: len({taps})
options.why: Braces around a list do not convert it. This raises TypeError, because a list cannot be put inside a set.

quiz.question: A different situation: a bookshop with two branches merges their customer email lists. It wants to email every customer exactly once, and to find the customers who shop only at the first branch. What fits?

options.text: Make both into sets. The union gives each customer once, and first - second gives the first-branch-only customers.
options.why: The register's shape: repeats collapse, and difference answers who is in one group but not the other.

options.text: Join the two lists with + and email everyone on the result
options.why: Anyone on both lists gets two emails. + keeps repeats, which is the 64-present problem again.

options.text: Sort the combined list
options.why: Sorting puts repeats next to each other, but it does not remove them.

options.text: A dictionary with each branch as a key
options.why: That groups customers by branch, but anyone who shops at both still appears twice.

title: Six Digits
source: Real system · India Post PIN codes · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — Postal Index Number

blurb: The checkout never reads your address. It looks up six digits.

panels.text: Before 1972, a letter in India was sorted by reading its address, and plenty of places shared a name or were spelled five different ways. On 15 August 1972 India Post introduced the PIN code: six digits that say where a letter is going, however the address is written.
panels.alt: An envelope with a handwritten address and six empty boxes marked PIN.

panels.text: The digits are read left to right, from wide to narrow. The first names one of nine regions: eight are parts of the country, and 9 is kept for the Army Postal Service. The second narrows it to a sub-region, the third to a sorting district, and the last three to the post office that delivers.
panels.alt: The digits 560034, split into the region, the sub-region, the sorting district, and the three digits of the delivering post office.

panels.text: Today you meet the same six digits at every online checkout. You type 560034, and the city and state fill themselves in. The shop's system never reads your street address to do it. It takes the six digits you typed and finds what is stored against them.
panels.alt: A checkout form with 560034 typed in, and the city and state filled in and ticked.

panels.text: Type one digit wrong, 560304, and one of two things happens. If that number belongs to some other place, the form fills in a town you have never visited. If no place has that number, the form stops and asks you to check your PIN. It has nothing to fill in with.
panels.alt: A checkout form with 560304 typed in, the city and state left as question marks, and a stamp reading check your PIN.

bridge.hook: A PIN code is a key, and the place it names is the value. The checkout never searches your address; it looks up six digits.

mapping.story: The six-digit PIN
mapping.detail: Exact and unique, and the thing you look up by. Close is not good enough: 560034 and 560043 are different keys.

mapping.story: The city and state it names
mapping.detail: What comes back from the lookup.

mapping.story: Typing a PIN and watching the form fill in
mapping.detail: One step, however many places are stored. Nothing is read through one by one.

mapping.story: No place has that number: check your PIN
mapping.detail: Square brackets raise. .get() returns None, or a default you choose, so the form can ask again.

bridge.code:
pincodes = {
    "560034": ("Bengaluru", "Karnataka"),
    "110001": ("New Delhi", "Delhi"),
    "400001": ("Mumbai", "Maharashtra"),
}

typed = "560034"
city, state = pincodes[typed]
print(city, state)                        # Bengaluru Karnataka

typo = "560304"
print(typo in pincodes)                   # False
print(pincodes.get(typo, "check your PIN"))

# the first digit is its own, smaller lookup
zone = {"1": "North", "5": "South", "9": "Army Postal Service"}
print(zone[typed[0]])                     # South
bridge.codeNotes: pincodes[typed] is the form filling itself in. typed[0] reads only the first digit, the region, and uses it as the key into a second, smaller dictionary.
bridge.gotcha: A key must match exactly, type included. The PIN codes here are stored as text, so pincodes[560034] (the number, with no quotes) raises KeyError even though 560034 is plainly there. A missing key raises KeyError too. A checkout that puts whatever the user typed into square brackets will crash on the first typo. Use "in" or .get() for anything a person typed.

quiz.question: At the checkout, which part is the dictionary's key?

options.text: The six digits you typed
options.why: Right. The lookup is done by it, and it has to match exactly.

options.text: The city and state that fill in
options.why: Those are the value, what comes back once the key is found.

options.text: Your full street address
options.why: The lookup never reads it. That is the whole point of the PIN.

options.text: The number of post offices in India
options.why: That is how many entries there are, len() of the dictionary, not what you look up by.

quiz.question: A user types a PIN that no place has. Which code lets the form ask again instead of crashing?

options.why: Yes. .get() returns None for a missing key, and the form can respond to that.

options.text: place = pincodes[typed]
options.why: Square brackets demand an answer. A missing key raises KeyError and the checkout falls over.

options.text: place = pincodes.get(typed, typed)
options.why: It no longer crashes, but it fills the city field with the digits the user typed. A default should be something the form can recognise as missing.

options.text:
if typed in pincodes.values():
    place = pincodes[typed]
options.why: values() holds the cities and states, not the PINs. This check is never true for a PIN, so the form never fills in.

quiz.question: A different situation: a college stores each student's hostel room, and roll numbers look like "21CS045". The warden wants any student's room in one step. What structure should it be, and what is the key?

options.text: A dictionary with roll numbers as keys and rooms as values
options.why: The PIN's shape: an exact identifier you look up by, and the thing it names.

options.text: A dictionary with rooms as keys and roll numbers as values
options.why: Right structure, wrong direction. The warden starts from the roll number, so that is the key.

options.text: A list of rooms, in roll-number order
options.why: Then the warden has to work out a position from "21CS045", and every new admission shifts the others.

options.text: A dictionary keyed by the student's name
options.why: Names repeat and get spelled different ways. That is exactly the problem the PIN code was invented to escape.

title: 1-Sep
source: Real incident · gene symbols rewritten as dates by spreadsheet software · original account

sources.label: PLOS Computational Biology — Gene name errors: lessons not learned (2021)
Nucleic Acids Research — Genenames.org: the HGNC and VGNC resources in 2021 (the renaming)
Scientific Reports — Gene Updater: a web tool that autocorrects Excel-misidentified gene names (2022)

blurb: Nobody typed 1-Sep. The software decided that was what they meant.

panels.text: A research team finishes a study and publishes the results as a table: one row per gene, the name of the gene in the first column. Months later a reader downloads that table and finds a row named 1-Sep. There is no gene called 1-Sep. Nobody typed it.
panels.alt: A published results table. The first column holds gene names, and one row near the middle reads 1-Sep, circled.

panels.text: Someone had opened the table in a spreadsheet. On the way in, the software looked at each cell and decided what it was. SEPT1 looked like the first of September, so it became the first of September. The change was saved. No warning appeared, because as far as the software was concerned nothing had gone wrong.
panels.alt: One cell drawn twice: SEPT1 as typed on the left, 1-Sep after saving on the right, with a thick arrow between them.

panels.text: This is not rare. In 2021 a group screened more than eleven thousand published papers whose extra files carried gene names. Nearly a third of them held names that had been turned into dates. Five years earlier the same count had been about one in five. Between the two studies the problem had grown.
panels.alt: Two bars side by side: a shorter one marked 2016, one in five, and a taller one marked 2021, nearly one in three.

panels.text: In 2020 the committee that names human genes stopped waiting for the software to be fixed and changed the names instead. Every SEPT gene became a SEPTIN gene. Every MARCH gene became a MARCHF gene. Whole families were rewritten worldwide, so that opening a file could no longer damage them.
panels.alt: Two name plates. SEPT1 struck through with SEPTIN1 beneath it, and MARCH1 struck through with MARCHF1 beneath it.

bridge.hook: The spreadsheet did not store what was typed. It stored what it guessed the typing meant, and the guess could not be undone.

mapping.story: SEPT1, sitting in a cell
mapping.detail: What arrives is characters. Nothing about the characters says what kind of value they were meant to be.

mapping.story: The software deciding it is a date
mapping.python: A conversion applied on the way in
mapping.detail: Something picks a kind for you, and it picks by appearance, one column at a time.

mapping.story: 1-Sep stored in place of SEPT1
mapping.python: The converted value replaces the original
mapping.detail: Once the cell holds a date, the characters that were typed are gone. Converting back gives you the date spelled out, not the name.

mapping.story: Renaming the gene to SEPTIN1
mapping.detail: Two ways out: declare the kind you want, or change the values so there is nothing left to guess at.

bridge.codeNotes: The first pass is the spreadsheet: every cell is inspected and re-made as whatever it resembles. The second pass is what the researchers wanted — characters kept as characters. In pandas the whole difference is one keyword: read_csv(path) guesses a kind per column, read_csv(path, dtype=str) does not guess at all.
bridge.gotcha: Nothing raises an error here, which is what makes it expensive. From the reader's side nothing failed: you asked for a table and you got a table. The same guess strips the leading zero from a mobile number, reads a product code like 1E5 as 100000, and turns a long account number into a rounded one. The rule worth keeping: if a field is an identifier rather than a quantity, say so when you read it, not after.

quiz.question: Which moment in the story is the conversion — the point where the value changes kind?

options.text: The spreadsheet storing 1-Sep in place of SEPT1 when the file is opened
options.why: Right. The characters go in, a date comes out, and the original is overwritten in the same step.

options.text: The researcher typing SEPT1 into the first column
options.why: That is the value before anything touched it. At this point the cell holds exactly what was meant.

options.text: The reader noticing a row named 1-Sep months later
options.why: That is the discovery, not the change. The damage happened when the file was opened and saved.

options.text: The committee renaming SEPT1 to SEPTIN1 in 2020
options.why: That is the fix, applied years afterwards. It removes the resemblance so that no guess can be made.

quiz.question: You are loading that file of gene symbols. Which line keeps every symbol exactly as it was written?

options.text: genes = pd.read_csv("genes.csv", dtype=str)
options.why: Yes. You declare the kind before anything is read, so no column is inspected and no value is remade.

options.text: genes = pd.read_csv("genes.csv")
options.why: This is the default, and the default is to guess a kind per column. It is exactly what produced 1-Sep.

options.text: genes = pd.read_csv("genes.csv").astype(str)
options.why: Too late. The guess already happened while reading; this converts the result of the guess, so you get '1900-09-01' rather than 'SEPT1'.

options.text: genes = pd.read_csv("genes.csv", parse_dates=True)
options.why: This asks for more guessing, not less. It is the same mistake with the volume turned up.

quiz.question: A different situation: you load a spreadsheet of customer records and every mobile number has lost its leading zero. What happened, and what would have prevented it?

options.text: The reader saw digits and made them numbers, and a number has no leading zero. Read that column as text from the start.
options.why: The same shape as the gene symbols. A phone number is an identifier that happens to be written in digits, so it has to be declared, not deduced.

options.text: The numbers were too long for the column and were cut short.
options.why: Nothing was truncated — the zeros were never stored, because the value was kept as a quantity and quantities do not carry leading zeros.

options.text: The file was saved with the wrong character encoding.
options.why: Encoding damage looks like mangled letters and stray symbols. Here every digit that remains is correct; the issue is which kind of value was chosen.

options.text: Nothing was lost. Convert the column back to text after loading and the zeros return.
options.why: They do not return. The zeros were discarded at read time, and converting 9876543210 back to text gives you those ten characters and no more.

title: Safely Remove
source: Real system · write caching on removable drives, and the Windows 10 default change · original account

sources.label: Microsoft Learn — Windows default media removal policy (Quick removal vs Better performance)

blurb: The copy said it had finished. The drive had not heard about it yet.

panels.text: You copy a presentation onto a pen drive with ten minutes to spare. The progress window fills, reaches the end, and closes itself. You pull the drive out of the port and walk down to the hall.
panels.alt: A pen drive drawn clear of a dark machine and its empty port, moving away from it, beside a progress bar filled to the far end.

panels.text: On the machine in the hall the presentation opens, and it is yesterday's. Everything you changed this morning is missing. Nothing warned you. The window that closed had said the copy was done, and from where that window sat, it was.
panels.alt: A slide headed SLIDE 1 whose last line reads YESTERDAY and is flagged, and beside it a slip listing this morning's edits with a MISSING stamp under it.

panels.text: Windows had accepted your edits and kept them in memory. It planned to put them on the drive in one go a moment later, because one large write to a drive costs far less than a hundred small ones. Safely Remove Hardware is the command that finishes those held writes and then says the drive is done. You had not run it.
panels.alt: Three blocks of text stacked inside a box marked MEMORY, a thin dotted arrow from the box to a pen drive, and a thick arrow labelled ON EJECT.

panels.text: From Windows 10 version 1809 the default changed. A removable drive is now set to quick removal: nothing is held back, so the drive can be pulled at any moment. Writes are a little slower. Far fewer presentations are yesterday's.
panels.alt: A settings panel with two choices. Better performance is greyed out; quick removal is ticked and marked default.

bridge.hook: The copy said it was finished. What it meant was that the words had been handed over, not that they had arrived.

mapping.story: The progress window reaching the end
mapping.detail: The call finishes the moment the bytes are accepted. Accepted is not stored.

mapping.story: Windows holding the edits in memory
mapping.detail: Small writes are collected so they can be sent once, because the cost is per trip to the disk, not per byte.

mapping.story: Safely Remove Hardware
mapping.python: close(), or the end of a with block
mapping.detail: This is the step that empties the buffer onto the disk. Until it runs, the disk does not have your work.

mapping.story: Pulling the drive early
mapping.detail: Whatever was still being held is simply gone, and what survives is the last version that was fully written.

bridge.code:
import os

path = "notes.txt"

handle = open(path, "w")
handle.write("slide 1\n")
handle.write("slide 2\n")
print("two writes done, on disk:", os.path.getsize(path), "bytes")   # 0

handle.flush()                      # this is Safely Remove Hardware
print("after flush, on disk:", os.path.getsize(path), "bytes")       # 16
handle.close()

# The same thing with the emptying done for you on the way out of the block.
with open(path, "a") as handle:
    handle.write("slide 3\n")
print("after the with block:", os.path.getsize(path), "bytes")       # 24

os.remove(path)
bridge.codeNotes: The first number is the whole story: two writes have returned, and the disk still holds nothing. flush() is the eject. A "with" block does the same on the way out, which is why it is the habit worth having — you cannot forget a step you never type.
bridge.gotcha: Buffering hides this in small programs. Write a few lines, let the program end, and it works, because the interpreter closes the file as it exits — so you learn the wrong lesson. Then the program is long-running, or it is killed, or the power goes, and the last few thousand lines were never on disk. For records you genuinely cannot lose, flush() is still not the end of it: the operating system keeps a cache of its own, and os.fsync() is what empties that one.

quiz.question: Which moment in the story does close() correspond to?

options.text: Running Safely Remove Hardware before the drive is pulled
options.why: Right. It is the step whose job is to finish the held writes, and after it the drive really holds what you copied.

options.text: The progress window reaching the end and closing
options.why: That is the write returning. It reports that the bytes were accepted, which is the thing the story shows you cannot trust.

options.text: Dragging the presentation onto the drive
options.why: That is the write itself — the data being handed over. Nothing about it says where the data has got to.

options.text: Opening the presentation on the machine in the hall
options.why: That is a read, and it happens afterwards. It is how you discovered the problem, not part of causing it.

quiz.question: Which of these cannot leave the last lines unwritten if the process is killed straight after?

options.text:
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write(text)
options.why: Yes. Leaving the block empties the buffer and closes the file, and it happens even if the code inside raises.

options.text:
f = open(path, "w")
f.write(text)
options.why: Nothing in your code ever closes it. It usually survives because the interpreter tidies up on exit — but a kill or a power cut does not give it that chance.

options.text: open(path, "w").write(text)
options.why: The handle is dropped the instant the line ends, and CPython happens to close it then. That is an implementation detail, not a promise, and it is not true on every interpreter.

options.text:
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.flush()
    f.write(text)
options.why: The flush runs before the write, so it empties an empty buffer. Order matters: you cannot push out something that has not been put in yet.

quiz.question: A different situation: a long-running program appends one line to a log for every order it processes. The server is rebooted, and the last few hundred lines are gone even though the program had reached those orders. Why?

options.text: Those lines were still being held, waiting to be written in one go, and the reboot took them with it. Flush after each line, or each batch, if the log has to survive a crash.
options.why: Same shape as the pen drive. The writes returned, the disk never received them, and nothing unusual had to happen for that to be true.

options.text: Opening the file in append mode overwrites the end of it each time.
options.why: Append mode does the opposite: every write goes after what is already there. That is the one mode that never overwrites.

options.text: The disk was full, so the last writes had nowhere to go.
options.why: A full disk announces itself — the write raises an error rather than going quiet. Here the program had no reason to think anything was wrong.

options.text: The reboot rolled the file back to its last saved version.
options.why: Files have no versions to roll back to. What was on the disk stayed on the disk; what had not reached it was never there to keep.

title: Eleven Lines
source: Real incident · the left-pad unpublishing on npm, March 2016 · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — npm left-pad incident
npm blog — kik, left-pad, and npm (the registry's own account)

blurb: Eleven lines nobody thought about, removed one afternoon in 2016.

panels.text: On 22 March 2016 a developer fell out with the shared registry where programmers publish small pieces of code for anyone to use. He withdrew everything he had published there. One of the pieces was eleven lines long. All it did was add spaces to the front of some text until it reached a given width.
panels.alt: A card of eleven numbered lines on the left; on the right a shelf marked REGISTRY whose middle space is an empty dashed outline, with an arrow running from that gap across to the card.

panels.text: Within minutes, builds were failing around the world. Hardly anyone used those eleven lines on purpose. They used tools that used them: the ones that turn modern code into code older browsers can run, the ones that bundle a site together. The build machines at some very large companies stopped.
panels.alt: Four build machines in a row, each stamped with a red cross, all wired back to one empty slot on a shelf.

panels.text: Nobody had a copy. Each project held the name of the piece it wanted, and fetched it fresh from the registry every time it was built. Naming a thing is not the same as holding it. Once the registry no longer had those eleven lines, every name pointing at them pointed at nothing.
panels.alt: A project card whose entry is a name, with an arrow leading from it to an empty shelf space.

panels.text: About two hours later the registry put the eleven lines back from its own backup — the first time it had ever undone someone's withdrawal. Then it changed the rules. Once a day has passed and anything else depends on what you published, you can no longer take it down.
panels.alt: The card of eleven lines with RESTORED stamped across it, beside a dark-headed note titled NEW RULE giving the condition for withdrawing anything.

bridge.hook: Those projects did not contain the eleven lines. They contained the name of the eleven lines, and went and got them every single time.

mapping.story: Eleven lines someone else wrote and published
mapping.detail: Capability you did not write and do not maintain, doing one small job well enough that writing it again would be silly.

mapping.story: Your project naming the piece it needs
mapping.python: The import line, and the entry in requirements.txt
mapping.detail: The name is the whole of the dependency. None of the code itself lives in your project.

mapping.story: Fetching it from the registry at build time
mapping.python: pip install turning that name into real code
mapping.detail: The name becomes code at install time, on that machine, from a service you do not run.

mapping.story: The name pointing at an empty shelf
mapping.detail: Your own code is exactly as correct as it was yesterday. What changed is what the name resolves to.

bridge.code:
# Capability you did not write, and did not have to fetch: this ships with Python.
import textwrap
from datetime import date

print(textwrap.shorten("the eleven lines everyone depended on", width=24, placeholder="..."))
print(date(2016, 3, 22).strftime("%d %B %Y"))

# left-pad's entire job, built in, where no registry can withdraw it:
print("7".rjust(3, "0"))        # 007

# What a name that resolves to nothing looks like, and how to survive one.
try:
    import leftpad              # not installed here, and never will be
except ImportError:
    leftpad = None
    print("leftpad is not here — falling back")

width = 3
print(leftpad.left_pad("7", width) if leftpad else "7".rjust(width, "0"))
bridge.codeNotes: "textwrap" and "datetime" resolve without anyone's registry being awake — that is what the standard library buys you. "rjust" is left-pad, already in your hands. The last block is the pattern for a name that might not resolve: catch it at the point it fails and decide what to do, rather than letting the whole program die on its first line.
bridge.gotcha: "ModuleNotFoundError" is confusing precisely because nothing you wrote is wrong. Names are resolved when the program starts, against whatever happens to be installed on that machine at that moment — so the same code runs on your laptop and fails on the server. That is why a pinned version in requirements.txt is worth more than it looks, and why the standard library is worth learning first. "rjust" was always there, and nobody can take it away.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the import line?

options.text: A project naming the piece of code it needs, without keeping a copy of it
options.why: Right. The name is the dependency in full — that is why removing what it pointed at broke so much so fast.

options.text: The eleven lines themselves
options.why: Those are the thing being named. The import is the reference to them, and the reference is what every project actually held.

options.text: The registry handing the code over during a build
options.why: That is installation — the step that turns the name into real code on a real machine. It happens because of the import, but it is not the import.

options.text: The build machines failing
options.why: That is the error the missing name produced, several steps later.

quiz.question: Which change would have kept a build working on the afternoon those eleven lines vanished?

options.text: padded = value.rjust(width, "0")
options.why: The job was always available without a dependency. The cheapest dependency to survive is the one you never took.

options.text: leftpad==1.0.0   # pin the version in requirements.txt
options.why: Pinning fixes which version you want, not whether it exists. When the package is withdrawn, the pinned version is withdrawn with it.
This swallows the import error and carries on, so the program dies a few lines later on the name "leftpad" instead. Catching without a fallback just moves the failure.

options.text: import leftpad as lp
options.why: Renaming changes what you call it in your file. It is the same name being resolved against the same registry.

quiz.question: A different situation: your program fetches today's currency rates from a free public web service every time it starts. What is the same risk, and the cheapest way to reduce it?

options.text: You hold the address of the rates, not the rates. If the service is slow, moved or gone, your program cannot start — so keep the last good rates on disk and fall back to them.
options.why: The same shape as the eleven lines: a name resolved at run time against something outside your control, with no copy of your own.

options.text: There is no real risk. Availability is the web service's responsibility, not yours.
options.why: Their outage is your outage. Whoever is at fault, it is your program that will not start.

options.text: Call the service more often, so the rates are always fresh.
options.why: More calls means more chances to be caught by an outage, and it does nothing at all when the service is unreachable.

options.text: Copy the code that calls the service into your own project, so you no longer depend on anything.
options.why: You would be copying the caller, not the rates. The dependency is the service at the other end, and it is untouched by where the calling code lives.

title: Six Minutes
source: Real incident · the GTA Online load-time investigation of February 2021 · original account

sources.label: t0st — How I cut GTA Online loading times by 70% (28 February 2021)

blurb: Seven years of a six-minute load screen, and one core doing all of it.

panels.text: A very popular game took about six minutes to reach its online mode. Players had lived with it for years. In February 2021 one of them decided to find out why. While the screen waited, one processor core sat at full for four minutes, and the disk, the network and the graphics card did nothing at all.
panels.alt: A load screen with a timer reading six minutes, beside a graph of four cores where one is at the top of the scale and three are flat.

panels.text: The four minutes were spent reading one thing: a catalogue of everything a player can buy. Ten megabytes of text, about sixty-three thousand entries. Nothing in it was complicated, and nothing in it was wrong.
panels.alt: A tall stack of printed sheets labelled 10 MB and 63,000 ENTRIES, next to the words four minutes, spent reading it.

panels.text: There were two faults, and the second is the expensive one. Every time an entry was read, the program compared it against every entry it had already stored, to be sure it was not a repeat. The first entry was compared against nothing. The last was compared against sixty-three thousand. Added up, that is nearly two billion comparisons, on a catalogue that contained no repeats at all.
panels.alt: One new entry on the left with arrows fanning out to every entry in a tall stored column, and the number 1,984,531,500 printed beneath.

panels.text: He wrote a fix, explained it in public, and the load time fell from six minutes to one minute fifty — a cut of about seventy per cent. The studio shipped the same change in an official patch and paid him ten thousand dollars.
panels.alt: The same timer now reading one minute fifty, a stamp beside it reading 70% LESS, and a payment slip reading paid to the finder, $10,000.

bridge.hook: Storing one more entry was cheap. Storing one more entry after looking at every entry already stored was not, and it got dearer with every single one.

mapping.story: Going through the sixty-three thousand entries once
mapping.detail: One pass over the catalogue. This part is unavoidable, and on its own it takes no time worth measuring.

mapping.story: Comparing the new entry against everything stored so far
mapping.python: The inner loop, over the results built so far
mapping.detail: A second pass, run once for every step of the first. The two do not add — they multiply.

mapping.story: Nearly two billion comparisons
mapping.python: About n × n / 2 work, with n = 63,000
mapping.detail: Double the catalogue and the cost does not double, it quadruples. That is the shape to recognise.

mapping.story: A catalogue that had no repeats in it anyway
mapping.python: A set, where the check costs the same at any size
mapping.detail: The inner pass vanishes: membership is answered by how the container is built, not by searching it.

bridge.code:
import time

items = [f"item-{n}" for n in range(6000)]      # the real catalogue held 63,000

def load(rows, fast):
    kept, seen = [], set()
    for row in rows:                             # one pass over the catalogue
        known = row in seen if fast else row in kept
        if not known:                            # row in kept is a pass inside the pass
            seen.add(row)
            kept.append(row)
    return kept

for fast in (False, True):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    load(items, fast)
    print("set     " if fast else "scanning", f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

n = 63000
print("comparisons the scanning version makes:", (n * n + n) // 2)
bridge.codeNotes: The inner pass is hiding inside row in kept. It reads as one small operation and it is a walk over everything kept so far — which is why the cost climbs as the run goes on. Only the container changes between the two versions. The amount of code is the same; the shape of the work is not.
bridge.gotcha: Nested loops are not slow. Nested loops over the same growing collection are. The tell is a membership test against a list inside a loop over that list, because "in" on a list is itself a loop you did not write and cannot see. On ten items you will never notice; on sixty-three thousand it is four minutes of one core at full. The moment the question is "have I seen this one before", reach for a set or a dict.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is the inner loop?

options.text: Comparing each entry that has just been read against every entry already stored
options.why: Right. It runs in full once per entry of the outer pass, and it grows as the outer pass goes on, which is where the two billion comes from.

options.text: Reading the sixty-three thousand entries once, start to finish
options.why: That is the outer loop. One pass over sixty-three thousand entries is quick — it is what happens inside it that cost four minutes.

options.text: Measuring the length of the remaining text at every step
options.why: That was the first of the two faults and a real cost, but it is a separate problem. It is not a pass over the entries already stored.

options.text: The six-minute wait on the load screen
options.why: That is what the player saw — the result, not the structure that produced it.

quiz.question: The check is if row not in kept: where "kept" is a list. Which replacement actually removes the second pass?

options.text:
seen = set()
...
if row not in seen:
    seen.add(row)
options.why: Yes. A set answers membership by where the value would live, so the check costs about the same whether it holds ten entries or sixty-three thousand.

options.text: if kept.count(row) == 0:
options.why: The same walk with a different name — and slightly worse, because "count" cannot stop at the first match and always reads to the end.

options.text: if row not in tuple(kept):
options.why: This adds work rather than removing it: a fresh copy of everything kept so far is built on every entry, and then walked anyway.

options.text:
kept.sort()
if row not in kept:
options.why: Sorting does not change how "in" searches a list — it still walks it — and sorting on every entry is far more expensive than the check ever was.

quiz.question: A different situation: you have ten thousand order IDs exported from one system and ten thousand from another, and you need the IDs that appear in both. Which approach stays fast as those numbers grow?

options.text: Put one side into a set, then go through the other side once, checking membership as you go
options.why: One pass, with a check that does not depend on size. This is the same fix as the catalogue, in a different setting.

options.text: For each ID on the first side, go through the second side until you find it
options.why: This is exactly the pattern that cost four minutes: a pass inside a pass. Ten thousand against ten thousand is a hundred million comparisons.

options.text: Sort the second side, then for each ID on the first side scan it from the beginning
options.why: Sorting is wasted here, because the scan still starts at the front every time. The work is unchanged and you have paid for the sort as well.

options.text: Nothing needs changing — ten thousand is a tiny number for a computer
options.why: Ten thousand is tiny; ten thousand times ten thousand is not. The size that matters is the product, and that is the habit this story is trying to build.

title: Say It Back
source: Real incident · the OpenSSL heartbeat defect disclosed 7 April 2014 · original account

sources.label: heartbleed.com — the disclosure page (affected versions, what could be read)
CISA — OpenSSL 'Heartbleed' vulnerability alert, 8 April 2014

blurb: The request said how much to send back, and the server took its word for it.

panels.text: A secure connection keeps itself alive with a small exchange. One side sends a short message and asks the other to say it back. If the words come back, the connection is still there and still working. Millions of machines did this quietly, all day, for years.
panels.alt: Two machines joined by a line, a small envelope travelling one way and an identical envelope coming back.

panels.text: The request carried two things: the message, and a number stating how long that message was. The machine answering it copied out as many characters as the number asked for and sent them back. It never compared the number against the message that had actually arrived.
panels.alt: A request slip with two fields. The message field reads HELLO; the length field reads 64000 and is circled.

panels.text: So a request could carry one character and state a length of sixty-four thousand. The machine sent back the one character, and then whatever else happened to be lying beside it in memory: other people's details, the contents of recent conversations, the secrets that made the connection private to begin with. Nothing was forced. It was asked, and it answered.
panels.alt: A long strip of memory. HELLO sits at the front, followed by rows of other people's details, with a bracket marked 64 KB reaching across all of them.

panels.text: The defect was made public on 7 April 2014 and corrected the same day. The correction was one comparison: measure what arrived, compare it with what was claimed, and refuse the request if the two disagree. Two years' worth of servers had to be updated, and their secrets replaced, because there was no way to tell who had already asked.
panels.alt: A note headed PATCH dated 7 April 2014 listing the change, and beside it the length field with an arrow down into a box reading equals len(received), and REFUSED below that.

bridge.hook: The request said how much to send back, and the machine believed it — while the thing being described was sitting right there, unmeasured.

mapping.story: The short message the caller sends
mapping.detail: The obvious input. This is the part everyone remembers to think about.

mapping.story: The number stating how long it is
mapping.python: A length or a count supplied by the caller
mapping.detail: Also input. It came in the same request from the same stranger and deserves exactly the same suspicion.

mapping.story: Copying out that many characters
mapping.python: Reading or slicing with a caller-supplied size
mapping.detail: The claim is used as an instruction before anything confirms it describes the data it came with.

mapping.story: The comparison added by the fix
mapping.detail: Validation is not checking that a value looks reasonable. It is checking it against what you actually hold.

bridge.codeNotes: "echo_trusting" is not badly written. It is short, it is clear, and it does exactly what it says. The defect is the thing it does not do. "echo_checked" differs by one comparison, placed before the number is used for anything at all — which is the only place a check is worth putting.
bridge.gotcha: The dangerous inputs are the ones that do not look like inputs. A length, a count, an offset, a page size, a record ID, a filename — each one gets used to decide how much to read or where to look, and each is as untrusted as the text sitting next to it. And a bound is not a validation: if n > 1000: reject still lets a five-character message ask for nine hundred. Check against what you hold — if n != len(data) — not against what sounds sensible.

quiz.question: Which piece of the request was the input nobody validated?

options.text: The number stating how long the message was
options.why: Right. It was supplied by the caller and used to decide how much memory to copy, and it was never tested against the message it claimed to describe.

options.text: The short message itself
options.why: The message was used as it arrived and caused no harm. It is the honest half of the request — which is why the other half went unexamined for so long.

options.text: The memory lying next to the message
options.why: That is what leaked, not what came in. It was never input at all; it was the machine's own working memory.

options.text: The release that carried the correction
options.why: That is the fix. It added the check whose absence is the answer to this question.

quiz.question: You are writing the echo yourself. Which line would have prevented this?

options.text:
if claimed_length != len(payload):
    raise ValueError("length does not match the payload")
options.why: Yes. It compares the claim against the thing it describes, which is the only comparison that can catch a claim that is simply untrue.

options.text:
if claimed_length > 65536:
    raise ValueError("too long")
options.why: An upper bound, not a validation. A five-character message asking for sixty-four thousand passes this happily, and sixty-four thousand is the whole problem.

options.text: claimed_length = min(claimed_length, 65536)
options.why: This quietly caps a bad request instead of refusing it. The caller still gets back far more than they sent, and now nothing is even logged.

options.text: payload = payload[:claimed_length]
options.why: Slicing past the end is harmless in Python, so this looks safe — but it silently hands back less than was asked for and never tells anyone the request was wrong. It checks nothing.

quiz.question: A different situation: an endpoint takes a page number and a page size from the URL and returns that many records. Which check belongs there?

options.text: Reject a size outside the range you decided on, and take the slice from the records you actually have rather than from the number alone
options.why: Both halves of the Heartbleed lesson: refuse what you did not agree to, and measure against what you hold instead of what you were told.

options.text: None — the values come from your own front end, which only ever sends sensible ones
options.why: Anyone can type a URL. What your front end sends is what you hope for; what arrives at the endpoint is what you must handle.

options.text: Confirm that both values are whole numbers, then use them
options.why: Checking the kind of a value is not checking its size. A page size of 5,000,000 is a perfectly good whole number.

options.text: Cap the page size at a large round figure such as 100000
options.why: A loose cap is the same mistake with a bigger ceiling. It permits a request nobody would ever legitimately make, which is what a limit is supposed to stop.

source: Real system · how file names are put in order, and what natural sort changed · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — Natural sort order
Microsoft Learn — StrCmpLogicalW: digits considered as numerical content rather than text (Windows XP and later)

blurb: Everything in order, and none of it in the order you meant.

panels.text: You photograph twenty pages of a document and save them one by one: page1, page2, page3, and on to page20. Every page is there. You open the folder to check them before sending them on.
panels.alt: Twenty small boxes in a tidy grid of four columns, labelled page1 through page20 in sequence.

panels.text: What you see is page1, page10, page11, page12, and so on to page19, then page2, page20, page3. Nothing is missing and nothing is damaged. The folder is in order. It is simply not the order you had in mind.
panels.alt: A folder listing reading page1, page10, page11, page12, page2, page20, page3, with the jump from page1 to page10 marked.

panels.text: Names are compared one character at a time, left to right, and the comparison stops at the first place they differ. Put page2 beside page10: p matches p, a matches a, g and e match — then 2 meets 1. One comes before two, so page10 is placed first. Nothing in that comparison ever learns that 10 means ten.
panels.alt: The names page2 and page10 drawn one above the other as boxed characters that line up in columns. The p, a, g and e columns are joined by equals signs; the column holding 2 above 1 is outlined in the accent colour and marked with a cross.

panels.text: Since Windows XP the file browser has treated a run of digits as one number, which is why a folder usually looks right today. Nothing about the saved names changed. What changed is what the comparison was told to look at.
panels.alt: The same folder shown twice side by side: plain order on the left, number order on the right, with identical file names in both.

bridge.hook: Nothing was out of order. It was in the order you get when you compare writing instead of numbers.

mapping.story: The name written on each file
mapping.detail: What gets compared is the characters, because characters are all a name is.

mapping.story: Comparing left to right, stopping at the first difference
mapping.detail: Position by position. The first position that differs settles it, and nothing after that position is even read.

mapping.story: page10 landing before page2
mapping.detail: '1' comes before '2' in character order, and that is the first difference there is to find.

mapping.story: The browser reading a run of digits as one number
mapping.detail: The values are untouched. You change what the comparison is handed, not what you are sorting.

bridge.code:
import re

names = ["page1", "page10", "page11", "page2", "page20", "page3"]

print(sorted(names))                 # page1, page10, page11, page2, page20, page3
print('"10" < "2" is', "10" < "2")   # True — the first character settles it

def by_number(name):
    digits = re.search(r"\d+", name)
    return (name[:digits.start()], int(digits.group()))

print(sorted(names, key=by_number))  # page1, page2, page3, page10, page11, page20

# Same idea wherever numbers arrive written down:
print(sorted(["9", "10", "2"]))
print(sorted(["9", "10", "2"], key=int))
bridge.codeNotes: "sorted" has no idea what your names mean; it compares what it is handed. key= is where you say what to hand it — the number inside the name rather than the name itself. The key here returns a pair, so the text before the digits is compared first and the number only breaks the tie. That keeps "chap2" and "page2" in their own groups instead of interleaving them.
bridge.gotcha: This bites hardest with numbers that arrive written down — a column read from a spreadsheet, a value out of a form, an ID out of a URL — where 9 and 10 are characters rather than quantities. The sort looks like it worked, because it did work: it sorted, correctly, by the thing you gave it. Mixed kinds are the kinder case, because sorted([2, "10"]) raises a TypeError and tells you.
