The silent wrong order is the one that reaches the printer.

quiz.question: Which step is the comparison that decides page10 comes before page2?

options.text: Reaching the fifth character of each name, finding 1 against 2, and stopping there
options.why: Right. The first differing position decides the whole comparison, and everything after it — including the 0 that makes ten ten — is never looked at.

options.text: Saving the files as page1 up to page20
options.why: That is the setup. Those names are perfectly good; the ordering is imposed later, by whatever reads them.

options.text: Opening the folder to check the pages
options.why: That is when you saw the result. The order was already decided before anything appeared on screen.

options.text: page10 having more characters in it than page2
options.why: A reasonable guess, and not what happens — length is only consulted when one name runs out first. Here the two differ at the fifth character, long before length matters.

quiz.question: "names" holds page1 through page20. Which line puts them in the order you meant?

options.text: ordered = sorted(names, key=lambda n: int(n.removeprefix("page")))
options.why: Yes. Each name is handed over as the number inside it, so the comparison is between 2 and 10 rather than between '2' and '1'.

options.text: ordered = sorted(names)
options.why: This is the order in the story. It compares the names as written, character by character, and that is what puts page10 second.

options.text: ordered = sorted(names, key=str)
options.why: "str" of something that is already text hands back the very same text, so this is the plain sort with an extra step.

options.text: ordered = names.sort(key=int)
options.why: Two faults: .sort() rearranges the names in place and returns None, so "ordered" is None — and int("page1") cannot work anyway, because the name is not all digits.

quiz.question: A different situation: exam roll numbers come out of an export as text, and the ranking sheet built from them puts roll 10 above roll 9. What fixes it?

options.text: Sort with a key that reads each roll number as a number
options.why: Same fix, different setting: leave the values alone and change what the comparison is given.

options.text: Re-export the file — text that sorts wrongly means the export was corrupted
options.why: The export is fine. Every character in it is correct, and a fresh copy will sort exactly the same way.

options.text: Convert the whole column to numbers after sorting it
options.why: The order is already fixed by then. Converting afterwards gives you correct numbers in the wrong sequence.

options.text: Sort with reverse=True and read the sheet from the bottom
options.why: Reversing a wrong order gives a different wrong order. Roll 10 still sits next to roll 1, because the comparison has not changed.

title: Still Running
source: Real incident · Ariane 5 Flight 501, 4 June 1996 · original account

sources.label: ESA — Ariane 501: presentation of the Inquiry Board report
Wikipedia — Ariane flight V88

blurb: Working equipment, moved to a faster rocket, still doing a job it no longer had.

panels.text: On 4 June 1996 a new rocket lifted off for the first time. Thirty seconds later it turned hard off its path, broke apart and destroyed itself about three and a half kilometres up. Nobody was aboard. The flight and its cargo were worth more than three hundred and seventy million dollars.
panels.alt: A rocket's climb drawn as a solid curve that turns into a dashed line veering away and ending in a burst, marked at thirty seconds and at 3,700 metres.

panels.text: The guidance unit was not new. It had been taken unchanged from the previous rocket in the family, where it had worked for years. One part of it lined the unit up with the ground before launch. That part had no job at all once the rocket left the pad, and it was left running for about forty seconds into the flight, because the older rocket had asked for that.
panels.alt: Two rockets side by side, the older one narrow and the newer one broader, with the same small guidance box drawn in each and an arrow copying it from left to right.

panels.text: The new rocket climbed sideways far faster than the old one ever had. A measure of that sideways motion grew larger than anything the older flights produced, and the software moved it into a space too small to hold it. Only four of the seven such measures had been guarded against this; guarding all seven had been judged too slow for the computer.
panels.alt: A wide number being pushed into a narrow slot with its left-hand digits spilling past the edge, and a row of seven boxes below of which four are ticked.

panels.text: Both units were the same equipment reading the same motion, so both stopped within moments of each other. The one in charge handed the main computer a fault report. The computer had no way to tell that from ordinary flight readings, took it as one, and swung the engine nozzles hard over. The airflow tore the rocket apart.
panels.alt: Two identical guidance boxes both stamped STOPPED, a fault report passing from one into a box marked FLIGHT READINGS, and engine nozzles below swung fully to one side.

bridge.hook: The part that failed was correct. It had been correct for years — on a rocket that never went that fast sideways.

mapping.story: The alignment code, taken unchanged from the older rocket
mapping.detail: Working code, moved to a new caller. Moving it re-checks none of what it quietly assumed.

mapping.story: The sideways speed it was handed
mapping.python: The argument at the new call site
mapping.detail: A new caller brings a new range of values, and the old range was never written down anywhere.

mapping.story: A number too large for the space it was put in
mapping.python: The unguarded operation inside the function
mapping.detail: The failure happens deep inside, far from the call that caused it, which is why it is hard to see coming.

mapping.story: Four of the seven guarded, three not
mapping.python: Partial validation, traded away for speed
mapping.detail: A deliberate decision, sound under the old assumptions, and never revisited when the assumptions changed.

bridge.codeNotes: "to_slot" is not wrong. It is right for one range of inputs, and that range lived in the heads of the people who wrote it rather than anywhere in the code. Reuse carries the function and leaves the assumption behind. The "raise" is the guard the real value did not have — four of seven had one.
bridge.gotcha: The dangerous sentence is "it already works." A function carries the assumptions of the caller it was written for, and copying it into a new project copies none of them. Write the precondition down — as a check, a docstring line, a test — because the caller you have not met yet will not guess it. And note the second half: stopping the whole unit was itself a choice. For a routine that by then had no job left to do, carrying on without it would have been the safer answer.

quiz.question: Which moment is the call with an argument outside the range the code was written for?

options.text: The alignment code being handed the new rocket's sideways speed
options.why: Right. The code is unchanged and the caller is new, and it is the value arriving from that new caller that it cannot handle.

options.text: The alignment code being copied across from the older rocket
options.why: That is the reuse — the setup that made the failure possible. On its own it breaks nothing, and it is why this looked safe.

options.text: Both units stopping within moments of each other
options.why: That is the consequence. It is also why the redundancy did not help: identical units given identical values fail identically.

options.text: The nozzles swinging hard over
options.why: Two steps further downstream, after a fault report had already been mistaken for a flight reading.

quiz.question: Which change removes the fault rather than moving it somewhere else?

options.text:
if not lifted_off:
    align()
options.why: The routine had no job after lift-off. Not calling it at all removes the failure completely — and this is what the inquiry pointed at first.
The unit survives, and its alignment output is now meaningless with nothing saying so. A silent wrong answer from a guidance system is worse than a loud stop.

options.text: bias = min(bias, MAX)
options.why: Now the number fits and is wrong. Guidance would act confidently on a value that was capped rather than measured.

options.text: bias = float(bias)
options.why: It was already a wide number. The problem is the narrow space it gets written into, and this does nothing about that.

quiz.question: A different situation: you lift a date-parsing helper out of an old project and drop it into a new one. It ran without complaint for five years. What should you establish first?

options.text: Which inputs the old project actually gave it, whether the new one stays inside that range, and then a check that says so out loud
options.why: Exactly the Ariane lesson. Five years of success documents the old caller, not the helper, and the assumption has to travel with the code.

options.text: Nothing — five years in production is strong evidence it has no bugs
options.why: It is evidence about the inputs it was given, not about the ones it is going to get. That is precisely the reasoning that lost the rocket.

options.text: Whether it is fast enough for the new project's load
options.why: Worth knowing, and not the risk here. A helper that is quick and quietly wrong is the more expensive outcome.

options.text: Whether the new project runs the same version of Python
options.why: A reasonable compatibility check that says nothing about the values the helper will be handed.

title: Amend
source: Real system · how Git names and stores a commit · original account

sources.label: Pro Git — Git Internals: Git Objects (content-addressed storage)
git-commit documentation — what --amend actually does

blurb: You cannot correct a commit. You can only make another one and move the label.

panels.text: Git records your work as a run of commits. Each one is given a name: a long stretch of letters and digits worked out from the thing itself — the files it holds, who wrote them, when, and the note attached. Nobody picks that name. It is a summary of the contents.
panels.alt: A box of files with a long name printed beneath it, and an arrow showing the name being worked out from the contents of the box.

panels.text: So you cannot correct one. You spot a typo in the note a minute after saving it, and there is nothing there to edit: any change to the contents produces a different summary, and a different summary is a different commit. The one you made is the one you made.
panels.alt: The same box with one letter of its note altered, and a completely different name printed beneath it, the two long names shown side by side and unalike.

panels.text: What Git's amend option does is build a second commit, holding your corrected note, and move the branch marker across to point at that one instead. The first commit is not altered. It is not removed either. It simply has nothing pointing at it any more.
panels.alt: Two boxes side by side, each under a long name. A marker reading main sits over the second; a faint dashed stub above the first shows where it used to sit, with an arrow running between them.

panels.text: And it is still there. Git keeps a record of where the branch has been, so the old name still finds it, right up until the housekeeping that clears away unreachable work eventually runs. Nothing was edited. Something new was made, and the marker moved.
panels.alt: The first box still drawn with no branch pointing at it, beside a panel headed REFLOG showing its long name on the second row.

bridge.hook: There is no way to change a commit, because its name is worked out from its contents. Change anything at all and what you have is a different one.

mapping.story: A commit's name, computed from what it holds
mapping.python: A value whose identity is its contents
mapping.detail: Two tuples holding the same items are the same value. Change an item and it is a different value, not a changed one.

mapping.story: Wanting to fix the note in place
mapping.python: Reaching for an operation that does not exist
mapping.detail: There is no assignment into a tuple and no method that edits text. The thing you want is simply not offered.

mapping.story: Amend building a second commit
mapping.detail: Every operation that looks like a change hands back something new and leaves the original alone.

mapping.story: The branch marker moving across
mapping.detail: What changed is which value the name refers to. The old value did not move and did not alter.

bridge.code:
note = "inital commit"

fixed = note.replace("inital", "initial")   # hands back a new value
print(note)    # 'inital commit'  — untouched
print(fixed)   # 'initial commit'

commit = ("a1b2c3", "inital commit", 1)
try:
    commit[1] = "initial commit"
except TypeError as problem:
    print("refused:", problem)

# An amend: new contents, so a new name, and the first one is still whole.
amended = ("d4e5f6", "initial commit", commit[2])
print(commit)
print(amended)

reflog = {"HEAD": amended, "HEAD@{1}": commit}   # both still reachable
print(sorted(reflog))
bridge.codeNotes: Read note.replace(...) as the amend: a corrected version is handed back, and the original is still sitting in "note", unharmed. The tuple shows the refusal outright — there is no way to write into it. "reflog" is the last panel: the old value has no branch pointing at it and is still perfectly reachable by name.
bridge.gotcha: The trap is expecting s.replace(...) or s.upper() to change "s". They do not — and they do not complain either. The new value is simply thrown away unless you catch it, so s.upper() alone on a line is a no-op and one of the most common pieces of dead code beginners write. Compare a list, which really does change in place: items.append(x) returns None precisely because the work is already done.

quiz.question: Which part of the story is a tuple refusing to be changed?

options.text: There being nothing to edit on a commit you have already made
options.why: Right. The operation does not exist, and it does not exist for the same reason: what the thing is called is what the thing contains.

options.text: The amend option building a second commit
options.why: That is the way around the refusal, not the refusal. It matches t + (x,) — a new value handed back.

options.text: The branch marker moving to the new commit
options.why: That is rebinding a name. It changes which commit the branch refers to and changes neither commit.

options.text: The old commit still being findable afterwards
options.why: That is the original surviving untouched — the consequence of immutability rather than the refusal itself.

quiz.question: "note" holds "inital commit". Which line actually leaves "note" holding the corrected text?

options.text: note = note.replace("inital", "initial")
options.why: Yes. The method hands back a new value and the assignment points "note" at it — the amend and the branch move, in one line.

options.text: note.replace("inital", "initial")
options.why: The corrected value is built and then dropped on the floor, because nothing catches it. No error, no change, no warning.

options.text: note[0] = "I"
options.why: Text does not accept assignment into it. This raises a TypeError — the same refusal the tuple gives.

options.text: note.append("!")
options.why: There is no such method here. "append" belongs to things that can be changed in place, which is exactly what this is not.

quiz.question: A different situation: one settings object is handed to a dozen parts of a program, and you want to be certain none of them quietly alters it. What do you reach for?

options.text: Hold it as a tuple or a frozen mapping, so an attempt to change it fails loudly instead of succeeding quietly
options.why: The commit's property, chosen deliberately: make the change impossible rather than merely discouraged, and the mistake announces itself at the point it is made.

options.text: Hand out a fresh copy each time, so the original is safe
options.why: The original is safe and the mistake is now hidden. A caller that edits its copy believes it has changed the settings, and nothing tells it otherwise.

options.text: Write a comment telling other developers not to modify it
options.why: A comment is a request. The reason a commit cannot be edited is not that Git asks nicely.

options.text: Name it in capitals, by convention
options.why: A convention communicates intent and enforces nothing. SETTINGS["retries"] = 5 works exactly as well as it would in lower case.

title: Where the Moon Will Be
source: Real system · the Nautical Almanac, first published 1766 for the year 1767 · original account

sources.label: US Naval Observatory — History of The Nautical Almanac
Wikipedia — Nautical almanac

blurb: Hours of arithmetic, done on land in 1766, so that nobody had to do it at sea.

panels.text: For centuries a ship could work out how far north it was from a single measurement of the sun. How far east or west was guesswork: speed, heading, and hope. Get that wrong and you meet a coast you believed was fifty miles off.
panels.alt: A ship on open water with a firm vertical line drawn through it labelled NORTH-SOUTH: KNOWN, and a dashed horizontal line across it labelled EAST-WEST with a question mark.

panels.text: A method was known. Measure the gap between the moon and a chosen star, and that gap tells you the time back in Greenwich; the difference from your own local noon gives you your longitude. But knowing where the moon ought to be takes hours of arithmetic, and hours of arithmetic are not available on a pitching deck.
panels.alt: A plain figure standing on a steeply tilted deck, and beside them a ruled page headed HOURS OF IT holding several lines of trigonometry.

panels.text: So in 1766 the Astronomer Royal had it done in advance. A team of people — sitting at desks, on land, with time — worked out the positions for every day of the coming year, and the results were printed and bound. The book went to sea. Aboard, the navigator finds the day, reads two numbers, and fills in the gap between them. Minutes, not hours.
panels.alt: On land, a row of desks with plain figures working through sums, feeding into a bound book, and an arrow carrying that book out to a waiting ship.

panels.text: It has come out every year since. From 1832 a dedicated office in Britain took charge of it, and since 1958 it has been produced jointly with the United States. The hard part is still done once, well before anybody needs it, by people who never go to sea.
panels.alt: A shelf of seven identical bound volumes standing side by side, the first marked 1767 and the last marked TODAY.

bridge.hook: Nobody aboard worked out where the moon would be. That had been settled years earlier, on land, by people who had the time to do it.

mapping.story: The moon's position, needed in the middle of a voyage
mapping.python: An expensive result you need at run time
mapping.detail: The answer is the same whenever you compute it. The only question is when you pay for it.

mapping.story: Doing the arithmetic on deck, every sighting
mapping.python: Computing it inside the loop, on every call
mapping.detail: The same sum repeated by everyone who needs it, at the moment least able to afford it.

mapping.story: Working out the whole year in advance, ashore
mapping.python: Building the table once, before the work begins
mapping.detail: Paid once, by one party, at a time when the cost does not matter.

mapping.story: Finding the day and reading two numbers
mapping.python: A dict lookup into the precomputed table
mapping.detail: What was hours becomes a read, and the cost stops depending on how hard the sum was.

bridge.code:
import time

def hard_way(day):          # stands in for hours of arithmetic; same answer every time
    total = 0
    for i in range(2000):
        total = (total + day * i) % 999983
    return total

SIGHTINGS = 2000

start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(SIGHTINGS):
    hard_way(97)
print("worked out on deck: ", f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

start = time.perf_counter()
almanac = {day: hard_way(day) for day in range(1, 366)}   # printed once, ashore
build = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(SIGHTINGS):
    almanac[97]
print("printed, then read:  ", f"{build:.3f}s to build +", f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.6f}s to use")
bridge.codeNotes: There are two costs here, not one. The table costs something to build, and after that every use is a read. The Almanac is worth printing because thousands of ships each take thousands of sightings, so the one build is divided among all of them. If a single ship had ever sailed, the arithmetic on deck would have been the cheaper answer.
bridge.gotcha: Precomputing is not free and is not always right. You pay memory for the table, you pay the build cost up front, and — the one that actually bites — you pay every time the real answer changes underneath you, because a stale table is confidently wrong. The Almanac gets away with it because the moon's position for 1767 will never need revising. A cached exchange rate has no such protection. Ask how often the answer changes before you decide to store it.

quiz.question: Which step in the story is the precomputation?

options.text: Working out every day of the coming year, ashore, before the book is printed
options.why: Right. The expensive work happens once, away from the place and moment where the answer is needed.

options.text: The navigator finding the day and reading two numbers off the page
options.why: That is the lookup — the cheap half that precomputing buys you. It is the payoff, not the investment.

options.text: Measuring the gap between the moon and a star through a sextant
options.why: That is the measurement the navigator must take whatever happens. No amount of precomputing can do it for them.

options.text: The book being reprinted every year since 1767
options.why: That is distribution, and it is why the build cost is worth paying — but the computing is what happens before the press runs.

quiz.question: A function is called thousands of times with a handful of repeated inputs, and always returns the same answer for the same input. Which change gives you the almanac's shape?

options.why: Each input is computed once and kept; every call after the first is a read. The table builds itself as it is needed, which is the same trade.

options.text:
answer = hard_way(day)
print(answer)
options.why: This reuses the result within one pass and nothing across passes. The next call for the same day pays the full cost again.
A table with one row in it. It helps only while the same day repeats back to back, and collapses the moment the days alternate.

options.text: Rewrite the body so the arithmetic runs twice as fast
options.why: Worth having, and a different thing. Halving a cost you pay thousands of times over is still paying it thousands of times over.

quiz.question: A different situation: a report page runs the same twelve database queries on every visit, and the underlying figures are updated once a night. What is the almanac here?

options.text: Run the twelve queries once after each nightly update, store the results, and have every visit read the stored copy
options.why: The build is tied to the rate the answer actually changes, and every reader afterwards pays only a read. That is the Almanac exactly.

options.text: Keep running them on every visit, because the figures might have changed
options.why: They change once a night, not once a visit. This pays the full cost thousands of times to catch a change that happens once.

options.text: Run them on the first visit and keep those results from then on
options.why: You have built the table and never reprinted it. By the second morning the page is showing yesterday's figures with complete confidence.

options.text: Tune the twelve queries until the page is fast enough
options.why: Useful, and it leaves the shape alone. Every visit still redoes work whose answer nobody expects to have changed.

title: How Big Is This Folder
source: Real system · how a folder's size is worked out, and why the number climbs · original account

sources.label: GNU coreutils manual — du: summarise usage, recursively for directories
POSIX specification — du utility

blurb: The number climbs for several seconds. Nothing is wrong — it cannot answer until it has been everywhere.

panels.text: You ask a folder how big it is. A window opens and the number starts climbing: forty megabytes, three hundred, nine hundred. It keeps going for several seconds before it settles. Nothing is broken. It cannot give you an answer until it has been everywhere.
panels.alt: A properties window listing type, a count of 12,404 files and a size of 912 MB, with three dots beside the size where the number is still climbing.

panels.text: The folder itself holds almost nothing. What it holds is names, and some of those names are files while others are more folders. To answer you have to add up the files. To add up the files inside one of those other folders, you have to ask that folder exactly the same question.
panels.alt: A single folder opened out to show what it contains: three file icons and two more folder icons.

panels.text: So the question asks itself, of smaller and smaller pieces. Photos contains 2024, which contains March, which contains forty files. A file answers immediately, because it knows its own size. A folder cannot, so it passes the question down. When the files at the bottom answer, the totals add up on the way back.
panels.alt: A tree drawn downward from Photos to 2024 to March to a row of files, with arrows pointing down labelled as the question and numbers travelling back up.

panels.text: It finishes because there is a bottom. A file contains nothing, so nothing further is asked, and every folder is smaller than the one holding it. Remove the bottom — a shortcut inside March pointing back at Photos — and the walk goes round and round and the number never settles.
panels.alt: The same tree with one extra arrow running from the bottom folder back up to Photos, drawn in the accent colour and marked with a warning.

bridge.hook: You cannot say how big a folder is without asking the very same thing of everything inside it.

mapping.story: Asking a folder inside a folder its size
mapping.detail: The same question, in the same shape, about a strictly smaller part of the problem.

mapping.story: A file answering on the spot
mapping.detail: Something that answers without asking anything further. With no such case, nothing ever comes back.

mapping.story: Totals adding up as they come back
mapping.python: Return values combining as the calls unwind
mapping.detail: Each level finishes only after the levels beneath it have. The addition happens on the way out, not the way in.

mapping.story: A shortcut pointing back up the tree
mapping.python: A call that is not smaller, and RecursionError
mapping.detail: This ends because every step shrinks. Break that and the depth limit is the only thing that stops you.

bridge.codeNotes: Two branches and nothing else: a file returns, a folder asks. The sum(...) is where the totals come back up — every call is waiting on the calls it made. Notice that nothing keeps track of how deep it has gone, because it does not need to. The tree runs out on its own.
bridge.gotcha: A missing base case is the classic, and it looks like a program that hangs and then dies with a RecursionError about a thousand levels down. The subtler fault is a call that is not actually smaller: follow a shortcut that points at a folder above you and the tree becomes a ring. "du" carries flags for exactly this, and your own walk needs the same care. Depth itself is rarely the problem with real folders — they are shallow — but a structure a million levels deep would want a stack you manage yourself.

quiz.question: What is the base case here?

options.text: A file, which knows its own size and asks nothing further
options.why: Right. It is the one thing that can answer on its own, and it is what guarantees the walk ends.

options.text: A folder that happens to contain nothing
options.why: A fair guess, and it is the recursive branch with nothing to recurse into — the sum of no items is zero. It ends the walk by accident, not by design.

options.text: The folder you asked about in the first place
options.why: That is the first call, the top of the tree. It is the last thing to finish, not the thing that lets anything finish.

options.text: The number settling in the window
options.why: That is what you see once the top call returns. It is the result of there being a base case, not the base case.

quiz.question: Which of these both finishes and gives the right total?

options.why: A base case that answers correctly, and a step that always moves one level down. Both halves are needed and both are here.

options.text:
def total(p):
    return sum(total(os.path.join(p, n)) for n in os.listdir(p))
options.why: No base case at all. The first file it meets is handed to os.listdir, which raises — and even if it did not, no call would ever return a number of its own.
It finishes, and it answers zero for everything. A base case has to return the right answer, not merely stop the descent.
Two faults. "getsize" on a folder gives the size of the folder's own entry, not its contents, and "listdir" on a file raises — so there is still no case that answers without asking.

quiz.question: A different situation: on a discussion page any comment can have replies, and those replies can have replies of their own. How do you count every comment under a post?

options.text: Count the comment itself, then ask the same question of each of its replies; a comment with no replies answers one
options.why: Same shape as the folder: a step that goes one level down, and a case that answers without going further.

options.text: Go through the top-level comments and add up how many replies each one has
options.why: That reaches two levels and stops. Every reply to a reply is missed, and nothing in the result tells you they were.

options.text: Count only the deepest replies, since everything above them led there
options.why: This has the direction backwards. The deepest replies are the smallest part of the thread, not a summary of it.

options.text: Count repeatedly until the total stops changing
options.why: Repeating a thing is not the same as descending into it. Nothing here makes the next pass reach any deeper than the last.

title: One Face, Three Messages
source: Real system · SMS alphabets and segment limits under 3GPP TS 23.038 and 23.040 · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — GSM 03.38: the 7-bit default alphabet and the fallback to UCS-2
Wikipedia — GSM 03.40: concatenated short messages and the per-segment header

blurb: The message grew by one character. The bill grew by eight thousand messages.

panels.text: A clinic writes one appointment reminder and sends it to four thousand patients. The note runs to 148 characters, comfortably under the 160 an ordinary SMS carries. The bill arrives for four thousand messages, which is what everyone expected.
panels.alt: A message box with a counter beneath it reading 148 of 160, and a single envelope beside it marked 4,000.

panels.text: The next month someone adds a small smiling face at the end, to warm it up. The counter on the screen now reads 149. The bill arrives for twelve thousand messages.
panels.alt: The same message box with a small round smiling face added at the end, its counter now reading 149, and three envelopes beside it marked 12,000.

panels.text: An SMS is not carried as letters. It is carried in a fixed alphabet with room for 160 of them. The smiling face is not in that alphabet, and one character outside it moves the whole message to a wider scheme where only 70 fit — 67 once it must be cut up and labelled so the phone can join it back together. A curly quote pasted from a word processor does the same. So does every letter of Devanagari.
panels.alt: Two measuring rules of different scale: an upper one divided into 160 slots and a lower one into 70, with an arrow from a single marked character on the upper rule switching the whole message down to the lower one.

panels.text: Nothing was mistyped and nothing failed. The screen counted 149, because that is how many things were typed. The network counted 150, because the smiling face takes two of its slots. The question was "how long is this", and it had more than one correct answer.
panels.alt: The number 149 shown on a phone screen and the number 150 on a billing slip, with a bracket joining them marked SAME MESSAGE.

bridge.hook: The message did not really get longer. What counts as one character changed, and then everything was measured again.

mapping.story: 148 plain letters, one to a slot
mapping.python: Text that is all ASCII, where len() matches what you typed
mapping.detail: Every way of counting agrees here, which is exactly why the assumption survives for years.

mapping.story: One smiling face, outside the alphabet
mapping.python: A character above the ASCII range
mapping.detail: A single one is enough to change how the whole thing is stored and measured.

mapping.story: The counter on the screen saying 149
mapping.detail: An honest answer to one question: how many units of text is this.

mapping.story: The network counting 150 and billing three
mapping.detail: An honest answer to a different question: how much room does it take. Neither number is wrong, and they are not the same.

bridge.code:
note = "Your appointment is at 10:30 am."
face = "\U0001F642"
namaste = "\u0928\u092e\u0938\u094d\u0924\u0947"

for label, s in (("plain", note), ("with a face", note + face), ("namaste", namaste)):
    print(f"{label:12} len={len(s):3}  "
          f"utf-8 bytes={len(s.encode('utf-8')):3}  "
          f"utf-16 units={len(s.encode('utf-16-le')) // 2:3}")

# One thing on the screen; four people and three invisible joiners underneath.
family = "\U0001F468\u200D\U0001F469\u200D\U0001F467\u200D\U0001F466"
print("family emoji: len() says", len(family))
bridge.codeNotes: Three different numbers for the same text, all of them correct. len() counts code points. The UTF-8 count is what a file or an HTTP request sees. The UTF-16 count is the one an SMS is billed in, and it is why the smiling face costs two. The family emoji is the clearest case of all: one picture, seven code points.
bridge.gotcha: len() is not "how many characters a person sees", and treating it that way breaks the moment your users stop typing plain English — which, in India, is immediately. text[:160] can cut a name in half, and slicing a joined emoji in the middle leaves you half a family. Whenever a limit has to match something real — an SMS segment, a column declared in characters, a 280-character box — go and find out which count that thing uses, because it is probably not the one len() gives you.

quiz.question: Which step tripled the bill?

options.text: Adding one character that is not in the message alphabet
options.why: Right. It is not the extra length — it is that a single outside character changes how every character in the message is carried.

options.text: The note going from 148 characters to 149
options.why: One character more would have been free. 159 plain letters would still have gone as one message.

options.text: Sending to four thousand patients
options.why: That number did not change between the two months. It is the multiplier, not the cause.

options.text: The message being cut into three parts
options.why: That is what the bill is counting, and it is downstream. The splitting happened because the limit had already dropped from 160 to 67.

quiz.question: You need to guarantee a note fits in a single 70-slot message. Which check is right?

options.text: len(note.encode("utf-16-le")) // 2 <= 70
options.why: This counts the units the message is actually carried in, so a smiling face correctly costs two of the seventy.

options.text: len(note) <= 70
options.why: This counts code points, so it lets through a note with several emoji that will not fit — each of them takes two slots, and this sees one.

options.text: len(note.encode("utf-8")) <= 70
options.why: The wrong unit in the other direction. A Devanagari letter is three bytes here, so this rejects a 24-letter note that would fit comfortably.

options.text: note = note[:70]
options.why: That is not a check, it is a silent cut — and it slices by code point, so it can leave half a joined character behind.

quiz.question: A different situation: a database column is declared to hold 50 characters, and a user's 30-letter name is rejected as too long. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The column counts bytes rather than characters, and those letters take more than one byte each
options.why: The same trap in a different place: two definitions of "character", and the one that enforces the limit is not the one the name was measured by.

options.text: The name contains a character the database cannot store at all
options.why: That failure reads differently — an encoding error or a replacement mark, not a complaint about length.

options.text: The user left trailing spaces on the end
options.why: Twenty invisible spaces would be an odd thing to type, and it would not explain a name that is barely more than half the stated limit.

options.text: The form is adding hidden formatting to the name before saving it
options.why: Possible in principle and rarely the answer. The simpler explanation is that the limit was never counting what you assumed.

title: Touchdown
source: Real incident · Mars Polar Lander, lost 3 December 1999 · original account

sources.label: Wikipedia — Mars Polar Lander
NASA — Report on the Loss of the Mars Polar Lander and Deep Space 2 Missions

blurb: The sensor was right. Nothing asked whether it could possibly be right yet.

panels.text: On 3 December 1999 a lander arrived at Mars after eleven months in flight and was never heard from again. The descent should have taken about six minutes. The review board that followed could not recover any data from it, so everything known was worked out on the ground afterwards.
panels.alt: A lander hanging beneath a parachute above a planet surface, with its radio trace to one side ending in a flat line.

panels.text: Each of its three legs carried a small sensor with one job: notice the moment the foot met the ground, so the descent engines could be shut off. Shutting them off early is as bad as never shutting them off at all. Once they stop, nothing is holding the craft up.
panels.alt: A single landing leg with a small sensor drawn at the foot, and an arrow running from it to a switch labelled ENGINES.

panels.text: The legs unfolded high above the surface, while the craft was still hanging from its parachute. That jolt was enough to make a sensor report contact. The software accepted a report as real if it was still there on the next reading, and it was. So the report was recorded and kept.
panels.alt: The legs unfolding high up beneath the parachute, a jolt mark drawn at the sensor, and a small box beside it flipping to CONTACT.

panels.text: The software was meant to disregard anything recorded before it started watching for a landing, which it did at forty metres. That part had not been built correctly. So at forty metres it began watching, found a contact already sitting there, and shut the engines off. The craft was descending at thirteen metres a second with nothing left to slow it.
panels.alt: An altitude scale with a shutter marked WATCHING opening at 40 m, the CONTACT box already ticked behind it, and the engines below stamped OFF.

bridge.hook: The sensor was not lying. It really had felt something. Nothing anywhere asked whether the craft was near enough to the ground for that to mean what it seemed to mean.

mapping.story: The sensor reporting contact
mapping.python: The test that was actually made
mapping.detail: One true thing — and true at a moment when it carried no information at all.

mapping.story: Being forty metres up
mapping.detail: The other half of the rule. Contact is only meaningful if you are low enough for contact to happen.

mapping.story: Acting on a reading taken minutes earlier
mapping.python: Reading a flag that was set outside the window you meant
mapping.detail: The value was recorded when the rule did not apply and read when it did. Timing is part of the test.

mapping.story: Engines off, nothing holding it up
mapping.python: The branch with no way back
mapping.detail: Some wrong branches can be retried. This one could not, which is what makes a missing half so expensive here.

bridge.codeNotes: The two are one "and" apart. The first is not missing its check because nobody had the altitude — it is being passed in and ignored. It simply was not part of the test. Read the second aloud and it is the sentence you would have written in English: cut the engines if something touched down "and" we are low enough for that to be possible.
bridge.gotcha: Two beginner shapes hide in here. One is a test that is true without being sufficient — if user_typed_something: where you also needed it to be valid. The other is "or" where you meant "and", which widens a rule instead of narrowing it and almost never shows up in a test that only tries the case you expected. And there is a timing trap sitting on top of both: this flag was set long before anyone looked at it, so even a correct "and" would need the flag cleared at the moment the window opens.

quiz.question: Which half of the rule was missing?

options.text: That the craft was low enough for a touchdown to be possible at all
options.why: Right. The altitude was known and available the whole time. It was simply never part of the test that shut the engines off.

options.text: That the sensor was working correctly
options.why: The sensor was working. It reported a real jolt — which is what makes this so much harder to catch than a broken part.

options.text: That the parachute had been released
options.why: A sensible thing to check and not the gap the board identified. The decisive missing fact is how far above the ground the craft was.

options.text: That the engines were still running
options.why: They were. Knowing that adds nothing about whether shutting them off is the right thing to do.

quiz.question: Which version cuts the engines only when a touchdown is actually possible?

options.text: return touchdown and altitude_m <= 2.0
options.why: Both halves, joined so that each one can veto. A jolt at 1500 m is now simply ignored.

options.text: return touchdown or altitude_m <= 2.0
options.why: "or" widens where you meant to narrow. This cuts the engines at two metres with no contact reported at all, which is a second way to fall.
Two separate ifs that each return True is an "or" written out longhand. It reads like a stricter rule and is a looser one.

options.text: return touchdown and touchdown_previous
options.why: This is the rule the lander already had — the same reading seen twice. The jolt from the legs lasted through two readings, so it passes this too.

quiz.question: A different situation: a delivery app marks an order delivered as soon as the rider's phone is within 50 metres of the address. Riders report orders being marked delivered while they are still riding. What does the rule need?

options.text: That the rider has actually stopped, and stayed stopped — being near an address while passing it is not delivering to it
options.why: The missing half, exactly as on the lander: one true fact that only means something in combination with a second one.

options.text: Tighten the distance from 50 metres to 10
options.why: It fires less often and fires for the same wrong reason. A rider going past the door is within ten metres too.

options.text: Require the phone to be within 50 metres on two readings in a row
options.why: This is the lander's own test, and it failed the same way. A rider on a slow road is inside the circle for several readings together.

options.text: Wait for the customer to confirm the order arrived
options.why: That is a different product, not a fixed rule. It blocks every delivery on someone who may be asleep, and says nothing about the faulty test.

title: The Printed Gate
source: Real system · airport departure boards and printed boarding passes · original account

sources.label: Frontier Airlines help centre — boarding passes, gate assignments and airport displays

blurb: The pass and the board agreed at check-in. Only one of them was ever going to change.

panels.text: At check-in the desk printed a boarding pass, and near the top, in large type, it said GATE B7. The passenger folded it into a pocket and went through security. Above the corridor a board showed every departure, one line to a flight, and that line said B7 as well. For the moment, the two agreed.
panels.alt: A paper boarding pass with GATE B7 in large letters beside a departures board whose highlighted row also reads B7.

panels.text: The board keeps no history. Each flight has one line and one place for its gate, and when the airport moves a flight, the new gate is written into that place and the old one is simply gone. Aircraft arrive late and stands get swapped, so gates change after passes have been printed. Airlines tell travellers to watch the screens.
panels.alt: A single row of the board drawn large: time, destination and one box for the gate, with grey smudges in the box where an earlier value was wiped away.

panels.text: Forty minutes before departure the aircraft was moved, and the flight's line on the board changed from B7 to C12. Nothing reached into the passenger's pocket. The pass had been made from what the board said at check-in, not tied to it, and it went on saying B7 as clearly as the day it was printed.
panels.alt: The board row now reading C12, with an arrow from a struck-out B7 above it down to the new value, and the boarding pass beside the board still reading B7, with no line joining the two.

panels.text: The passenger sat at B7, pass in hand, and watched a different flight board there. The pass was not wrong about what the gate had been. It had only ever been a record of one moment. The board was the one place that knew what the gate was now, and one look at it got them to C12 in time.
panels.alt: Two gate signs, B7 and C12. A plain figure stands under B7 beside a small pass reading B7, and a dashed arrow runs from the board line GOA C12 up to the C12 sign.

bridge.hook: The pass and the board said the same thing at check-in. Only one of them was ever going to be kept up to date.

mapping.story: The flight's line on the departure board
mapping.detail: One name, one current value. Look it up now and you get what it holds now.

mapping.story: Writing C12 where B7 was
mapping.detail: The old value is not kept anywhere under that name. The name now leads to the new one.

mapping.story: The pass printed at check-in
mapping.detail: The value is taken at that moment. Nothing connects printed back to gate afterwards.

mapping.story: Reading the board again at the gate
mapping.python: Using gate, not printed, when it matters
mapping.detail: If you want the current value, ask the name that is kept current.

bridge.code:
gate = "B7"                 # the board at check-in
printed = gate              # the pass takes the value as it is now

gate = "C12"                # the aircraft moves; the board is rewritten

print("board says:", gate)
print("pass says: ", printed)

gate.lower()                # works something out, then throws it away
print("board still says:", gate)
bridge.codeNotes: Read the second line as the desk printing the pass: it takes whatever gate holds at that instant. The third assignment rewrites the board and touches nothing else, so the two prints disagree, and the pass still says B7. The gate.lower() line is the other half of the idea: working something out from a value without writing it back changes nothing. The board would only change with gate = gate.lower().
bridge.gotcha: Beginners read = as "these two are now linked" and expect printed to follow gate. It does not. = means "make this name refer to that value, now". The mirror-image mistake is working something out from a name without assigning the result, like score + 10 on a line of its own, and expecting the name to have changed. Both come from treating a name as the value itself rather than a label that points at one.

quiz.question: In the story, which moment plays the part of printed = gate?

options.text: The desk printing the pass at check-in
options.why: Right. That is the moment the value is taken. Whatever the board held then is what the pass holds from then on.

options.text: The board changing from B7 to C12
options.why: That is the reassignment, gate = "C12". It changes what the board's name holds, and leaves the pass alone.

options.text: The passenger reading the board at the gate
options.why: That is reading the current value, using gate itself. It is the fix, not the copy.

options.text: The aircraft being moved to another stand
options.why: That is the reason the value changes, out in the world. The code only ever sees the result: a new value written to gate.

quiz.question: The gate has just changed to C12. Which lines leave printed saying C12?

options.text:
gate = "C12"
printed = gate
options.why: The copy is taken after the change, which is the desk printing a new pass. Taking it earlier can only ever give the old value.

options.text:
printed = gate
gate = "C12"
options.why: This is the story as it happened. printed took B7 on the first line, and the second line rewrites gate alone.

options.text:
gate = "C12"
printed == gate
options.why: == asks whether the two are equal and throws the answer away. It assigns nothing, so printed keeps whatever it had.

options.text:
gate = "C12"
gate = printed
options.why: Assignment runs right to left: this copies printed into gate. It undoes the gate change and leaves printed as it was.

quiz.question: A different situation: a currency app sets quote_rate = rate once, when it starts. Every hour it runs rate = fetch_rate() to get the latest exchange rate. Customers complain that quotes use a rate from the morning. Why?

options.text: quote_rate took the value of rate once, at start-up, and later assignments to rate never reach it. Quotes should read rate at the moment they are made.
options.why: The printed pass again. Assigning a new value to one name does nothing to another name that was given the old value earlier.

options.text: fetch_rate() is failing and handing back the morning's rate
options.why: Possible in general, but then rate would be stale too. The complaint is specifically about quotes, and quotes read a copy that nobody refreshes.

options.text: Python keeps the first value a name was ever given, so rate never really changes
options.why: Reassignment works: rate does hold the new value. It is quote_rate that was set once and never touched again.

options.text: The start-up line should be quote_rate == rate so the two stay linked
options.why: == compares, it does not link. Python has no way to make one name follow another's reassignments; you read the current name when you need it.

title: It Works on My Laptop
source: Real system · the name localhost, reserved under RFC 6761 · original account

sources.label: RFC 6761 — Special-Use Domain Names, §6.3 localhost

blurb: The link was not broken. It was read on the wrong laptop.

panels.text: Two students were building a project together. One got the sign-up page working and sent the other a link to try: localhost, a colon, and the number 3000. It had opened perfectly a minute earlier. On the teammate's laptop it opened nothing at all, only a message that the site could not be reached.
panels.alt: Two laptops side by side. The left screen shows a sign-up form; the right shows CAN'T BE REACHED. Below them a chat bubble reads localhost:3000, with an arrow toward the right laptop.

panels.text: Most addresses name one particular machine, and every computer that looks one up is sent to the same place. This one is different on purpose. The rule for it is written down: localhost always means the machine that is asking. It is never looked up anywhere else, and nobody is allowed to register it.
panels.alt: An ordinary address drawn with arrows from three machines all converging on one server, beside localhost drawn with each machine's arrow curling back to itself.

panels.text: So the link was not broken. It was read in the wrong place. On the first laptop, localhost meant that laptop, where the page was running. On the second, it meant the second laptop, where nothing was answering on 3000. The same words, carried across, pointed at whatever was at home on the other end.
panels.alt: Each laptop drawn inside its own boxed outline. Inside the left box a door marked 3000 is open with a page behind it; inside the right box the door marked 3000 opens onto nothing.

panels.text: The next week was worse. The teammate had their own copy of the project running on 3000, opened the same kind of link, saw a sign-up page and reported that it worked. It was their own page. The fix was an address that meant the first laptop from outside it, or putting the page somewhere both of them could reach.
panels.alt: The left laptop faded, its screen blank. The right laptop shows a sign-up form with a tick above it, and a circular arrow beside it labelled its own.

bridge.hook: The link carried a name, not a place. Each laptop filled in the place for itself.

mapping.story: localhost on the first laptop
mapping.python: A name assigned inside a function
mapping.detail: It means something only inside the call where it was made.

mapping.story: The teammate's laptop finding nothing
mapping.python: Using that name after the function returns: NameError
mapping.detail: Outside, the name is looked up again where you are, and there is nothing by that name there.

mapping.story: The teammate's own page answering
mapping.python: A different name that happens to be spelled the same, outside
mapping.detail: The worse case is not an error but a hit. The name finds something, only not the thing you meant.

mapping.story: An address that works from outside
mapping.python: return the value and let the caller keep it
mapping.detail: Hand back the thing itself, rather than a name that only means something where you are.

bridge.code:
page = "teammate's own page"     # what lives out here

def run_on_my_laptop():
    page = "sign-up page"          # a new name, belonging to this call
    visits = 1
    return page                    # hand back the thing, not the name

print(run_on_my_laptop())          # sign-up page
print(page)                        # same spelling, different thing

try:
    print(visits)
except NameError as err:
    print("NameError:", err)       # visits never existed out here
bridge.codeNotes: run_on_my_laptop is the first laptop: inside it, page means the sign-up page. The page outside belongs to the teammate, and printing it finds theirs with no complaint, which is the second week exactly. visits was only ever made inside the call, so outside there is nothing by that name at all: the first week. The only thing that crossed over correctly is the value that was returned.
bridge.gotcha: Two traps. The quiet one is a name that exists both inside and outside: reading it outside gets the outer thing with no error, which is the teammate saying it works. The loud one is assigning to a name anywhere in a function. Python then treats it as local for the whole function, so count = count + 1 fails with UnboundLocalError even though a count exists outside. If a function needs to change something, return the new value and let the caller assign it.

quiz.question: In the story, which moment corresponds to a NameError?

options.text: The first week: the teammate's laptop found nothing answering at localhost:3000
options.why: Right. The name was used somewhere it had never been given a meaning, and the lookup came back empty.

options.text: The second week: the teammate saw a sign-up page and said it worked
options.why: That is the other scope trap, a same-spelled name outside finding something else. There is no error, which is why it is worse.

options.text: The page opening on the first laptop
options.why: That is the name used inside the place it was made, where it means exactly what it was meant to mean.

options.text: The rule that nobody may register localhost
options.why: That rule is why the name can never be shared between machines. It explains the error; it is not the error.

quiz.question: A total lives outside a function that records a sign-up. Which version adds one to that total?

options.why: The function is handed the value, hands back a new one, and the caller writes it where the total lives. Nothing depends on names crossing over.
Assigning to total makes it local for the whole function, so reading it on the right-hand side fails with UnboundLocalError before anything is added.
No error, and nothing changes. This makes a new total inside the call that vanishes when it returns. The outer one never hears about it.
The parameter is a name inside the call. Reassigning it moves that inner name only, and the result is thrown away when the call ends.

quiz.question: A different situation: a school timetable script defines periods at the top of the file as a small sample for testing. A function load_timetable() reads the real file and sets periods inside itself. The report at the bottom prints periods and shows the sample. What happened?

options.text: periods inside the function was a new name local to that call. The report found the sample, which has the same spelling. load_timetable() should return the timetable and the report should use what it returns.
options.why: The second week on the laptops: no error, a confident answer, and the wrong thing, because the name was filled in from where the report stands.

options.text: The file was never read, so periods kept its old value
options.why: The file may have been read perfectly. The real timetable went into a name that only existed during the call.

options.text: print always shows the first value a name was given
options.why: print shows the current value of the name it can see. The name it can see from the bottom of the file is the sample.

options.text: The function needs to be called twice before its values are kept
options.why: Calling it any number of times makes a fresh inner periods each time and throws each one away.

title: The Row That Moved Up
source: Real system · how a spreadsheet closes the gap when a row is deleted · original account

sources.label: Microsoft Support — Insert or delete rows and columns in Excel
Python tutorial §4.2 — modifying a collection while iterating over it

blurb: Every closed supplier was checked, except the ones standing directly behind another.

panels.text: An office kept a register of forty suppliers in a spreadsheet, one to a row. Some had closed and needed to come off. The clerk wrote nothing down in advance. The plan was simple: start at row 2, look at each row in turn, and delete it on the spot if that supplier had closed.
panels.alt: A spreadsheet of numbered rows with supplier names, three of them marked CLOSED, and a marker arrow at row 2.

panels.text: A spreadsheet does not leave holes. Delete a row and every row beneath it moves up by one, so row 8 becomes row 7 and the gap closes at once. That is useful, since a register full of blank rows is harder to read. It also means a row's number is only where it sits right now, not a label it keeps.
panels.alt: One row struck out, and short upward arrows on every row below it showing each one moving up a place.

panels.text: At row 6 the clerk found a closed supplier and deleted it. The supplier that had been on row 7 slid up into row 6. The clerk, finished with row 6, moved on to row 7, which now held what had been row 8. The one that slid up was never looked at. Two closed suppliers had sat together, and only the first went.
panels.alt: Before and after columns of rows. On the left, rows 6 and 7 are both CLOSED and row 6 is struck out. On the right, the second has moved up to row 6, outlined, and the marker arrow has already moved on to row 7.

panels.text: The clerk reached the bottom, satisfied. A colleague filtering the sheet the next morning found three closed suppliers still in it, each sitting directly beneath one that had gone. Working from the bottom up, or marking every row first and deleting them all afterwards, would have looked at every one of them.
panels.alt: The finished sheet with three CLOSED rows still present, each circled, and a long arrow beside the sheet pointing upward, labelled BOTTOM UP.

bridge.hook: The clerk moved down one row every time. Every deletion moved the rows up by one. For exactly the row that mattered, the two moves cancelled out.

mapping.story: Going down the rows by number
mapping.detail: The loop keeps a position and moves it on by one each pass. It does not remember which item it saw there.

mapping.story: Deleting the row where you stand
mapping.detail: Everything after it shifts one place towards the front, into positions the loop is about to pass.

mapping.story: The supplier that slid up and was never read
mapping.python: The item after each removal, skipped
mapping.detail: It moved into the position the loop had just finished with, and the loop never goes back.

mapping.story: Marking first and deleting after
mapping.python: Build a new list of what to keep
mapping.detail: The thing being walked is no longer the thing being changed, so nothing moves under the loop.

bridge.code:
suppliers = ["Anand", "Bose", "Closed-1", "Closed-2", "Dutta", "Closed-3", "Closed-4"]

register = suppliers.copy()
for name in register:                 # walking the rows
    if name.startswith("Closed"):
        register.remove(name)         # deleting where you stand
print("as the clerk did it:", register)

kept = [name for name in suppliers if not name.startswith("Closed")]
print("mark first, then keep:", kept)
bridge.codeNotes: register is the sheet and the for line is the clerk moving down it. Each remove closes the gap, so the next name slides into the position the loop has just finished with, and the loop moves past it. Closed-2 and Closed-4 both survive, and each sits directly after a removed row, exactly as on the sheet. The last two lines build a new list of the rows to keep and never change the one being walked.
bridge.gotcha: There is no error, which is what makes this dangerous. The loop finishes normally, and only some of the items were checked. A test with one closed supplier passes, because the skip only bites when two to be removed sit next to each other. Dictionaries and sets are stricter: changing their size inside a loop over them raises RuntimeError. Lists just shift and carry on.

quiz.question: Which moment in the story is the skipped item?

options.text: The supplier that slid up into row 6 after the deletion
options.why: Right. It moved into a position the clerk had already finished with, so it was never looked at.

options.text: The supplier deleted at row 6
options.why: That one was checked and removed correctly. The damage lands on its neighbour.

options.text: The clerk reaching the bottom of the sheet
options.why: That is the loop ending normally, which it does. The fault never stops it early or raises anything.

options.text: The colleague filtering the sheet the next morning
options.why: That is the check that found the result afterwards, not the skip itself.

quiz.question: Which of these removes every closed supplier?

options.text: suppliers = [s for s in suppliers if not s.startswith("Closed")]
options.why: It reads the old list from start to end without changing it, and builds a new one of the rows to keep. Nothing moves under the loop.
This is the clerk's method. Each removal slides the next item into a position already visited, so two closed suppliers in a row leave one behind.
The same skip, plus a crash: range was worked out for the original length, so once the list has shrunk, the last positions no longer exist and you get IndexError.
This moves the loop's own name s to an empty text. The list itself is never touched, so nothing is removed at all.

quiz.question: A different situation: a game keeps a list of enemies. Each frame it loops over enemies and removes any whose health is 0. Players notice that when two enemies are defeated in the same frame, one of them stays on screen for an extra frame. Why?

options.text: Removing the first shifts the second into the position just checked, so it is skipped this frame and only caught on the next
options.why: The clerk's sheet exactly. It only shows when two to be removed sit together, which is why it depends on both being defeated at once.

options.text: The health check runs before the damage is applied
options.why: That would delay every defeated enemy by a frame, not only when two go at the same time.

options.text: The screen is drawn before the enemies are removed
options.why: Again, that would affect every enemy equally. The symptom depends on two going together, which points at positions shifting.

options.text: A loop may only remove one item per pass over the list, so the second removal is ignored
options.why: There is no such limit. The second enemy is not refused; it is never looked at, because it moved into a position already passed.

title: One Character
source: Real incident · the OpenSSH channel advisory of 7 March 2002 · original account

sources.label: OpenSSH Security Advisory (adv.channelalloc), 7 March 2002, with the patch

blurb: The guard was there, and it was right about every number but one.

panels.text: On 7 March 2002 the people who maintain OpenSSH, the program a great many servers use to let people log in from far away and type commands, published a warning. Every version from 2.0 to 3.0.2 had a fault in how it kept track of channels, the separate streams one connection can carry. Version 3.1 fixed it.
panels.alt: A typed notice headed SECURITY ADVISORY, dated 7 MAR 2002, naming OpenSSH, with the affected versions 2.0 to 3.0.2 underlined and 3.1 ticked as fixed.

panels.text: The program kept its channels in a row of numbered slots. With room for ten, the slots were numbered zero to nine. When a message arrived naming a channel, a guard checked the number first: turn it away if it was below zero, or above the number of slots. Anything else was treated as a real channel.
panels.alt: A row of ten boxes numbered 0 to 9, a bar standing in front of them, and a sign above reading REFUSE BELOW 0 OR ABOVE 10.

panels.text: Ten is not above ten. So a message naming channel ten passed the guard, and the program went to slot ten, counting from zero. That is the eleventh place, and it is not one of the slots at all. Whatever happened to lie just past the end was read and trusted as though it were a channel.
panels.alt: The same row of boxes 0 to 9, with a dashed box drawn just past the end and marked 10. An arrow arcs over the bar and lands on it, under the words IS 10 ABOVE 10? NO.

panels.text: Someone already logged in, or a hostile server a user connected to, could use this to gain more power over the machine than they had been given. The fix changed one character. The guard now turned away any number at or above the number of slots, and the gap of exactly one was closed.
panels.alt: Two versions of one line, one above the other: the first with a greater-than sign, the second with greater-than-or-equal, its added equals sign in the accent colour and circled.

bridge.hook: The guard was not missing. It was one short, and one was all it took.

mapping.story: Ten slots, numbered zero to nine
mapping.python: A list of length n has positions 0 to n - 1
mapping.detail: Counting from zero, the last position is one less than the count.

mapping.story: Turn away anything above the number of slots
mapping.detail: It lets the count itself through, the one number that is never a valid position.

mapping.story: Channel ten, one past the end
mapping.detail: Python raises IndexError here. The original was written in C, which reads whatever lies past the end, and that is the whole incident.

mapping.story: The one-character fix
mapping.detail: Say what a valid position is, at least 0 and strictly less than the count, rather than guessing at what an invalid one looks like.

bridge.codeNotes: Three slots, so the positions are 0, 1 and 2, and 3 is the first number that is not one. The shipped guard asks whether the number is bigger than 3, and 3 is not, so it goes through. Python stops at slots[3] with an IndexError; the C original had no such net and read the memory past the last slot. The fixed guard says in one line what a valid position is: at least 0, and strictly less than the count.
bridge.gotcha: The beginner versions are range(1, len(names)), which skips the first item, and range(len(names) + 1), which runs one past the end. Both come from forgetting that counting starts at zero and that range stops before its end number. When you write a bound by hand, test the edges: the first item, the last item, and the number equal to the count. The last two are where off-by-one lives.

quiz.question: Which number did the guard let through that it should have refused?

options.text: The number equal to the count of slots
options.why: Right. It is the one number that is never a valid position when you count from zero, and "above the count" misses it by exactly one.

options.text: Any number below zero
options.why: The guard turned those away correctly. Its first half was right.

options.text: Any number far larger than the count
options.why: Those were refused. The fault was at the edge, not far past it.

options.text: Zero itself
options.why: Zero is the first slot and a real channel. Refusing it would be the opposite off-by-one.

quiz.question: Which guard accepts exactly the valid positions in slots?

options.text: if 0 <= i < len(slots):
options.why: At least 0, strictly less than the count. That is the whole set of positions and nothing else.

options.text: if 0 <= i <= len(slots):
options.why: This is the shipped guard, written as what it lets in. It accepts len(slots), the one position past the end.

options.text: if 1 <= i <= len(slots):
options.why: Counting from one. It refuses the first slot and accepts one past the last, so it is wrong at both ends.

options.text: if 0 < i < len(slots):
options.why: The upper end is right, but it refuses 0, the first slot. Off by one at the other edge.

quiz.question: A different situation: a website shows search results ten to a page and works out the number of pages with pages = total // 10. There are 25 results. What do users see?

options.text: Two pages; the last five results never get a page. It should be (total + 9) // 10.
options.why: Floor division drops the part page, so the count is one short whenever the total is not a multiple of ten. Test 25, not only 30.

options.text: Three pages, the last one holding five results
options.why: That is what was wanted. // rounds down, so 2.5 becomes 2.

options.text: An error, because 25 does not divide evenly by 10
options.why: // never complains about a remainder. It quietly drops it, which is why this goes unnoticed.

options.text: Two pages holding twelve and thirteen results
options.why: The page size stays at ten. The page count is short; the results are not spread out to fit.
